lessons.title: V3·RB1 — Fetching by hand: races, aborts, stale answers
lessons.summary: Every app eventually fetches without a library, and the code that results is almost always wrong in the same four ways: a boolean pair that can express states that cannot exist, a spinner that flashes over data you already had, an error from a request nobody is waiting for, and a retry loop that keeps running after the component is gone. This sector rebuilds the fetch layer from the transport up.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RB1 — Fetching by hand: races, aborts, stale answers

`07_data_fetching` gave you the flag-in-a-cleanup, and `d13_race_abort` drilled
it until the shape was automatic. This sector assumes both and asks the harder
question: if you had to ship the data layer of a real application without
installing anything, what would you actually write?

The honest answer is that `useEffect` plus `fetch` is not a data layer. It is a
transport call and a lifecycle hook, and everything between them — the state
machine, the error taxonomy, the cancellation policy, the retry policy, the
deduplication — is code somebody has to write. Most teams write it by accident,
one `useState` at a time, and end up with the same four bugs.

**Bug one: impossible states.** The `loading` / `data` / `error` triple of
booleans-and-nullables has eight combinations and only three of them are real.
`loading === true` with a non-null `error` is not a state your UI has a design
for, but your code can reach it, and one day it will. A discriminated union
makes the illegal combinations unrepresentable, which is not a purity argument:
it is the difference between a render function with three branches and one with
an accidental fourth that nobody drew.

**Bug two: the flash.** The naive effect clears `data` before every request, so
changing a filter blanks the table and paints a spinner over content the user
was reading. A request is not always a reason to throw away what is on screen.
Distinguishing *loading* (I have nothing) from *fetching* (I have something,
and something newer is coming) is the single highest-value change you can make
to the perceived speed of a UI, and it costs one boolean — the right one.

**Bug three: errors from the past.** A superseded request can still reject, and
a rejection usually renders *instead of* data rather than beside it, so a dead
request does not merely show stale information, it destroys good information.
Worse, `AbortController.abort()` itself produces a rejection: an `AbortError`
on the `DOMException` class. Code that reports every rejection reports your own
cancellations to the user as failures.

**Bug four: work that outlives its reason.** A retry loop with a two-second
backoff will happily wake up four times after the component unmounted, each
time hitting the network and calling `setState` on nothing. Cancellation has to
reach into the *gaps between* attempts, not just the attempts.

## The shape of a request, precisely

A request has four terminal outcomes and you should be able to name all four
before writing any code:

- it **succeeds** — a response arrived and parsed;
- it **fails at the transport** — DNS, connection reset, CORS, offline. `fetch`
  rejects with a `TypeError` and no status code exists;
- it **fails at the protocol** — a response arrived and it says `404` or `503`.
  `fetch` *resolves*. This is the single most surprising thing about `fetch`
  and the reason `res.ok` exists;
- it is **cancelled** — you aborted it. `fetch` rejects with an `AbortError`,
  and this is not a failure, it is a success at doing nothing.

A wrapper that folds the second and third into one `Error` subclass carrying an
optional `status`, and rethrows the fourth untouched so callers can recognise
it, is about twenty lines and pays for itself immediately. Every exercise after
the second uses it.

```tsx
export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly status: number, readonly body: unknown) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}`);
    this.name = "HttpError";
  }
}
```

## Cancellation is composition

`AbortController` is a one-shot signal with a listener list, and the two
modern conveniences are worth knowing because writing them by hand is fiddly:

- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` returns a signal that aborts itself with a
  `TimeoutError`, not an `AbortError`. The distinction matters: a timeout is
  something to tell the user about, a cancel is not.
- `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` returns a signal that aborts when *either* input
  does. This is how you say "abort on unmount, or after five seconds,
  whichever comes first" without wiring listeners yourself.

Both are available in React 19's baseline environments. Exercise 4 builds the
composition and makes you distinguish the two reasons for stopping.

## Deduplication and the request key

Two components mount at once and both want `/api/user/7`. Two requests go out.
Nothing is broken, exactly — but at ten components it is ten requests, and at a
list of avatars it is the same request forty times. The fix is a module-level
`Map` from key to in-flight promise: the first caller creates the entry, later
callers get the same promise, and the entry is deleted when it settles so the
next caller gets fresh data. That is *deduplication*, not caching — the entry
lives only as long as the request. Confusing the two produces a "cache" that
never updates. Caching is the next sector; this one stops at dedupe on purpose,
because dedupe is correct with no policy attached and caching is not.

The key has to be derived from everything the request depends on. `"user/7"`
is fine; an object of query parameters is not, until you serialise it in a way
that does not depend on key insertion order.

## What you will build

Eight pieces of a data layer, in the order you would actually need them: the
state machine, the transport wrapper, keep-previous-data, composed
cancellation, abort-aware retry with backoff, in-flight deduplication, parallel
requests with a partial-failure policy, and paged accumulation. The challenge
assembles them into one `useResource` hook, and the review re-tests the whole
sector from the angle where these bugs actually reach users: search-as-you-type.

Every exercise injects its transport as a function prop, and the gate resolves
the injected promises out of order deliberately. Nothing depends on timing, on
the network, or on how fast your machine is.

# Reading — react/v3rb01_fetching_by_hand

## Notes

**Model the request, not the variables.** Three `useState` calls produce a
state space that is the product of their domains; one `useReducer` over a
discriminated union produces exactly the states you drew. The practical
difference shows up in the render function: with a union, TypeScript narrows
`state.data` to non-null inside the `success` branch and refuses to let you
read it anywhere else, so the "cannot read property of null" class of bug stops
compiling rather than stops working.

**`loading` and `fetching` are different questions.** "Do I have something to
show?" and "is a request out?" are independent, and a good list view answers
them separately: skeleton when the first is false, a dimmed table plus a subtle
progress hint when the first is true and the second is also true. The rule of
thumb: clear `data` when the *identity* of what you are showing changes (a
different user), keep it when only its *freshness* changes (the same user,
refetched). Exercise 3 makes you decide which one a parameter change is.

**`fetch` does not reject on 404.** It rejects only when no HTTP response was
obtained at all. Every wrapper you will ever write starts with `if (!res.ok)`,
and every wrapper somebody forgot to write ends with `undefined is not an
object` two components away, because a 500 body parsed as JSON is an error
envelope that does not look like your type.

**Aborting is not failing.** `controller.abort()` makes the pending `fetch`
reject with a `DOMException` whose `name` is `"AbortError"`. Reporting it puts
"The user aborted a request" on screen — a real string that has shipped to real
users. Check `signal.aborted` at the top of your error handler, or check
`err.name`, but check something. `AbortSignal.timeout` deliberately uses a
different name, `"TimeoutError"`, precisely so you can tell your own
cancellation from the deadline expiring.

**Retry needs three decisions, not one.** *Whether* (a 4xx will fail again;
retrying it is just noise and, for a `POST`, dangerous), *how long* (fixed
delays synchronise across clients and produce a thundering herd, so exponential
with jitter), and *whether still* (before each attempt and after each sleep,
ask the signal whether anybody still cares). The third is the one everybody
misses, because the sleep is where the component unmounts.

**Dedupe by promise, cache by value.** An in-flight map stores promises and
deletes on settle; a cache stores values and needs an expiry policy. Storing a
settled promise forever is the accidental cache that never revalidates and is
the most common self-inflicted staleness bug in hand-rolled data layers.

**Parallel by default.** `await a(); await b();` is a waterfall — a latency you
chose without meaning to. Requests that do not depend on each other belong in
one `Promise.all`, and requests where a partial answer is still useful belong
in `Promise.allSettled`. `Promise.all` rejects on the first failure but does
*not* cancel its siblings; if you want them stopped, you have to abort them.

## ex1 — the state machine

Tests whether you can make the illegal states unrepresentable. The classic
mistake is a union that still carries `data` in every variant "for
convenience", which restores exactly the nullability you were removing. The
model answer defines four variants — `idle`, `loading`, `success`, `error` —
each carrying only what that state actually has, and reduces over actions
tagged with a request id so an action from a retired request cannot move the
machine.

## ex2 — the transport wrapper

Tests the error taxonomy. The classic mistake is `catch (e) { setError(e) }`
around everything, which flattens abort, transport failure and a 422 with a
useful validation body into one useless string. The model answer resolves
non-ok responses into an `HttpError` carrying the status and the parsed body,
lets `AbortError` propagate untouched, and only ever parses the body once.

## ex3 — keep what you have

Tests the difference between loading and fetching. The classic mistake is
`setData(null)` at the top of the effect, which is correct-looking and produces
a spinner flash on every parameter change. The model answer keeps the previous
data and exposes `isFetching` alongside it, and — the part people miss — still
clears the previous *error*, because a stale error is not useful context the
way stale data is.

## ex4 — two reasons to stop

Tests signal composition. The classic mistake is creating a timeout signal and
passing it instead of the unmount controller's, so the component stops caring
but the request runs to completion. The model answer composes both with
`AbortSignal.any`, and distinguishes the outcomes by name: a timeout becomes a
message the user sees, an unmount becomes silence.

## ex5 — retry that can be interrupted

Tests whether cancellation reaches the gaps. The classic mistake is a
`setTimeout`-based sleep with no abort listener, so an unmounted component's
retry loop keeps waking up. The model answer's sleep rejects as soon as the
signal aborts, and the loop re-checks `signal.aborted` before every attempt.
It also refuses to retry a 4xx, which is not an optimisation — it is the
difference between one failed request and six.

## ex6 — one request, many callers

Tests dedupe. The classic mistake is caching the settled promise, which makes
the second render of the page show yesterday's data forever. The model answer
deletes the map entry in a `finally`, so the sharing window is exactly the
lifetime of the request, and it shares the *rejection* too, which is what you
want: five callers of a failing endpoint should see one failure, not five.

## ex7 — parallel, with a policy

Tests whether you can express "some of this is optional". The classic mistake
is `Promise.all` over a required and an optional request, so a failing sidebar
takes down the page. The model answer runs both under one controller, uses
`allSettled` for the optional part, and rejects the whole thing only when the
required part fails — aborting the sibling on the way out.

## ex8 — pages that stay in order

Tests accumulation under a race. The classic mistake is `setPages(p => [...p,
next])` with no check, so a slow page two lands after page three and the list
is out of order — or worse, a parameter change resets the query and the old
page appends into the new list. The model answer ties every page to the
parameter generation that requested it and drops anything from an older
generation, which is the same request-id idea from ex1 applied to a list.

## Further reading

- [You Might Not Need an Effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [`useReducer` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useReducer)
- [MDN: Using the Fetch API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch)
- [MDN: `AbortSignal.any()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal/any_static)
- [MDN: `AbortSignal.timeout()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal/timeout_static)
- [MDN: `Promise.allSettled()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/allSettled)

# Long reading — fetching by hand

## Where `fetch` came from, and what it decided

`XMLHttpRequest` was an accident of history: a component Microsoft shipped for
Outlook Web Access that the rest of the web adopted because it worked. It had
an event-based API, an implicit global-ish state machine (`readyState` 0 to 4),
and — the detail that matters here — an `abort()` method that had been there
from the beginning. When the Fetch standard replaced it in 2015, cancellation
was left out entirely. There was no way to stop a `fetch`. That gap lasted
until 2017, when `AbortController` was specified as a general-purpose
cancellation primitive rather than a fetch-specific one, which is why it now
also cancels event listeners, streams, `addEventListener`, and anything else
that accepts a signal.

That history explains the API's two oddities. First, cancellation is
*outside-in*: you do not cancel a promise, you abort a controller that the
operation was told to watch. Promises are values, not processes; a value cannot
be cancelled. Every "cancellable promise" library that tried to paper over this
eventually died of it. Second, aborting surfaces as a rejection, because that
is the only channel `fetch` has. The rejection is a `DOMException` named
`AbortError`, and — a detail added later — `signal.reason` lets you supply your
own object, which is how `AbortSignal.timeout` manages to reject with a
`TimeoutError` through the same machinery.

The other decision worth understanding is that `fetch` resolves on any HTTP
response, including `500`. This is not an oversight. `fetch` models the
*network operation*, and receiving a 500 is a successful network operation that
returned a document saying something went wrong. `XMLHttpRequest` behaved the
same way; jQuery's `$.ajax` hid it behind an `error` callback, and a generation
of developers learned the wrong model from jQuery. The consequence is that
`res.ok` is not a convenience — it is the boundary between "the network worked"
and "the application worked", and any wrapper that does not draw it forces
every caller to draw it, which means most callers will not.

## Why `useEffect` is the wrong place, and why you use it anyway

React's own documentation now opens the data-fetching discussion by
discouraging effects for it, and lists the reasons plainly: effects do not run
on the server, so effect-fetching guarantees a client waterfall; effects fire
after paint, so the request starts later than it could; effects have no
built-in deduplication, caching, or preloading; and StrictMode's deliberate
double-invocation in development exposes any non-idempotent request.

The recommended answers are a framework's loader, or a library. Both are
correct advice and both are unavailable in the two situations where this
material matters: an app that is not on a framework with a loader, and an
interview. So the practical position is this — use an effect, but be precise
about what an effect actually gives you. It gives you exactly one thing that is
hard to get otherwise: a cleanup function scoped to a single run, closing over
that run's variables. That is a per-request box, created and destroyed at
exactly the right moments. Everything else in a good data layer — the state
machine, the error taxonomy, the retry policy, dedupe — is plain functions that
neither know nor care about React, and they should be written that way. The
test is whether you can unit-test your fetching logic without rendering
anything. If you cannot, too much of it is inside the hook.

## StrictMode, and the double request

In development, React 19 mounts, unmounts and remounts every component once,
running effects twice. This is not a bug simulator; it is a check that your
effect is *resumable*, because concurrent rendering can genuinely discard and
recreate work.

The right reaction is not to add a ref guard that skips the second run. That
guard also skips the legitimate re-run when a real remount happens, and it
disables exactly the check StrictMode was performing. The right reaction is to
make the second run harmless, which is what abort-on-cleanup already does: run
one starts, cleanup aborts it, run two starts. You will see two entries in the
network panel in development and one in production, and the first will show as
cancelled.

There is one case where this is genuinely unsafe, and it is worth being blunt
about: a non-idempotent request. `POST /orders` in an effect is a bug in
production too — it fires on every remount, every fast-refresh, every
navigation back — and StrictMode simply makes the bug visible sooner. Mutations
belong in event handlers or actions, never in effects.

## The performance story of a waterfall

Serial dependent requests are the most expensive mistake in the list, and it
compounds silently. A component that fetches a user, then a team from the
user's `teamId`, then permissions from the team, costs three round trips. At
40ms of latency that is 120ms and nobody notices. At 300ms — a mobile
connection, or a user two continents away from your region — it is 900ms of
blank screen, and it is invisible in local development because localhost has no
latency. Nesting components that each fetch is worse: the child cannot start
until the parent has rendered, which cannot happen until the parent's data
arrives, so the component tree becomes a request tree with the same depth.

Three mitigations, in order of preference. Restructure the API so one request
answers the question — the fix that actually removes the latency. Hoist the
requests to a common ancestor and fire them in parallel with `Promise.all`,
accepting that you have coupled the ancestor to its descendants' data needs.
Or preload: start the request at the moment of *intent* (hover, focus,
`pointerdown`) rather than the moment of render, which buys you a hundred
milliseconds for free and is the trick behind most "instant" navigations you
have admired.

## Retry, and the ethics of it

Retrying is a load multiplier applied by every client simultaneously. If a
service fails and ten thousand clients each retry three times with a fixed
one-second delay, the service receives thirty thousand requests one second
after it started failing — a synchronised wave precisely when it is least able
to absorb one. Exponential backoff spreads the wave out in time; jitter
de-synchronises the clients from each other. Both are needed: exponential
backoff without jitter still has every client retrying at the same instants.

The policy question — *what* to retry — is a correctness question, not a
politeness one. A `422` means the request was understood and rejected; the
identical request will be rejected again. A `401` means you need new
credentials, and retrying without refreshing them is a good way to get an
account locked. A `429` is the server telling you to slow down, and it often
includes a `Retry-After` header, which your backoff should respect over its own
arithmetic. And a `POST` that timed out may well have succeeded — the response
was lost, not the effect — so retrying it without an idempotency key can create
two orders. That is why idempotency keys exist, and why "retry everything three
times" is a policy that eventually charges a customer twice.

## When not to write any of this

There is a real cost to a hand-rolled data layer, and it is not the code you
write in the first week — it is the code you do not write. React Query,
SWR and the framework loaders give you request deduplication across the whole
tree, a normalised cache with a documented invalidation model, background
revalidation on focus and reconnect, retry policy, pagination and infinite
query helpers, devtools that show you what is cached and why, and — the one
people underestimate — a *shared vocabulary*, so a new engineer already knows
what `staleTime` means in your codebase.

Write it by hand when: the app has a handful of endpoints and no shared server
state; you are on a framework whose loader already solves it and adding a
client cache would create a second source of truth; or you are learning, in
which case building it once is the fastest possible way to understand what the
library is doing on your behalf. Do not write it by hand because the bundle
size of a five-kilobyte library offended you, and then spend six months
reinventing invalidation badly.

The next sector takes the honest next step: it writes the cache. Not because
you should ship it, but because after you have written `staleTime`,
`gcTime`, structural sharing and focus revalidation with your own hands, the
library stops being magic and starts being a set of decisions you can argue
with.

## Exercise 1 — a state machine with no illegal states

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Export a type and a hook.

```tsx
export type Resource<T> =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; error: Error };

export function useResource<T>(
  key: string | null,
  load: (key: string) => Promise<T>,
): Resource<T>;
```

Rules:

- `key === null` means "nothing to ask for": the resource stays `idle` and
  `load` is never called.
- A non-null `key` puts the resource in `loading` and calls `load(key)` once.
- A resolved value moves it to `success`; a rejection moves it to `error`,
  with a real `Error` (wrap non-`Error` rejections with `new Error(String(r))`).
- A change of `key` starts again from `loading` and **retires** the previous
  request: its answer, resolved or rejected, must not move the machine.

The gate renders with `key="a"`, switches to `key="b"`, resolves `b`, then
resolves `a` — the machine must still read `{ status: "success", data: <b's
value> }`. It then switches to `key={null}` and expects `idle`.

Do the retirement with a request counter inside the reducer, not with a flag in
the effect: exercise 5 needs a guard that survives event handlers too.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb01_fetching_by_hand ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reason three `useState` calls go wrong here is that nothing stops
`setError` and `setLoading(true)` from both being true. Ask instead: what are
the *four* things this component can be, and what does each one actually carry?
Once that is a union type, the render branches are forced to be exhaustive.

## Hint 2

Give the reducer a private field the union does not expose. Something like:

```tsx
type Internal<T> = { seq: number; view: Resource<T> };

function reduce<T>(state: Internal<T>, action: Action<T>): Internal<T> {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "start":
      return { seq: state.seq + 1, view: { status: "loading" } };
    // ...
  }
}
```

`start` is the only action that may increase `seq`. Every other action arrives
carrying the `seq` it was issued under.

## Hint 3

The effect body dispatches `start`, then needs to know which sequence number it
just created so the `.then` can quote it back. Reading `state.seq + 1` in the
effect works but is fragile. The cleaner shape is a `useRef` counter that the
effect increments itself, passing the same number to both the dispatch and the
callbacks — the reducer then only has to compare. Do not forget the `idle`
branch: a `null` key must reset the machine, and must not leave the previous
request able to answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the render side and work backwards. Write the `switch (r.status)`
that consumes this hook first — all four branches, with a `default` that
assigns `r` to `never`. The type you needed in order to write that switch is
the type the hook must return, and anything you find yourself wanting to add
"just in case" is a state you have not drawn.

## Hint 2

There are two independent clocks here and confusing them is the whole
difficulty. One is React's render clock, which you do not control. The other is
your request clock, which you do. The request clock must tick in exactly one
place — the moment a request goes out — and every message from a request must
carry the tick it was born on. That is why a boolean cannot work with more than
one request in flight: a boolean has one tick.

## Hint 3

Two traps at the edges. If the effect dispatches `start` unconditionally, a
`null` key still moves the machine out of `idle` — guard the whole body. And if
`load` is an inline arrow in the test's render, it is a new function identity
every render; putting it in the dependency array would refetch forever. Depend
on `key`, and read `load` through a ref if your linter insists on more, but do
not put an unstable function in the deps of an effect that starts requests.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The core insight is one sentence: `fetch` only rejects when *no HTTP response
happened*. A 503 is a successful network operation that returned a document
saying the server is unwell. So the shape is `await fetch(...)` with no
try/catch around it — a rejection there is a transport failure or an abort, and
both should propagate — followed by an explicit `res.ok` decision.

## Hint 2

You may read a response body exactly once. This throws:

```tsx
const body = await res.json();
if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, await res.text()); // already read
```

Read `text()` first, unconditionally, and derive everything from that string.
Parsing is then a local operation you can wrap in its own try/catch without
touching the network call.

## Hint 3

Subclassing `Error` in TypeScript compiled to ES5 breaks `instanceof`; the
project targets modern output, so a plain `class HttpError extends Error` works
— but set `this.name` yourself, because it inherits `"Error"` otherwise.
Prefer parameter properties or explicit assignment; either is fine as long as
`status` and `body` are readable afterwards.

The four-way table you are implementing: (ok, parses) → resolve; (ok, does not
parse) → `Error("Invalid JSON…")`; (not ok, parses) → `HttpError(status,
parsed)`; (not ok, does not parse) → `HttpError(status, rawText)`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the *caller* needs to decide, and write the error type that answers
it. A caller wants to know: should I show a message, retry, redirect to login,
or say nothing? A bare string answers none of those. A status code answers
three of them, and the parsed body answers the fourth for a 422. That is why
the status and body are on the error rather than baked into a message.

## Hint 2

Empty bodies are more common than you think: `204 No Content` from a DELETE,
`200` with `Content-Length: 0` from an endpoint that returns nothing useful.
`JSON.parse("")` throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input`, and if you
treat that as "invalid JSON" you turn a perfectly good response into an error.
Check the string for emptiness before parsing, and remember to trim.

## Hint 3

Do not put a `try` around the whole function. That catch will swallow the abort
rejection and every transport failure, and you will find yourself re-throwing
based on `err.name` — which works, but backwards. Keep the try narrow: it
belongs around `JSON.parse(text)` and nothing else. Everything outside it is
either a value you decide about or a rejection you have deliberately chosen not
to intercept.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are being asked to treat two dependencies of the same effect differently,
which sounds impossible for one effect and is not. The effect still depends on
both. What differs is what happens to the *state* when each one changes — and
state changes do not have to live in the effect that starts the request.

## Hint 2

Two things want to be tracked separately:

```tsx
const [rows, setRows] = useState<string[] | null>(null);
const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
```

`rows === null` answers "have I got anything?"; `busy` answers "is something
coming?". The four combinations are all meaningful here, which is why this is
the one place a pair of variables beats a union.

## Hint 3

To clear rows only when `reportId` changes, you need to notice that it changed.
The two respectable ways: a second effect that depends only on `reportId`
(runs before the fetch effect commits its own state, so ordering is
predictable), or the adjust-state-during-render pattern — keep the previous
`reportId` in state, compare during render, and `setRows(null)` immediately
when it differs. React re-runs the component before touching the DOM, so no
flash occurs. The second avoids an extra commit; pick one and be able to
explain it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the user is doing at the moment each parameter changes. They
change `range` while looking at a table they are reading — blanking it steals
their place. They change `reportId` because they want something else — leaving
the old numbers up, dimmed, means for a few hundred milliseconds the screen is
confidently wrong. The code follows from the product decision, so make the
product decision first.

## Hint 2

`aria-busy` exists precisely for this pattern. It marks a region as being
updated without removing it, without moving focus, and without an announcement,
which is exactly what "the table you are reading is refreshing" should feel
like to a screen-reader user. A `role="status"` region, by contrast, is a live
region and *is* announced — so using it for a background refresh talks over the
user every time a filter changes.

## Hint 3

The error rule has a trap in it. If you only clear the error on success, a
failing report that then succeeds shows both. If you clear it in the effect
cleanup, you clear it on unmount for no reason. Clear it at the moment a new
request goes out — the same place you set `busy` to true — and the invariant
"an alert on screen describes the most recent completed request" holds without
any further thought.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both stop conditions must reach the same request, so there is exactly one
signal passed to `fetchQuote` and it is not either of the originals. Build the
two sources, compose them, hand over the composition — and keep a reference to
the one you own, because you will need to ask it a question later.

## Hint 2

```tsx
const controller = new AbortController();
const timeout = AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs);
const signal = AbortSignal.any([controller.signal, timeout]);
```

`AbortSignal.any` aborts as soon as any input does, and adopts that input's
`reason`. So after a timeout, `signal.reason.name === "TimeoutError"`; after
your own abort, `"AbortError"`.

## Hint 3

The guard in the rejection handler is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the
whole exercise. Checking `signal.aborted` and returning would silence the
timeout too. Check `controller.signal.aborted` — *your* reason to stop — and
return only for that. Everything that gets past it is either a timeout, which
you name, or a real failure, which you report.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the three sentences the user could end up reading, then decide which
events produce them. "Loading AAPL." "The quote service did not answer in
time." "Rate limit exceeded." Now notice there is a fourth event — you navigated
away — that produces *no* sentence at all. A single catch block cannot express
four outcomes; it needs to interrogate what stopped it.

## Hint 2

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` starts its clock the moment it is created, not the
moment it is passed anywhere. Creating it outside the effect, or in a `useMemo`
with the wrong dependencies, gives you a clock that started at mount and fires
part-way through the third request. One timeout signal per effect run, created
in the effect body, is the only arrangement that means what it says.

## Hint 3

`DOMException` is the type both cancellations arrive as, and `name` is what
separates them. Prefer reading it off the signal (`controller.signal.aborted`,
`signal.reason`) rather than off the caught value: a well-behaved fetch rejects
with the signal's reason, but an injected fake — or a transport that abandons
the request some other way — may not, and code that only trusts the caught
error is one implementation detail away from silence.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — retry that can be interrupted

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export two functions — no React in this file.

```tsx
export function isRetryable(error: unknown): boolean;

export async function withRetry<T>(
  attempt: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<T>,
  options: { signal: AbortSignal; tries?: number; baseMs?: number },
): Promise<T>;
```

`isRetryable` returns `true` for a `TypeError` (transport failure) and for an
`HttpError` — imported from `../ex2/solution` — whose `status` is `408`, `429`,
or anything `>= 500`. Everything else is `false`.

`withRetry` runs `attempt(signal)` up to `tries` times (default `3`), waiting
`baseMs * 2 ** i` milliseconds multiplied by a jitter factor in `[0.5, 1.5)`
between attempts (default `baseMs` `100`). It must:

- reject immediately with the caught error when `isRetryable` says no;
- reject with the **last** error when the tries run out;
- check the signal before every attempt and reject with `signal.reason` if it
  is already aborted — use `signal.throwIfAborted()`;
- abort **during the sleep**: if the signal aborts while waiting, the pending
  wait rejects with `signal.reason`, the timer is cleared, and no further
  attempt is made;
- register its abort listener with `{ once: true }` so repeated attempts on one
  signal do not accumulate listeners.

The gate uses fake timers. It asserts three attempts for a 503, one attempt for
a 404, that aborting mid-sleep rejects within one tick and leaves no pending
timers, and that the listener count on the signal never exceeds one.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb01_fetching_by_hand ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Retry policy is three separate decisions and writing them as three separate
pieces of code makes the exercise easy. *Whether* is a pure function of the
error — that is `isRetryable`, testable on its own with no timers. *How long*
is a pure function of the attempt number. *Whether still* is a question to the
signal. Mixing them into one loop body is how the abort check gets forgotten.

## Hint 2

Jitter is not decoration. Without it, every client that started failing at the
same moment retries at the same moments forever, and a service that fell over
under load gets a synchronised wave precisely when it is least able to take
one. Multiplying by `0.5 + Math.random()` spreads a 200ms delay over
100–300ms, which is enough to de-synchronise a fleet. A gate that pins
`Math.random` will still see the exponential growth, so compute the base delay
and the jitter as separate factors.

## Hint 3

`signal.throwIfAborted()` is the modern spelling of `if (signal.aborted) throw
signal.reason` and it is worth using because it throws the *reason*, which
carries the difference between an abort and a timeout that ex4 depended on.
Note where it goes: at the top of every loop iteration, not once before the
loop. The whole point is that time passes inside the loop.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — one request, many callers

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export a deduplicating wrapper and a small hook.

```tsx
export function dedupe<T>(key: string, run: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T>;

export function inFlightCount(): number;

export function useShared<T>(
  key: string,
  run: () => Promise<T>,
): { data: T | null; error: Error | null };
```

`dedupe` returns the promise already in flight for `key` if there is one, and
otherwise starts `run()`, records it, and removes the record **when it
settles**, success or failure. All callers of one key share one outcome —
including the rejection.

`inFlightCount()` returns the number of live entries; the gate uses it to prove
the map empties out.

`useShared` calls `dedupe(key, run)` in an effect keyed on `key`, stores the
resolved value or the error, and ignores answers after unmount or a key change.

The gate renders four components with the same key at once, resolves, and
asserts `run` was called **once** and all four show the value. It then asserts
`inFlightCount() === 0`, re-renders with the same key, and asserts `run` was
called a **second** time — this is deduplication, not caching, and the
distinction is the exercise. Finally it fails a shared key and asserts all
subscribers see the error and the entry is still removed.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb01_fetching_by_hand ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The map is not a cache. Ask exactly how long an entry should live and the whole
design follows: from the moment the request goes out to the moment it comes
back, and not one millisecond longer. Anything that keeps the entry after it
settles has built a cache with no expiry, which is why the page never updates
after a deploy.

## Hint 2

```tsx
const promise = run().finally(() => {
  inFlight.delete(key);
});
inFlight.set(key, promise);
return promise;
```

Two things to notice. `finally` runs on both paths, so a failed request cleans
up too. And `finally` returns a *new* promise that adopts the original's
outcome — store and return the same one, or callers and the map will disagree
about what they are holding.

## Hint 3

Sharing a rejection has a sharp edge in Node and in some test environments: if
you store `run()` and every caller attaches handlers later, you are fine, but
if a rejection settles before anyone attaches a `catch`, you get an
unhandled-rejection warning. Attaching the `finally` immediately gives the
promise a handler, which is another quiet reason the shape above is the right
one.

For `useShared`, remember there is no cleanup that can cancel a *shared*
request — cancelling it would break the other three subscribers. Guard the
answer, do not abort the work.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Draw the timeline. Four components mount in the same commit; all four call
`dedupe("user/7", ...)` synchronously during their effects. The first finds
nothing and starts a request. The second, third and fourth find the entry the
first one just wrote. That only works because the write happens *before* any
`await`, in the same synchronous turn — an `async function dedupe` that awaits
before setting the map would let all four through.

## Hint 2

The distinction the gate is testing has a name in every real client:
deduplication collapses *concurrent* callers, caching serves *later* ones. They
have different failure modes. Dedupe cannot serve stale data because the entry
does not outlive the request. A cache can, which is exactly why a cache needs
`staleTime`, revalidation and invalidation — three policies dedupe does not
need and should not pretend to have.

## Hint 3

Think about who owns cancellation in a shared request. If caller two unmounts
and aborts, callers one, three and four lose their answer for no reason. The
honest options are: the shared request carries its own controller and nobody
can abort it; or you reference-count subscribers and abort when the count hits
zero. This exercise takes the first, and the ability to say why — and what it
costs — is worth more than the code.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Both start in the same tick" is a statement about where the `await` is. Call
both functions first, keep the two promises in variables, and only then start
awaiting. The moment you write `const p = await fetchProfile(...)` before
calling `fetchActivity`, you have chosen a waterfall.

## Hint 2

You need a controller of your own, downstream of the caller's signal, because
you sometimes want to abort the sibling without the caller having asked:

```tsx
const inner = new AbortController();
const childSignal = AbortSignal.any([signal, inner.signal]);
```

Hand `childSignal` to both requests. Now `inner.abort()` stops the activity
request when the profile fails, and the caller's signal still stops everything.

## Hint 3

`Promise.all` rejects on the first rejection but does not cancel the siblings —
that is why the `inner.abort()` is needed and is not automatic. And an
unhandled rejection is waiting for you: if the activity promise rejects while
you are awaiting the profile, and nothing has attached a handler yet, the
runtime complains. Attach the optional promise's `catch` *immediately*, turning
it into a promise that always resolves, and await that.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Name the policy before writing it. There are exactly three sensible ones for a
two-request screen: all-or-nothing (`Promise.all`), best-effort
(`Promise.allSettled`, render whatever arrived), and required-plus-optional,
which is what a dashboard usually is. The third has no single built-in and that
is why people reach for the wrong one — writing it out is four lines and a
comment.

## Hint 2

The idiom that turns a rejection into a value is worth having at your
fingertips:

```tsx
const activityResult = fetchActivity(id, childSignal).then(
  (rows) => ({ ok: true as const, rows }),
  (err: unknown) => ({ ok: false as const, err }),
);
```

Now `activityResult` never rejects, so it can sit in a `Promise.all` beside a
required request without taking it down, and it has a handler attached from the
first tick.

## Hint 3

Two ordering details. Abort the sibling in the profile's failure path *before*
rethrowing, or the abort never happens. And when the outer signal aborts, both
requests reject with the same reason — make sure you rethrow that reason rather
than resolving a `Dashboard` whose `activityError` says "The operation was
aborted", which is a partial success the caller never asked for.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — pages that stay in order Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export a component. ```tsx export function Feed({ topic, fetchPage, }: { topic: string; fetchPage: ( topic: string, cursor: string | null, signal: AbortSignal, ) => Promise<{ items: { id: string; title: string }[]; next: string | null }>; }): JSX.Element; ``` Behaviour: - On mount and whenever `topic` changes, reset to an empty list and load the first page with `cursor === null`. - Render one `
  • ` per item, in arrival order, showing the title. Duplicate ids across pages must appear **once** — servers repeat rows when the underlying data shifts between pages, and a duplicate key is a React warning and a visual bug. - A button labelled `Load more` requests the next page with the stored cursor. It is disabled while a request is in flight and absent entirely when `next` is `null`. - While the first page is loading, render `

    Loading

    `. While a later page is loading, keep the list and show `

    Loading more

    ` after it. - A page belonging to an **older topic** must never append. The gate switches topic mid-flight and resolves the abandoned page afterwards; the list must be the new topic's only. - Double-clicking `Load more` must not send two requests for the same cursor. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rb01_fetching_by_hand ex8 ```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the *identity* of a request is here, and you will see there are two
axes, not one. A request is identified by (topic, cursor). A topic change
invalidates every outstanding request; a cursor advance invalidates nothing —
the earlier pages are still wanted. That is why a single "ignore superseded
answers" flag is the wrong tool: it would throw away page one when page two
goes out.

## Hint 2

The first page is not a special case if you model it as "the page whose cursor
is `null`". Where it *is* special is in rendering: the difference between
`Loading` and `Loading more` is exactly whether the list is empty, which you
already know. Resist adding an `isFirstPage` boolean; it will drift.

## Hint 3

Two edges worth checking before you run the gate. When a topic changes while a
`Load more` is in flight, the stale page must not append *and* the busy flag
must clear, or the button stays disabled forever — so reset `busy` on topic
change rather than only in the response handler. And when `next` comes back
`null`, the button disappears; make sure the "loading more" status disappears
with it rather than being stranded under an empty list.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do not start from the hook. Start from a single private function inside the
file — `run(seq, isRefresh)` — that does the whole request: build the
controller, compose the signal, call `withRetry`, and dispatch the outcome
guarded by `seq`. Once that exists, the hook is two callers of it: an effect
for key changes, and `refetch` for refreshes. Every requirement in the list
lands in exactly one of those three places.

## Hint 2

`isLoading` and `isFetching` are not two pieces of state. One piece of state —
"is a request out" — plus `data === null` gives you both:

```tsx
const isFetching = pending;
const isLoading = pending && data === null;
```

Which also makes requirement 3 free: a refetch with data present cannot be
`isLoading`, because `data` is not null.

## Hint 3

Requirement 6's second half is the fiddly one. Keep the previous data on a
*refresh* failure — the user was reading something and a background update
failed — but not on a *key change* failure, where the data on screen belongs to
a different resource. You already clear `data` on key change (requirement 2),
so if you never clear it in the failure path, both behaviours fall out for
free. That is the trick: put the clearing where the identity changes, not where
the failure happens.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the invariants down as assertions and keep them beside you: `isLoading`
implies `data === null`; `isLoading` implies `isFetching`; `error !== null`
implies `!isFetching`; a `null` key implies all three of `data`, `error` and
`isFetching` are empty. Any implementation that satisfies all four is almost
certainly right, and each one maps to a line of code you can point at.

## Hint 2

The double-refetch guard is where people put a `useState` and then read stale
values from a closure. `refetch` is called from an event handler, so it sees
whatever `pending` was when that render happened — which is correct here only
because React re-renders between clicks. The robust version keeps `pending` in
a ref *as well*, or checks a ref that the request path sets synchronously. Pick
one and be able to say why the other is a hazard.

## Hint 3

Composition order matters when you combine ex4 and ex5. `withRetry` receives
the *composed* signal, so a timeout ends the retry loop rather than being
retried — which is a policy choice worth making deliberately. If you wanted
timeouts to be retryable you would give `withRetry` the outer controller's
signal and create a fresh timeout inside each attempt. Say which one you built
in a comment; an interviewer will ask.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — search as you type, from the other end `review1/solution.tsx`. The sector's ideas meet the interaction that produces all of them at once. ```tsx export function ProductSearch({ search, }: { search: (query: string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise; }): JSX.Element; ``` - One text input labelled `Search products`. - A query shorter than two characters after trimming asks nothing and renders `

Type at least two characters

`. - Otherwise the query is **debounced by 300ms** — typing `sh`, `sho`, `shoe` within the window sends one request, for `shoe`. - While a request is out and there are no results yet, render `

Searching

`. While a request is out and previous results are on screen, keep them and set `aria-busy="true"` on the `
    `. - Results render as `
  • `s. An empty array renders `

    No matches for ""

    ` — with the query that produced it, not whatever is in the box now. - A superseded request is aborted, and neither its results nor its rejection may appear. - A rejection renders in `

    `, and the next keystroke clears it. - Clearing the box back below two characters cancels any in-flight request and returns to the "type at least two characters" state with no results left behind. The gate types out of order, resolves out of order, advances fake timers, and inspects the signals it was handed. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rb01_fetching_by_hand review1 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three separate clocks, and the bug in every hand-rolled search box is that they
get tangled. The *input* changes on every keystroke and must stay instant. The
*query* changes 300ms after the last keystroke. The *results* change when a
request for the current query lands. Give each one its own piece of state and
the wiring becomes obvious; try to make one variable do two jobs and it will
not.

## Hint 2

The debounce belongs in an effect, not in the change handler:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const t = setTimeout(() => setQuery(input.trim()), 300);
  return () => clearTimeout(t);
}, [input]);
```

Each keystroke's cleanup cancels the previous timer, so only the last one
survives — the same "cleanup retires the previous run" idea, applied to a timer
instead of a request. Then a second effect fetches on `query`.

## Hint 3

The `No matches for "..."` message is the detail that catches people. If you
render it from the input value, it changes as the user keeps typing and starts
claiming there are no matches for a query you never ran. Store the query
*alongside* the results — `{ query, items }` in one piece of state — so the
message and the list can only ever describe the same request.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a state machine and the eight bullet points collapse into five
states: `too-short`, `searching-empty`, `searching-with-results`, `results`
(possibly zero), and `error`. Write the union first. The debounce is not a
state — it is an edge that moves you from one to another after a delay — and
noticing that keeps it out of the render logic entirely.

## Hint 2

Two abort obligations that are easy to satisfy by accident and easy to miss.
Superseding: the effect keyed on `query` aborts its predecessor in cleanup, so
this is free if the request lives in that effect. Clearing the box: the query
becomes too short, the effect re-runs, its cleanup aborts — also free, *if* the
short-query branch is inside the same effect rather than being an early return
before the effect is set up. Conditional hooks are not allowed; conditional
work inside a hook is.

## Hint 3

`aria-busy` on the `<ul>` and `role="status"` are mutually exclusive by design
here. The first says "what you are reading is being updated" without
interrupting; the second is a live region and will be announced. Rendering both
means a screen-reader user hears "Searching" over every keystroke while the
results they were reading are still on screen — technically correct, actively
hostile. The rule that keeps it straight: announce state changes, mark
freshness.

lessons.title: V3·RB2 — Caching, revalidation, and a query client you write
lessons.summary: A cache is four decisions wearing a Map as a disguise: when an entry is stale, who is still listening, what invalidates it, and what happens to the render tree when the answer comes back identical. This sector writes the whole thing — subscriptions, staleTime, garbage collection, tag invalidation, structural sharing, focus revalidation — so the library stops being magic.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RB2 — Caching, revalidation, and a query client you write

The previous sector stopped deliberately at deduplication, because dedupe is
correct with no policy attached. An entry that lives exactly as long as the
request it represents cannot be stale, cannot be wrong, and needs no
configuration. The moment you keep an answer past the request, you have taken
on four questions that will not go away:

1. **How long is this answer good for?** Serving it forever is a bug; refetching
   it on every mount is the cache doing nothing.
2. **Who is still listening?** An entry nobody is rendering should eventually be
   dropped, but "eventually" has to be long enough that navigating away and
   straight back is instant.
3. **What makes it wrong?** A mutation somewhere else in the app just changed
   the data this entry describes. How does the entry find out?
4. **What happens when the new answer equals the old one?** A fresh object with
   identical contents is a new reference, and a new reference re-renders every
   memoised consumer of it for no reason at all.

Those four questions are `staleTime`, `gcTime`, invalidation, and structural
sharing, and every serious client — React Query, SWR, Apollo, RTK Query, the
framework loaders — answers all four. They differ in vocabulary, not in
substance. Once you have written them yourself, reading a library's
configuration stops being guesswork.

## Stale is not the same as absent

The single most useful idea in this sector: an entry has **data** and it has a
**freshness**, and they are independent. `staleTime` is not an expiry. When it
elapses, nothing is deleted and nothing stops rendering. All that happens is
that the entry becomes *eligible to be revalidated* the next time somebody
asks for it. The data stays on screen the whole time.

That is stale-while-revalidate, and it is the reason a well-configured app
feels instant: navigating back to a list you saw thirty seconds ago paints
immediately from cache and quietly updates underneath. Contrast the two failure
modes either side of it. A `staleTime` of zero refetches on every mount, so
every navigation shows a spinner over data you already had. A `staleTime` of
infinity never refetches, so your app shows the world as it was when the tab
was opened.

`gcTime` is the different question — how long to keep an entry **after the last
component stopped rendering it**. That timer starts when the subscriber count
hits zero and is cancelled if anyone subscribes again. Getting this wrong in
the other direction is a memory leak: a cache that never evicts, in a
long-lived SPA, holding every list the user ever scrolled.

## The store is not React state

The cache has to be shared by components that are not related, so it cannot
live in a component. It could live in context, and many hand-rolled caches do —
but then every write re-renders the entire subtree under the provider, because
context has no selector. The right primitive is an **external store**: a plain
object with `getSnapshot`, `subscribe` and mutation methods, connected to React
by `useSyncExternalStore`.

`useSyncExternalStore` exists for exactly this and has one sharp edge that
catches everybody once:

```tsx
// Infinite loop. getSnapshot returns a new object every call.
useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, () => ({ data: store.get(key) }));
```

React calls `getSnapshot` during render and compares the result with
`Object.is` to decide whether anything changed. A fresh object is never `is` to
the previous one, so React re-renders, calls `getSnapshot` again, gets another
new object, and in development throws `The result of getSnapshot should be
cached`. The snapshot must be a value the store already holds — which means the
store must build the entry object once, when it changes, and hand back the same
reference until it changes again. Exercise 2 makes you build that.

## Invalidation, and the honest version of it

Phil Karlton's line about cache invalidation being one of the two hard problems
is quoted so often it has stopped meaning anything. Here is the concrete
version. When a mutation succeeds, some set of cached entries is now wrong.
Nothing in the system knows which ones — the cache stores answers, not the
relationships between them. So you have exactly two strategies:

- **Tag and sweep.** Entries carry keys (`["users"]`, `["users", 7]`), a
  mutation names a prefix, and everything matching is marked stale.
  Subscribed entries refetch immediately; unsubscribed ones refetch whenever
  somebody next needs them. Coarse, cheap, always correct.
- **Write through.** The mutation's response *is* the new value, so put it in
  the cache directly with no extra round trip. Precise and fast, and wrong the
  moment the server computes anything the client cannot — a derived count, an
  audit trail, another user's concurrent edit.

Real applications use both: write through for the entity, invalidate the lists
that mention it. And there is a third thing to get right that neither strategy
mentions — a write-through must not overwrite data that is *newer* than it. If
a background fetch started before the mutation and lands after it, the entry
reverts. Every entry needs an `updatedAt`, and every write needs to check it.

## Structural sharing

A revalidation that returns identical JSON produces a brand-new object graph.
Handing it to React means every `React.memo` below is defeated, every
`useEffect` that depends on it re-runs, every `useMemo` recomputes. React Query
solves this with structural sharing: walk the old and new values together and,
wherever they are deeply equal, keep the *old* reference. A list where one row
changed then produces a new array with 99 old row objects and one new one, so
99 memoised rows do not re-render.

It is thirty lines and it is the difference between a table that stutters every
five seconds and one that does not. Exercise 6 writes it.

## What you will build

Eight parts of a query client — the entry model, the subscribable store bound
with `useSyncExternalStore`, stale-while-revalidate, reference-counted garbage
collection, tag invalidation, structural sharing, focus and reconnect
revalidation, and `setQueryData` with `updatedAt` protection. The challenge
assembles `createQueryClient` and a `useQuery` hook on top of them. The review
comes at it from the angle that breaks hand-rolled caches most often in
practice: the key.

# Reading — react/v3rb02_query_client

## Notes

**An entry is five fields, not one.** `data`, `error`, `updatedAt`, `status`,
and `isFetching`. Dropping `updatedAt` is the mistake that makes staleness
unknowable and lets a slow response overwrite a fast one. Dropping the
separation between `status` and `isFetching` is the mistake that makes
stale-while-revalidate impossible to express — you need to say "I have data,
and I am also fetching", which one enum cannot say.

**Subscribers are the unit of liveness.** Almost every policy in a cache is
phrased in terms of subscribers: refetch on mount if stale *and someone is
mounting*; garbage collect when the count reaches zero; on invalidation,
refetch subscribed entries eagerly and unsubscribed ones lazily. If your store
does not count subscribers, you will find yourself unable to express any of
these and will reach for timers instead, which is how caches start refetching
in background tabs.

**`useSyncExternalStore` has three arguments and each has a trap.** `subscribe`
must be stable — an inline arrow re-subscribes on every render, which is
usually harmless and occasionally a storm. `getSnapshot` must return a cached,
referentially stable value. `getServerSnapshot` is required if the component
ever renders on the server, and omitting it turns SSR into a runtime error
rather than a warning.

**Cache keys must be canonical.** `JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: 2 })` and
`JSON.stringify({ b: 2, a: 1 })` are different strings for the same query.
Property order in JavaScript objects is insertion order, and two call sites
that build the same filter object in a different order will miss each other's
cache entries — silently, with no symptom other than double the requests.
Serialise with sorted keys, recursively.

**Revalidation triggers are events, not intervals.** Polling is a blunt
instrument that burns battery in a background tab. The three events worth
listening to are: a component mounted and its entry is stale; the window
regained focus; the browser came back online. All three mean "the user is
looking, and time has passed". All three need a floor — refocusing four times
in a second should not send four requests.

**Structural sharing is not deep equality.** Deep equality answers "are these
the same?" and throws away the new value if so. Structural sharing answers "how
much of the old value can I keep?" and builds a hybrid. The distinction matters
for a list of 100 rows where one changed: deep equality says "different",
replaces everything, and re-renders 100 rows. Structural sharing replaces one.

## ex1 — the entry model

Tests whether you can name what an entry holds. The classic mistake is a `Map<
string, T>` — data and nothing else — which cannot answer "is this stale?",
"did this fail?", or "is a request out?" and therefore forces every one of
those into component state, where it stops being shared. The model answer keeps
an entry record and derives staleness from `updatedAt` and a `staleTime`,
because a stored boolean would need somebody to flip it.

## ex2 — the store, and the snapshot that must not change

Tests `useSyncExternalStore`. The classic mistake is a `getSnapshot` that
constructs its return value, which produces an infinite render loop and a
warning most people fix by memoising in the component — which does not work,
because React calls `getSnapshot` outside the memo. The model answer keeps the
entry objects immutable inside the store: every mutation replaces an entry with
a new object, and `getSnapshot` just reads the map.

## ex3 — stale-while-revalidate

Tests the central policy. The classic mistake is treating the cache as an
either/or: hit means show, miss means fetch. The model answer has three cases —
miss (fetch, show loading), fresh hit (show, do nothing), stale hit (show *and*
fetch) — and, crucially, only replaces the data on success, so a failed
revalidation leaves the good data alone with an error beside it rather than
instead of it.

## ex4 — reference counting and the collection timer

Tests lifetime. The classic mistake is deleting an entry the moment the last
subscriber unsubscribes, which makes back-navigation a full reload and defeats
the entire cache on exactly the interaction it exists for. The model answer
starts a timer on zero and clears it on resubscribe — and clears it in the
right order, because a subscribe that runs after the timer fired must fetch
rather than resurrect a deleted entry.

## ex5 — tag invalidation

Tests prefix matching and the eager/lazy split. The classic mistake is
refetching every matching entry, including the forty the user is not looking
at, which turns one mutation into forty requests. The model answer marks all
matches stale and refetches only those with subscribers, which is what every
real client does and is the reason `invalidateQueries` is cheap.

## ex6 — structural sharing

Tests whether you can preserve references. The classic mistake is a deep-equal
check that returns the old value wholesale when equal and the new value
wholesale when not — which is right at the top level and useless one level
down. The model answer recurses, rebuilding arrays and objects only where a
child actually changed, and returns the old reference whenever every child was
kept.

## ex7 — focus and reconnect

Tests event-driven revalidation and listener hygiene. The classic mistake is
adding a `visibilitychange` listener per query, so a page with thirty queries
has thirty listeners all firing at once. The model answer registers one
listener in the client, applies a minimum interval, and removes it when the
last query goes away.

## ex8 — writing to the cache

Tests `setQueryData` and the ordering hazard. The classic mistake is a plain
assignment, which lets an in-flight background fetch that started earlier land
afterwards and revert the mutation's result — a bug that looks like "the UI
flickers back to the old value about a second after saving". The model answer
stamps every write with a timestamp and refuses writes older than what is
already there.

## Further reading

- [`useSyncExternalStore` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore)
- [Scaling up with reducer and context](https://react.dev/learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)
- [MDN: `Page Visibility API`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Page_Visibility_API)
- [MDN: `navigator.onLine`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Navigator/onLine)
- [HTTP `Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate` (RFC 5861)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5861)
