# Long reading — the cache you did not want to write

## Where this design came from

Client-side caching of server state used to be a solved problem for exactly one
kind of app: the ones that used a normalising GraphQL client. Relay, and later
Apollo, cached *entities* by id, so a mutation returning an updated `User`
patched every query result that mentioned that user, automatically, because the
client knew the shape of the graph. It was elegant, and it cost a schema, a
compiler and a large runtime.

The REST world had nothing comparable until 2019, when Zeit published SWR and
Tanner Linsley published React Query. Both made the opposite bet: do not
normalise, do not model the graph, cache *responses* under *keys* the developer
chooses, and make invalidation an explicit operation. That sounds like a step
backwards and it was a step forwards, because the hard part of normalisation is
not the storage, it is teaching the client which queries a mutation affects —
and for REST there is no schema to teach it from. A key like `["orders",
{status: "open"}]` plus `invalidateQueries(["orders"])` puts the developer in
charge of a decision the machine could not make anyway.

The name SWR is the giveaway: `stale-while-revalidate` is an HTTP
`Cache-Control` extension standardised in RFC 5861 in 2010. It lets a cache
serve a stale response immediately while asynchronously checking for a fresh
one, on the grounds that a slightly old answer now beats a correct answer in
400ms. Moving that directive from the CDN into the browser tab is the entire
idea, and it is why the pattern felt instantly familiar to anyone who had
configured a CDN.

## How the pieces actually behave at runtime

Consider a user clicking through a list to a detail page and back, twice, on a
client configured with `staleTime: 30_000` and `gcTime: 300_000`.

At `t=0` the list mounts. Cache miss: an entry is created with `updatedAt: 0`,
`isFetching: true`, a promise stored for dedupe. Three sibling components that
also need the list find the promise and attach to it — one request. The
response lands, `structuralShare` runs against `undefined` and returns the new
value, `updatedAt` is stamped, listeners fire, one render.

At `t=2s` the user opens a detail page. The list unmounts; its subscriber count
hits zero; a five-minute eviction timer starts. The entry is still there, fully
intact.

At `t=6s` the user goes back. The list mounts, subscribes, the eviction timer
is cancelled. `getSnapshot` returns the existing entry, so the first render
already has data — no skeleton, no layout shift. `isStale` says `6s < 30s`, so
no request goes out at all. This is the interaction the whole design is for.

At `t=45s` they go back again. Same instant paint from cache, but now the entry
is stale, so a background revalidation starts. The user reads the old list for
80ms while the new one arrives; `structuralShare` finds that 49 of 50 rows are
deeply equal and returns an array reusing those 49 objects; `React.memo` on the
row means one row re-renders.

At `t=8min`, if they never came back, the eviction timer fires and the entry is
gone. The next visit is a cold miss.

Every number in that story is a knob, and every knob is a trade between
requests and staleness. That is the whole configuration surface, and it is why
"what should `staleTime` be?" has the honest answer: how wrong is this data
allowed to be? A currency rate, a second. A user's own profile, minutes. A list
of countries, hours.

## The reference-identity problem, in detail

React's rendering model rests on `Object.is`. `React.memo` skips a re-render
when every prop is `is` to its previous value. `useMemo` and `useCallback`
recompute when any dependency is not. `useEffect` re-runs on the same rule. So
the identity of the objects your cache hands out is not a stylistic concern —
it is the input to every optimisation in the framework.

A `fetch` + `JSON.parse` produces a completely fresh object graph every time,
sharing nothing with the previous one. Without structural sharing, a polling
query that returns identical data every five seconds invalidates every memo
below it, five times a minute, forever. Users describe this as "the page feels
heavy" and profilers describe it as a flame graph with a regular heartbeat.

Structural sharing has a cost — a full recursive walk of both values on every
response — and it is almost always the right trade, because the walk is cheap
relative to the renders it prevents. It stops being the right trade for very
large payloads that always change (a live log stream, a large binary-ish blob),
which is why real clients let you turn it off per query. The other thing to
know: it only helps if consumers actually compare references. Structural
sharing plus a component that reads `data.rows.map(...)` inline and passes new
objects down saves you nothing, because you rebuilt the identities one level
lower.

## Why keys are the hard part in practice

Everything above assumes two call sites asking the same question produce the
same key. In practice they do not, and the failures are quiet.

`JSON.stringify` depends on property insertion order, so
`{ status: "open", page: 1 }` and `{ page: 1, status: "open" }` serialise
differently. `undefined` values disappear entirely, so `{ page: 1, q: undefined
}` and `{ page: 1 }` collide — which is usually what you want, and occasionally
is not. `Date` objects serialise to ISO strings, which is fine, while `Map` and
`Set` serialise to `{}`, which is a catastrophe: every distinct filter set maps
to the same key. And a function or a class instance in the key object — an
accidental inclusion of a callback in a filters object — produces either a
crash or a silent collision.

The fix is a canonical serialiser: recurse, sort object keys, refuse or
normalise the types that do not have a stable textual form. Twenty lines, and
it belongs in the client rather than at every call site, because the call sites
will forget.

There is a second, subtler key problem: keys that are too coarse and keys that
are too fine. Too coarse — `["orders"]` for a paginated, filtered list — and
page two overwrites page one in the same entry, producing a list that flickers
between pages. Too fine — including a timestamp or a random request id — and
every render is a cache miss, which looks exactly like the cache being broken.
The rule that works: the key is the *complete set of inputs the fetcher reads*,
and nothing else. If your fetcher closes over a variable that is not in the
key, you have a bug that will appear the first time that variable changes.

## When not to write this

Everything in this sector is between three hundred and five hundred lines to do
properly, and the properly is the problem — the version you write in an
afternoon handles none of the ordering hazards, and you will discover each of
them in production over the following year.

Use a library when the app has shared server state across many screens: that is
precisely the situation the library is built for, and the marginal cost of
adding it is about five kilobytes and one provider.

Do not build a client cache at all when your framework already has one. An app
on a modern router with loaders has a cache keyed by route, revalidating on
navigation and after actions; adding a second client cache on top gives you two
sources of truth for the same data and a class of bug where the two disagree.
The framework's cache is usually the better one because it can prefetch on the
server, before the JavaScript has even arrived.

And do not cache at all when the data has no reuse. A one-off analytics
submission, a form's dependent dropdown that changes on every keystroke, a
one-screen app with three endpoints — the cache adds configuration, a staleness
model, and an invalidation story, in exchange for nothing.

The reason to write it once anyway is the one that motivates this whole volume:
after you have implemented `staleTime`, subscriber counting, tag invalidation
and structural sharing yourself, the library's documentation reads like a set
of decisions you have already made, and its defaults stop being mysterious.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The ordering of the checks in `entryStatus` *is* the exercise. Write the five
answers down and ask, for each pair, which one wins when both conditions hold.
`isFetching` and `data` both true is `refetching`. `error` and `data` both true
is `success`. Once the precedence is decided, the code is a chain of
`if`s in that exact order.

## Hint 2

`isStale` with `staleTime: Infinity` needs no special case if you write the
comparison as `now - updatedAt > staleTime`: anything minus anything is never
greater than `Infinity`. The `updatedAt === 0` check has to come first, though,
or a never-loaded entry with an infinite stale time is reported as fresh and
never fetched at all.

## Hint 3

Why derive staleness rather than storing an `isStale` boolean? Because a stored
flag needs somebody to flip it when time passes, and nothing in the system runs
when time passes. Deriving it means the answer is correct at the moment it is
asked, which is the only moment that matters. Keep that reasoning — the next
exercise's store depends on entries only changing when something *happens*.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach `entryStatus` from the render side. Write out the JSX each of the five
answers should produce: skeleton, table, table with a busy flag, error panel,
nothing. Now ask which of those you would want to see for an entry that has
last week's data *and* a failed refresh. The answer — the table, plus a
warning — is why `success` beats `error` when both are present.

## Hint 2

`updatedAt: 0` is doing double duty and it is worth naming: it means "never
successfully loaded", which is different from "loaded a long time ago". The
sentinel works because `Date.now()` is never zero in any environment you will
meet. The alternative, `updatedAt: number | null`, is more honest and forces a
null check at every comparison; both are defensible, and knowing why you picked
one is the point.

## Hint 3

Watch the boundary in `isStale`. With `staleTime: 1000` and exactly 1000ms
elapsed, `>` says fresh and `>=` says stale. Either is defensible, but the gate
pins `>`, and the reason is that `staleTime: 0` should mean "stale as soon as
any time has passed", which `>` gives you at 1ms — while `>=` would call an
entry written in this very millisecond stale, causing a refetch loop for any
component that mounts twice in one tick.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the store, and a snapshot that stays put

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. Export a store class and a hook.

```tsx
export class EntryStore {
  get(key: string): Entry | undefined;
  set(key: string, patch: Partial<Entry>): void;
  subscribe(key: string, listener: () => void): () => void;
  listenerCount(key: string): number;
}

export function useEntry(store: EntryStore, key: string): Entry | undefined;
```

Rules:

- `set` merges the patch over the existing entry (or over `blankEntry(key)`
  when there is none) and stores a **new object**. It then notifies only the
  listeners registered for that key.
- Reading the same key twice with no intervening `set` must return the **same
  object reference**. The gate asserts `store.get(k) === store.get(k)`.
- `subscribe` returns an unsubscribe function; `listenerCount` reports the
  current number for a key, and must go back to `0`.
- `useEntry` binds the store with `useSyncExternalStore`, passing a stable
  `subscribe` and a `getSnapshot` that returns the store's own entry object.
  The same function serves as `getServerSnapshot`.

The gate renders two components on key `a` and one on key `b`, patches `a`, and
asserts the `b` component did **not** re-render. It also renders under
`StrictMode` and fails on React's `The result of getSnapshot should be cached`
warning.

Import `Entry` and `blankEntry` from `../ex1/solution`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

React calls `getSnapshot` during render and compares the result to the previous
one with `Object.is`. So the question is not "how do I memoise the snapshot in
my component" — the component is the wrong place, React calls the function
outside your memo. The question is: what does the *store* have to guarantee?
Answer: the same reference until something actually changes.

## Hint 2

That guarantee comes for free if entries are immutable inside the store:

```tsx
set(key: string, patch: Partial<Entry>): void {
  const prev = this.entries.get(key) ?? blankEntry(key);
  this.entries.set(key, { ...prev, ...patch });   // new object, only here
  this.listeners.get(key)?.forEach((fn) => fn());
}
```

Never mutate an entry in place. `get` then just reads the map and hands back
whatever object is there.

## Hint 3

The two `useCallback`s in the hook are not an optimisation, they are the
contract. `subscribe` must be stable, or React tears down and re-establishes
the subscription on every render:

```tsx
const subscribe = useCallback((fn: () => void) => store.subscribe(key, fn), [store, key]);
const getSnapshot = useCallback(() => store.get(key), [store, key]);
return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getSnapshot);
```

Copy the listener set before iterating it, or an unsubscribe that happens
during notification will mutate the set you are looping over.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why this is not a context value, because the answer determines the design.
Context has no selector: a provider holding the whole cache re-renders every
consumer on every write, so a component watching `b` re-renders when `a`
changes. The gate tests exactly that. An external store subscribes per key,
which is the entire reason Redux, Zustand, Jotai and every query client are
external stores rather than context.

## Hint 2

Per-key listener sets are the difference between this design and a naive one
with a single global listener list. The naive version is correct — every
component re-renders and reads its own snapshot, which is unchanged, so React
bails out — but it is O(components) work on every write, and the bail-out only
happens *after* the component function has run. Per-key sets do the filtering
before React is involved.

## Hint 3

Two hazards to check. The unsubscribe you return must be idempotent — React may
call it during a StrictMode remount and again on real unmount — so `set.delete`
rather than anything that assumes presence. And clean up empty listener sets,
or a long-lived app accumulates an empty `Set` per key ever subscribed, which
is a small leak that shows up in a heap snapshot as tens of thousands of empty
sets.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — stale while revalidate

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export one function; it takes the store from ex2.

```tsx
export function ensureData<T>(
  store: EntryStore,
  key: string,
  fetcher: () => Promise<T>,
  options: { staleTime: number; now?: () => number },
): Promise<T> | undefined;
```

Three cases and their behaviour:

- **Miss** (no entry, or `updatedAt === 0`): set `isFetching: true`, call the
  fetcher, return the promise.
- **Fresh hit**: return `undefined` and call **nothing**. The gate asserts the
  fetcher was not called.
- **Stale hit**: set `isFetching: true` **without touching `data`**, fetch,
  return the promise. The gate asserts `store.get(key)!.data` is unchanged
  during the request.

On success: write `data`, clear `error`, set `updatedAt` to `now()`, clear
`isFetching`. On failure: write `error`, clear `isFetching`, and **leave `data`
exactly as it was** — a failed revalidation has not made the previous answer
wrong, only unconfirmed. The returned promise still rejects, and the gate
attaches a handler, so do not swallow it.

Deduplication: while a request for a key is in flight, a second call must
return the **same promise** and must not call the fetcher again. Track it
outside the entry, in a `Map` the function owns, and clear it when the request
settles.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the three cases as a decision at the top of the function before any
fetching code exists:

```tsx
const entry = store.get(key);
if (inFlight.has(key)) return inFlight.get(key);
if (entry && !isStale(entry, staleTime, now())) return undefined;
// ... fetch
```

Everything else is the success and failure handlers. Getting the order right —
dedupe before freshness — matters: a request already out for a stale entry
should be joined, not duplicated.

## Hint 2

The instruction "without touching data" is a statement about the patch you
send. `store.set(key, { isFetching: true })` merges, so it leaves `data` alone
by construction. The mistake is writing `store.set(key, { ...blankEntry(key),
isFetching: true })`, which clears everything and produces a spinner flash on
every revalidation.

## Hint 3

The failure handler has two jobs that pull against each other: record the error
in the store, and let the promise reject so callers can react. Both, not one:

```tsx
(error) => {
  store.set(key, { error: toError(error), isFetching: false });
  inFlight.delete(key);
  throw error;      // the caller's .catch still needs to fire
},
```

`throw` inside a rejection handler returns a rejected promise, which is what
the caller is holding. Note the `inFlight.delete` on both paths — a `finally`
is tidier and does it once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The phrase "stale-while-revalidate" contains its own specification. *Stale*:
the entry is past its freshness window. *While*: at the same time, not
afterwards — the data stays rendered for the whole request. *Revalidate*: check
whether it is still true, which may end in "yes, unchanged". If your
implementation ever has a moment where a stale entry has no data, it is not
implementing this pattern; it is implementing expiry.

## Hint 2

The dedupe map here does something the ex1 entry cannot: it holds a promise,
and promises do not belong in a snapshot that React compares by reference. If
you put the promise on the entry, every `set` that touches it notifies
subscribers about something they cannot render. Keeping it in a side map next
to the store is the pragmatic answer; a real client keeps it on the entry but
excludes it from the comparison, which is more machinery than this needs.

## Hint 3

The `now` injection point exists so the gate can control time, and it is worth
noticing what it implies about your code: `Date.now()` must be called *at the
moment of the decision* and *at the moment of the write*, not captured once at
the top. A single `const t = now()` at the top of the function is a subtle bug —
the write should be stamped when the response arrives, not when the request
went out, or a slow request will look fresher than it is.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — reference counting and the eviction timer

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Extend the store with a lifetime policy.

```tsx
export class GcStore extends EntryStore {
  constructor(options?: { gcTime?: number });
  subscribe(key: string, listener: () => void): () => void;
  has(key: string): boolean;
  pendingEvictions(): number;
}
```

- `gcTime` defaults to `300_000`.
- When the last listener for a key unsubscribes, schedule the entry's deletion
  `gcTime` milliseconds later.
- When anybody subscribes to a key with a pending eviction, **cancel** it. The
  gate unsubscribes, advances timers halfway, resubscribes, advances well past
  `gcTime`, and asserts the data is still there — this is the
  navigate-away-and-back interaction the whole cache exists for.
- If the timer fires, delete the entry *and* the timer record.
- `pendingEvictions()` reports how many timers are scheduled; the gate asserts
  it returns to `0`.
- A `set` on a key that has a pending eviction must **not** cancel it: writing
  to an entry nobody is watching is a background revalidation finishing, not a
  reason to keep it forever.

The gate uses fake timers and also asserts that subscribing to a key whose
entry was already evicted yields `undefined` from `get` rather than a resurrected
stale entry.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The timer is not attached to the entry, it is attached to the *transition* from
one subscriber to zero. So the code lives in the function `subscribe` returns,
after the delete, guarded by a size check:

```tsx
return () => {
  owned.delete(listener);
  if (owned.size === 0) this.scheduleEviction(key);
};
```

And the cancellation lives at the top of `subscribe`, before anything else.

## Hint 2

Order matters in `subscribe`. Cancel the eviction *first*, then add the
listener. If you add first and cancel second it still works, but if you ever
add a check like "do not cancel if the entry is gone", the two orders behave
differently. Cancelling first also makes the invariant easy to state: while a
key has listeners, it has no pending eviction.

## Hint 3

Extending a class whose fields are `private` means you cannot reach the map
from the subclass. Two ways out: change the base's `entries` to `protected`, or
give the base a `delete(key)` method and call that. The second is better
design — the subclass should not know how the base stores things — and it is
what a real client does, because eviction and storage are different concerns.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Pick the number by picturing the interaction rather than by taste. Five minutes
is React Query's default and it is chosen for: user opens a detail page, reads
it, goes back, opens another, goes back, opens the first again. All of that
should be instant. Evicting at zero subscribers makes every one of those
navigations a cold load, which is a cache that costs memory and buys nothing.
An hour, on the other hand, means a long session accumulates every list the
user ever scrolled.

## Hint 2

There is a race worth thinking about even though the gate does not force it.
The timer fires and deletes the entry. A component was in the middle of
mounting and subscribes one tick later. It finds no entry, so it fetches — which
is correct, and is why "subscribing to an evicted key yields `undefined`"
matters. The failure mode you are avoiding is a subscribe that *cancels* a
timer which has already fired, leaving a deleted entry with no timer and no
data, and code elsewhere assuming it is present.

## Hint 3

`setTimeout` in a long-lived SPA is a leak if nothing ever clears it. Two
disciplines keep it honest: always store the handle so it can be cancelled, and
always delete the handle when it fires. `pendingEvictions()` exists in this
exercise precisely so the gate can prove you did the second — a timer map that
only grows is the kind of bug nothing surfaces until a heap snapshot.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — invalidation by tag

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export a key serialiser and an invalidator.

```tsx
export function serializeKey(parts: readonly unknown[]): string;

export function matchesPrefix(key: string, prefix: readonly unknown[]): boolean;

export function invalidate(
  store: EntryStore,
  prefix: readonly unknown[],
  refetch: (key: string) => void,
): { marked: string[]; refetched: string[] };
```

- `serializeKey` turns `["orders", { status: "open", page: 2 }]` into a stable
  string. Object keys are sorted **recursively**, so `{ status, page }` and
  `{ page, status }` serialise identically. Arrays keep their order.
- `matchesPrefix` is true when the key was built from a parts array whose first
  `prefix.length` elements serialise to the same values. `["orders"]` matches
  `["orders", {...}]` and `["orders", 7]` but not `["ordersArchive"]` — prefix
  matching is per **segment**, not per character.
- `invalidate` walks every entry in the store, and for each match:
  - sets `updatedAt: 0` — marked stale, **not deleted**, so the user keeps
    reading what is on screen;
  - calls `refetch(key)` **only if the key has listeners**. Unwatched entries
    are refetched lazily, whenever somebody next needs them.
- It returns the keys it marked and the subset it refetched.

The gate builds eight entries, subscribes to two of them, invalidates a prefix
matching five, and asserts five marked and two refetched — and that the marked
entries still have their `data`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what invalidation actually knows. It knows a mutation happened and
it knows a prefix. It does *not* know which cached answers are genuinely now
wrong — the cache stores responses, not the relationships between them. That is
why the operation is deliberately coarse and deliberately cheap: over-marking
costs one background request that usually returns identical data (and
structural sharing makes it free to render), while under-marking shows the user
a stale screen after their own action.

## Hint 2

`JSON.stringify` has three failure modes worth knowing before you rely on it.
`undefined` values vanish from objects, so `{page: 1, q: undefined}` and
`{page: 1}` collide — usually desirable. `Map` and `Set` both serialise to
`{}`, so every distinct filter set collapses to one key, which is a
catastrophe. And property order is insertion order, which is the bug this
exercise exists to prevent.

## Hint 3

Two edges the gate probes. An empty prefix `[]` matches everything — that is
"invalidate the whole cache", and it should work rather than throw. And a
prefix longer than a key cannot match: `["orders", 7]` must not match the entry
whose key is just `["orders"]`, because that entry is the list and this prefix
is one order. Compare lengths before comparing contents.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — structural sharing

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export one pure function — no React.

```tsx
export function structuralShare<T>(prev: unknown, next: T): T;
```

It returns a value **deeply equal to `next`** that reuses as many object
references from `prev` as possible.

- Primitives, `null`, functions, and mismatched shapes (array vs object): return
  `next`.
- Objects: recurse over `next`'s own enumerable keys. If every child came back
  `===` to the corresponding child of `prev`, **and** `prev` has the same number
  of keys, return `prev` itself. Otherwise return a new object built from the
  recursed children.
- Arrays: the same, indexed, with lengths compared.
- `prev === next` short-circuits.

The gate asserts, in order:

1. `structuralShare(a, structuredClone(a)) === a` for a nested fixture — a
   response with identical content produces zero new references.
2. For a 50-row array where row 12's `title` changed, the result is a new array,
   `result[12] !== prev[12]`, and `result[i] === prev[i]` for every other `i`.
3. Removing a key from an object produces a new object, not `prev`.
4. It does not recurse into `Date`, `Map` or `Set` — those come back as `next`.
5. It handles `null` on either side without throwing.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difference between this and a deep-equality check is what you do with the
answer. Deep equality returns a boolean and forces an all-or-nothing choice.
This returns a *value*, built bottom-up, so a 50-row array where one row
changed comes back as a new array containing 49 old row objects. That is the
whole point: `React.memo` on the row then skips 49 re-renders.

## Hint 2

The recursion has one accumulator and one flag:

```tsx
let changed = false;
const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
for (const k of Object.keys(nextObj)) {
  const child = structuralShare(prevObj[k], nextObj[k]);
  out[k] = child;
  if (child !== prevObj[k]) changed = true;
}
return (changed ? out : prev) as T;
```

Note that `changed` is decided by reference comparison of the *results*, not by
comparing inputs — the recursion has already done the deep work.

## Hint 3

Three shape checks before you recurse, and each catches a real case.
`typeof x !== "object"` catches primitives and functions. `Array.isArray(prev)
!== Array.isArray(next)` catches an endpoint that changed a field from an
object to a list. And the key-count comparison catches deletion: iterating
`next`'s keys alone cannot notice that `prev` had one more.

`Date`, `Map` and `Set` are `typeof "object"` but have no enumerable own keys,
so a naive recursion would return `prev` for two *different* dates. Check
`constructor === Object` or use `Object.getPrototypeOf`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the cost you are avoiding. React's whole optimisation layer —
`memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, effect dependencies — is built on
`Object.is`. A `fetch` plus `JSON.parse` shares nothing with the previous
response, so a query that polls every five seconds invalidates every memo below
it twelve times a minute even when the bytes are identical. Users call that
"the page feels heavy"; a profiler shows a regular heartbeat of full re-renders.

## Hint 2

There is a trap in the phrase "as many references as possible". Reusing `prev`
when it is deeply equal is correct. Reusing a *child* of `prev` that happens to
be deeply equal to a *different* child of `next` is not — you would be matching
by content across positions, which is the same error as keying a list by value.
Recurse position by position and key by key, never by search.

## Hint 3

Know the limit of this optimisation, because an interviewer will ask. It only
helps if consumers actually compare references. A component that does
`data.rows.map(r => ({ ...r, label: fmt(r) }))` inline rebuilds every identity
one level lower and throws away everything you just preserved. Structural
sharing at the cache boundary plus fresh object creation in render is a
no-op with extra steps.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — focus and reconnect revalidation

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. Export an installer.

```tsx
export function installRevalidators(options: {
  onRevalidate: () => void;
  minIntervalMs?: number;
  now?: () => number;
}): () => void;
```

It registers **one** `visibilitychange` listener on `document` and **one**
`online` listener on `window`, and returns a function that removes both.

- `onRevalidate` fires when the document becomes visible, or when the browser
  comes back online.
- It must **not** fire on `visibilitychange` when
  `document.visibilityState !== "visible"` — the event fires on hide as well,
  and revalidating a tab the user just left is exactly wrong.
- A minimum interval, default `2000`ms, throttles it: a burst of focus events
  produces one call. The clock starts at the call that was allowed through.
- The very first eligible event fires immediately — the floor is between calls,
  not before the first.
- The returned function removes both listeners; calling it twice is harmless.

The gate installs, dispatches a hide (expects nothing), a show (expects one
call), three more shows within the window (expects still one), advances past
the interval, dispatches another show (expects two), tears down and dispatches
more (expects still two), and asserts the listener count on `document` returned
to its starting value.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex7
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why these two events and not a timer. Both mean the same thing: *the user
is looking, and time has passed while they were not*. A `setInterval` means
neither — it fires in a hidden tab, on a laptop lid that just closed, on a
phone in a pocket, burning battery and quota to refresh a screen nobody is
looking at. Browsers throttle background timers precisely because so much code
gets this wrong.

## Hint 2

`visibilitychange` is the modern choice over `window.onfocus`, and the
difference matters. Focus fires when the window gains keyboard focus, which
misses the case of a visible-but-unfocused window and fires for a tab that was
never hidden. `visibilityState` describes whether the document is actually
being rendered, which is the question. Mobile browsers fire `visibilitychange`
on app switching, where `focus` behaves inconsistently.

## Hint 3

Teardown discipline is the whole reason this is a function returning a
function. In an app where the client is created once, the listeners live
forever and nobody notices. In tests, in StrictMode, and in any app that
recreates the client on route change, a missing removal means handlers
accumulate and one focus event triggers as many revalidations as there have
been mounts. Make the returned function idempotent so a double call is safe.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — writing to the cache without losing a race

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export one function.

```tsx
export function setQueryData<T>(
  store: EntryStore,
  key: string,
  updater: T | ((prev: T | undefined) => T),
  options?: { at?: number },
): boolean;
```

- `updater` may be a value or a function of the previous value. Detect the
  function form with `typeof updater === "function"`.
- `at` defaults to `Date.now()` and becomes the entry's new `updatedAt`.
- **The guard**: if the existing entry's `updatedAt` is **greater than** `at`,
  the write is stale on arrival and must be dropped entirely — no `set` call,
  no listener notification. Return `false`. Otherwise write and return `true`.
- A successful write clears `error` and sets `isFetching` to its existing value
  (do not touch it — a background request may still be out).
- Run the new value through `structuralShare` from `../ex6/solution` against
  the previous data, so a write that changes nothing produces no new references
  and no re-render of memoised consumers.

The gate walks the bug this exists to prevent: a background revalidation
starting at `t=100`, a mutation writing at `t=200`, and the revalidation landing
at `t=300` carrying the pre-mutation value stamped `at: 100`. The second write
must be dropped and the mutation's value must survive.

It also asserts that writing deeply-equal data leaves `store.get(key)!.data`
`===` to what it was.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb02_query_client ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The bug this prevents is worth picturing before you write the guard. A
background refetch goes out at 100ms carrying the world as it was. At 200ms the
user saves, and the mutation response writes the new value. At 300ms the
refetch lands with the *old* value and overwrites the save. The user sees their
change appear and then silently revert about a second later — one of the
hardest bugs to reproduce and the easiest to prevent.

## Hint 2

The comparison is on the *timestamp the data describes*, not the moment the
write executes. So the caller passes `at`, and a fetch stamps it with the time
the request went out — or, better, with a server-provided version. Your job is
just the ordering:

```tsx
const entry = store.get(key);
if (entry && entry.updatedAt > at) return false;
```

Note `>` and not `>=`: two writes stamped identically should let the later
caller win, and there is no way to order them anyway.

## Hint 3

`typeof updater === "function"` narrows in TypeScript but not helpfully when
`T` could itself be a function type. The pragmatic cast is fine here — real
clients do exactly this and document that functional updaters win the ambiguity:

```tsx
const next =
  typeof updater === "function"
    ? (updater as (prev: T | undefined) => T)(prev)
    : updater;
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two ways to update a cache after a mutation, and this is the precise one.
*Invalidate* says "I do not know what changed, go ask" — always correct, costs a
round trip. *Write through* says "the response I just got is the new truth" —
free, and wrong the moment the server computes something the client cannot: a
derived count, a modified timestamp, another user's concurrent edit. Real code
uses both, and this exercise is the half that needs the ordering guard.

## Hint 2

Think about what `updatedAt` really means once you allow writes from two
sources. It is not "when we last touched this entry" — it is *the time of the
world this data describes*. A response that took 400ms describes the world as
of when it was generated, not when it arrived. Stamping it on arrival makes a
slow response look newer than a fast one, which is exactly backwards, and is
why the parameter is `at` rather than being read inside the function.

## Hint 3

Returning `false` rather than throwing is deliberate. A dropped write is not an
error — it is the system working. Callers occasionally want to know (to decide
whether to invalidate instead), which is why the boolean exists, but the common
case ignores it. Throwing would force every call site into a try/catch for
normal behaviour, which is how a good guard becomes a thing people disable.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build the client as a closure over the store rather than a class hierarchy —
you need `ensureData`, invalidation and `setQueryData` to share one `Map` and
one set of options, and a closure says that more plainly than four files of
inheritance. The exported object is six methods, each three to ten lines,
delegating to the functions you already wrote.

## Hint 2

`useQuery`'s effect is the only new thinking. Its job is: subscribe (done by
`useSyncExternalStore`), then *on every render where the key changed or the
entry is stale*, ask the client to ensure data. That second half belongs in an
effect keyed on the serialised key and `enabled`:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (!enabled) return;
  void client.fetchQuery(key, fetcher)?.catch(() => {});
}, [serialized, enabled]);
```

The `catch` is not laziness — the error is already recorded in the store, and
an unhandled rejection here would be noise.

## Hint 3

Two ordering hazards to design around. The eviction timer and the mount: if a
component mounts and the entry was evicted a tick earlier, `getSnapshot`
returns `undefined` and the effect fetches — which is correct, so make sure
subscribe does not resurrect a deleted entry. And invalidation's refetch
callback needs the *fetcher*, which the client does not store unless you keep
it: stash the last fetcher per key when `fetchQuery` runs, or invalidation can
mark but never refetch.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the nine requirements as nine one-line tests you can run in your head
against the finished code, and keep them visible. Most of the difficulty in
assembling this is not any single piece — you have written all of them — it is
that a change made for requirement 6 quietly breaks requirement 3. The
requirements that interact most: eviction and dedupe (both key off the entry's
existence), and `enabled` and mount-fetching (both decide whether a request
happens).

## Hint 2

`enabled: false` is more subtle than it looks. It must not fetch, but it must
still subscribe, because the entry may be populated by *another* component or
by `setQueryData`, and this one should re-render when that happens. A
implementation that skips the subscription when disabled produces a component
that ignores data arriving from elsewhere — a bug that only appears in an app
with two components on one key.

## Hint 3

The fetcher-per-key store is the piece people leave out and then cannot explain
why `invalidateQueries` does nothing visible. Invalidation knows a key; it does
not know how to fetch it. Keeping `Map<string, () => Promise<unknown>>`
alongside the entries, written on every `fetchQuery`, is the simplest fix, and
its lifetime should follow the entry's — evict both together, or you leak a
closure per key that ever existed.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`JSON.stringify` is the tempting one-liner and it fails on four things, each of
which you should be able to name: property order (insertion, so `{a,b}` and
`{b,a}` differ), `undefined` (vanishes from objects, which is usually what you
want), `Map` and `Set` (both become `{}`, so every distinct filter set collapses
to one key), and functions (also vanish, silently). This exercise is the
twenty-line fix.

## Hint 2

Normalise into plain JSON-safe values first, then serialise. Two passes are
much easier to reason about than one clever recursion:

```tsx
function normalise(value: unknown): unknown {
  if (value instanceof Date) return value.toISOString();
  if (value instanceof Set) return [...value].map(normalise).sort(byString);
  if (value instanceof Map) return [...value].map(([k, v]) => [normalise(k), normalise(v)]).sort(...);
  // ... reject the unserialisable, recurse into plain objects and arrays
}
```

Sorting a `Set` matters because sets have no order and two sets with the same
members must produce the same key.

## Hint 3

The 13-digit check for `suspicious` is a heuristic, and saying so is part of
the answer: it catches `Date.now()` accidentally included in a key, which is
the single most common cause of "my cache never hits". It will also flag a
legitimate 13-digit id, which is why the function reports rather than throws.

Watch the `null` versus `undefined` distinction the prompt draws — it is not
pedantry. `status: undefined` means "I did not filter by status"; `status:
null` means "show me the ones with no status". Different queries, different
keys.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The rule that makes keys correct is one sentence: **the key is the complete set
of inputs the fetcher reads, and nothing else.** Everything in this exercise
follows from it. A fetcher that closes over a variable not in the key has a bug
that appears the first time that variable changes. A key containing something
the fetcher does not read — a timestamp, a render counter, a callback — is a
guaranteed miss on every render.

## Hint 2

Think about the two directions of failure, because they look completely
different in production. Keys too *coarse*: page two and page one share an
entry, so the list flickers between them and a user reports "pagination is
broken". Keys too *fine*: every render is a miss, so the network panel is a
wall of identical requests and a user reports "the app is slow". The first is
usually a forgotten parameter; the second is usually an object rebuilt in
render with an unstable member.

## Hint 3

Throwing on unserialisable values is a deliberate choice worth defending.
Silently dropping a function from a params object gives you a key that ignores
part of the query — the failure is invisible and arrives months later. Throwing
happens on the first render in development, names the offending key, and takes
thirty seconds to fix. The general principle: a cache should fail loudly at
build-the-key time rather than quietly at serve-the-answer time.

lessons.title: V3·RB3 — Suspense, streaming and loading states that do not flash
lessons.summary: Suspense is not a loading-spinner component. It is a mechanism for letting a component say "not yet" during render, and everything that makes it useful — streaming HTML, transitions that keep the old screen, deferred values, spinners that refuse to appear for fast responses — follows from that one idea. This sector builds the mechanism, then the discipline of not flashing.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RB3 — Suspense, streaming and loading states that do not flash

Two sectors ago you built a request state machine, and every component that
used it had the same three branches: loading, error, data. That is fine, and it
is also the reason a page with six data-dependent regions has eighteen branches
of loading logic scattered through it, each one making its own decision about
what to show and when.

Suspense inverts it. A component that does not have its data yet does not
render a fallback — it *suspends*, which means it throws a promise (or, in
React 19, calls `use()` on one), and the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary above it
renders the fallback instead. The component's own code contains no loading
branch at all. It reads its data as a value, because by the time its body runs
to completion, the data is there.

This is a bigger change than it sounds. The loading state stops being a
property of the component and becomes a property of the *region of the tree*
you drew a boundary around, which is exactly where a designer would put it. It
also makes loading states composable: three components under one boundary
produce one fallback, and the same three under three boundaries produce three.
You choose the granularity, in the layout, without touching the components.

## What actually happens when a component suspends

React renders your component. Your component calls `use(promise)` with a
promise that is still pending. `use` throws — a special exception carrying the
promise. React catches it while rendering, discards the work-in-progress for
that subtree, walks up to the nearest `<Suspense>`, renders its `fallback`
instead, and attaches a `.then` to the promise so it can try again when it
settles.

Three consequences follow immediately and all three trip people up.

**Your component's body ran and its effects did not.** Anything before the
`use()` call executed; anything after did not. React then discards the render
entirely. Side effects in a render body were always a bug; with Suspense they
are a bug that runs an unpredictable number of times.

**The promise must not be created during render.** `use(fetch(url))` creates a
new promise every render, suspends on it, re-renders when it settles, creates
another new promise, and suspends again — forever. The promise has to come from
somewhere stable: a cache, a parent that created it, a framework loader. This
is the single most common Suspense bug, and it is why "Suspense for data
fetching" needs a cache underneath it and why the sector before this one
existed.

**A boundary that is already showing content behaves differently from one that
is not.** If a boundary has already revealed its children and something inside
suspends again — because a prop changed and a new promise is being read — React
hides the content and shows the fallback again. That is a *flash*, and avoiding
it is what `startTransition` and `useDeferredValue` are for.

## Streaming: the same mechanism over the wire

On the server, `renderToPipeableStream` uses the same suspension signal to
decide what to send first. Content outside any boundary is rendered and flushed
immediately; a boundary whose children suspend emits its fallback plus a
placeholder, and the real HTML is streamed later, followed by a tiny inline
script that swaps it into place. The user sees the shell — header, nav, layout
— in the first flush, and each region fills in as its data arrives.

The important consequence for you as an author is that **`<Suspense>`
boundaries are your streaming boundaries**. They are not a styling decision.
Wrapping your entire page in one boundary means nothing streams until the
slowest query finishes; wrapping each region means the fast ones arrive first.
The layout of your boundaries is the shape of your page's loading experience,
and it is worth drawing before writing any of it.

## The two ways a loading state hurts

A loading state can be too slow to appear or too eager. Both are worse than
they sound.

**Too eager** is the flash: a skeleton that appears for 80ms and vanishes. The
eye registers the change, the layout jumps twice, and the perceived experience
is worse than if nothing had appeared at all. The standard remedy comes from
Jakob Nielsen's response-time thresholds: below about 100ms an interaction
feels instantaneous and needs no feedback; up to a second the user stays in
flow but wants *something*; past a second they need a progress indicator or
they will assume it is broken. So: do not show a spinner before ~200ms, and if
you do show one, keep it up for a minimum time so it does not strobe.

**Too eager also means throwing away good content.** A user changes a filter on
a table they are reading. If the boundary falls back, the table is replaced by a
skeleton — a strictly worse screen than the stale table. `startTransition` tells
React that an update is non-urgent and that it should *keep showing the old UI*
until the new one is ready rather than falling back. `useDeferredValue` is the
same idea expressed as a value rather than an event.

## What you will build

The raw suspending resource, so the mechanism is not magic. Boundary placement
and its effect on reveal order. `use()` with a cached promise. Transitions that
prevent fallbacks. `useDeferredValue` with a staleness indicator. A delayed,
minimum-duration spinner. Ordered reveal without `SuspenseList`, which React 19
does not ship. And skeletons that match their content's geometry so nothing
shifts. The challenge is a search page with none of the flashes; the review
pairs Suspense with an error boundary and makes retry work.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3rb03_suspense_streaming

## Notes

**Suspending is a render-time signal, not a lifecycle.** There is no
`onSuspend`. A component either completes its render or it does not, and the
boundary above reacts. That is why the rules about purity get sharper here: a
render that gets thrown away must leave nothing behind.

**`use()` is not `useEffect` with a nicer face.** It can be called
conditionally, inside loops and after early returns, because it is not backed
by the hook-order array. What it needs instead is a stable promise, which the
caller must supply. React caches the promise's result per-promise-identity for
the duration of the render pass; it does not cache the promise for you.

**Reading a promise you created in render is the canonical infinite loop.**
Symptoms: the fallback shows forever, the network tab fills with identical
requests, no error appears. The rule: promises come from outside the render —
a cache keyed by query, a prop, a context value, a loader.

**A boundary that has revealed content will hide it again.** This is the
behaviour transitions exist to override. `startTransition(() => setQuery(next))`
marks the resulting render as non-urgent; if it suspends, React keeps the
previous committed UI on screen and finishes the new one in the background.
`isPending` from `useTransition` is how you show that something is happening
without destroying what is there.

**`useDeferredValue` is a transition you did not have to schedule.** You pass
the current value; it returns the previous one during the re-render that the
new value triggered, then re-renders with the new one at lower priority.
Comparing `value !== deferred` tells you the screen is showing stale content,
which is the hook for a dim-the-list-while-updating treatment. It differs from
a debounce in a way worth knowing: a debounce delays the *work* by a fixed time
regardless of machine speed; a deferred value starts the work immediately and
lets React interrupt it, so on a fast machine there is no delay at all.

**Spinner timing is two thresholds, not one.** A delay before appearing
(200–300ms) prevents the flash on fast responses. A minimum visible duration
(300–500ms) once it has appeared prevents the strobe when the response lands
just after the delay elapsed. Implementing only the first still lets a 210ms
response flash a spinner for 10ms.

**Skeletons must match geometry.** A skeleton that is not the same height as
the content it replaces guarantees a layout shift on reveal, which is
measurable as Cumulative Layout Shift and is felt as the page jumping under
your finger. The skeleton's job is to reserve the space, not to entertain.

## ex1 — the raw resource

Tests the mechanism. The classic mistake is believing Suspense involves
`try`/`catch` in your own code — it does not; you throw and React catches. The
model answer stores the promise's status and value on a wrapper, throws the
promise while pending, throws the error when rejected, and returns the value
when fulfilled, which is exactly what `use` does internally.

## ex2 — where the boundary goes

Tests granularity. The classic mistake is one boundary around the whole page,
which converts three independent slow queries into one slow page. The model
answer places a boundary per region so each reveals independently, and keeps
the shell — heading, nav — outside every boundary so it paints in the first
flush.

## ex3 — `use()` and the cached promise

Tests the promise-identity rule. The classic mistake is calling the fetcher in
render. The model answer keeps a module-level `Map` from key to promise, so the
same key always yields the same promise object and the second render finds a
settled one.

## ex4 — transitions

Tests fallback avoidance. The classic mistake is wrapping the *fetch* in
`startTransition` instead of the *state update* — the transition is about which
render is urgent, not about which work is async. The model answer wraps
`setQuery`, reads `isPending`, and dims rather than replaces.

## ex5 — deferred values

Tests the difference from debouncing. The classic mistake is deferring the
input's own value, which makes typing itself laggy. The model answer keeps the
input fully controlled and urgent, and defers only the value passed to the
expensive subtree, marking it stale while they disagree.

## ex6 — the honest spinner

Tests timing discipline. The classic mistake is a single `setTimeout` that
shows the spinner and nothing that governs how long it stays. The model answer
tracks both thresholds with a small state machine and cleans up both timers,
including the case where the response arrives during the delay and no spinner
should ever appear.

## ex7 — ordered reveal

Tests composition without `SuspenseList`. The classic mistake is assuming React
reveals boundaries in tree order — it reveals them in *settle* order, so a fast

# Long reading — the mechanism under Suspense

## A short history, because it explains the API

Suspense shipped in React 16.6 (2018) for exactly one purpose: code splitting.
`React.lazy` returns a component that throws a promise for its own module while
the chunk downloads, and `<Suspense>` renders a fallback meanwhile. That was
the entire supported surface for years, and it is worth noticing what it
implies — the mechanism was never about data. It is about *a component that
cannot finish rendering yet*, and a module that has not arrived is one instance
of that.

"Suspense for data fetching" was demonstrated in 2018 and then spent five years
in an unstable state, for a reason that is instructive: the mechanism was
finished, and the *cache* was not. Throwing a promise requires that the same
render, repeated, throws the same promise — which means something outside the
component must remember it. React did not want to ship an opinionated cache,
and without a cache the feature is a footgun. The gap was filled by userland:
Relay first, then React Query and SWR, then the framework loaders in Next.js
and React Router. React 19's `use()` finally blesses the pattern while still
leaving the cache to you or your framework.

The other thread is server rendering. `renderToString` was synchronous and
all-or-nothing: no data fetching, no streaming, and the whole page waited for
the slowest part. React 18's `renderToPipeableStream` uses the *same*
suspension signal to decide flush boundaries, which is why the API has no
separate concept for streaming. You do not mark something streamable; you wrap
it in `<Suspense>` and it becomes streamable, because "this part is not ready"
is exactly the information the streamer needs.

## What the reconciler actually does

When `use()` is called with a pending promise, React throws an internal
exception. The reconciler catches it in `handleThrow`, checks whether the
thrown value is thenable, and if so marks the work-in-progress fiber as
suspended. It then walks up the fiber tree looking for a boundary — a fiber
with `SuspenseComponent` tag — and marks *that* fiber for re-render with its
fallback children. The partially-built subtree is discarded: no DOM was
committed, no effects were flushed, no state was persisted. React attaches a
continuation to the promise (`promise.then(retry, retry)`) and, when it fires,
schedules a re-render of the boundary.

Two subtleties fall out of that description.

The first is that your component's body *did* run, up to the `use()` call, and
will run again from the top when React retries. Anything you did on the way —
mutating a module variable, pushing to an array, incrementing a counter — has
happened once and will happen again, an unknown number of times. This is the
same rule as StrictMode's double-invocation, with sharper teeth: the number of
runs is genuinely unpredictable because it depends on how many times the
subtree suspends.

The second is that React caches the *outcome* per promise identity within a
render pass, but has no way to associate two different promise objects with the
same logical request. `Object.is` on the promise is the whole identity model.
This is not a limitation React could fix without inventing the cache it
deliberately declined to invent.

## Streaming, in detail

`renderToPipeableStream` produces HTML in flushes. The first contains
everything renderable without suspending, with each unresolved boundary
represented by its fallback wrapped in a template comment that marks the
insertion point. As each boundary's data resolves, React renders that subtree
and writes it into the stream inside a hidden `<div>`, followed by a very small
inline script that moves the nodes into the placeholder position and removes
the fallback. No client JavaScript framework code is required for this swap —
it works before hydration, which is the point.

This has a consequence people find surprising: the HTML arrives out of document
order. A boundary near the bottom of the page whose data is fast will be
streamed before a boundary near the top whose data is slow, and inserted into
its correct place by the inline script. It also means the `<head>` has already
been sent by the time you know whether a page errored, which is why frameworks
have specific handling for late errors and why a 500 status cannot be set once
streaming has begun.

Selective hydration is the companion feature. React hydrates boundaries
independently, and prioritises the one the user just interacted with: if
someone clicks inside a not-yet-hydrated boundary, React hydrates that boundary
first and replays the event. Before this, a single slow component blocked
hydration of the entire page.

## The perception research behind the timings

The numbers in this sector are not folklore. Robert Miller's 1968 paper on
response time in conversational transactions established the thresholds that
Jakob Nielsen popularised in 1993: 0.1 seconds is the limit for the user to feel
the system is reacting instantaneously; 1 second is the limit for their flow of
thought to stay uninterrupted, though they will notice the delay; 10 seconds is
the limit for keeping attention on the task.

Applied to loading indicators, that yields three rules. Below ~100ms, showing
anything is worse than showing nothing, because the appearance and disappearance
of an element is itself a change the eye must process. Between 100ms and 1s, a
subtle indication of activity — dimming, `aria-busy`, a thin progress bar — keeps
the user informed without implying a long wait. Beyond 1s, a real indicator is
required, and beyond ~4s it should ideally be a determinate one, because
uncertainty is what makes waiting feel long.

The minimum-visible-duration rule comes from a different place: change
blindness research and the practical observation that an element which appears
and disappears within about 300ms reads as a glitch rather than as information.
This is why every mature design system's loading component has both a delay and
a floor, and why implementing only the delay produces the most annoying
possible behaviour — a spinner that flickers precisely on the medium-speed
responses that make up most of real traffic.

## Performance notes

Suspense is not free, but its costs are unusual. The discarded render is real
work: a component that suspends at the bottom of a deep tree has rendered
everything above it for nothing. In practice this rarely matters, because the
work is bounded by the boundary and React does it once per settle. What does
matter is the *number* of boundaries: each one is a fiber with its own retry
scheduling, and a list of 500 rows each in its own boundary is a genuine
regression. Boundaries are for regions, not for items.

Streaming's cost is on the server, and it is a trade: total time-to-last-byte
gets slightly worse (more flushes, more overhead) in exchange for a much better
time-to-first-byte and first-contentful-paint. For anything user-facing that is
the right trade, which is why the framework defaults went that way.

Transitions have a subtler cost. A transition render can be interrupted and
restarted, so an expensive render may happen several times before it commits.
On a fast machine that is invisible; on a slow one it is the mechanism working
as designed, spending CPU to keep the main thread responsive. If you find a
transition making things worse, the usual cause is a component that is
expensive *and* not memoised, so every restart redoes work that did not change.

## When not to use it

Do not put a Suspense boundary around something that is not slow. The boundary
adds a fallback, a reveal, and a potential layout shift in exchange for
managing a wait that does not exist.

Do not use Suspense for mutations. It is a read primitive: it describes a
component that cannot render yet, not an action in progress. Actions,
`useActionState` and `useOptimistic` are the mutation-side tools, and the next
sector is about them.

Do not reach for Suspense-based data fetching in a client-only app with no
framework and no cache. You will end up writing the cache — which is the
previous sector — and if you are not going to do that carefully, the explicit
loading branches of a `useQuery`-shaped hook are clearer, testable, and produce
no surprises about promise identity.

And do not use `useDeferredValue` to paper over a component that is slow for
avoidable reasons. Deferring makes an expensive render interruptible; it does
not make it cheap. If your list re-renders 5,000 rows on every keystroke
because none of them are memoised and the parent rebuilds every row object,
fix that first. Deferring is the last 20% after the structural work, not a
substitute for it.

## Hint 1

The whole protocol is two `throw` statements with different destinations.
A thrown *promise* is caught by React's reconciler and routed to the nearest
`<Suspense>`. A thrown *error* is caught by the nearest error boundary. Your
`read()` does both, depending on state, and nothing in your file ever catches
anything.

## Hint 2

State lives in a closure variable, not in React:

```tsx
let status: "pending" | "fulfilled" | "rejected" = "pending";
let value: T;
let reason: unknown;

const settled = promise.then(
  (v) => { status = "fulfilled"; value = v; },
  (e: unknown) => { status = "rejected"; reason = e; },
);
```

Throw `settled` rather than `promise` — it never rejects, so React's retry
subscription cannot itself produce an unhandled rejection.

## Hint 3

"Attaches handlers immediately" is the requirement that forces the `.then` to
run in `createResource`'s body rather than lazily inside `read`. A lazy version
looks tidier and has a real bug: a promise that rejects before anyone reads it
has no handler, and Node prints an unhandled-rejection warning — or, in some
configurations, exits.

## Hint 1

Ask what React can possibly observe about your component. It calls your
function. Either it returns elements, or it throws. There is no third channel —
no callback, no lifecycle, no way to say "wait" other than not finishing. Once
that is clear, the design of `read()` writes itself: it is the only place that
can decide, and it decides by throwing.

## Hint 2

Notice that `read()` is called *during render*, which means it must be
synchronous and must be safe to call many times. React may render your
component several times before committing — StrictMode, transitions,
interrupted renders — and each one calls `read()` again. A `read` with a side
effect, or one that mutates the resource, breaks in ways that only appear under
concurrent rendering.

## Hint 3

Two variants of the same throw are worth distinguishing. Throwing the original
promise works and is what the 2018 demos did. Throwing the *derived* promise —
the one returned by `.then(...)` with both handlers attached — is better,
because that promise always fulfils. React attaches its retry to whatever you
throw, and attaching a retry to a promise that rejects means React's own
internal handler is the one absorbing your rejection.

## Hint 3

Do not disable the buttons during the transition, even though it is tempting.
The entire point of a transition is that the interface stays interactive while
non-urgent work happens; disabling the controls throws that away and reproduces
the blocking behaviour you were avoiding. React handles the superseded
transition for you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — deferring the expensive half

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

```tsx
export function FilterList({
  items,
  renderCount,
}: {
  items: string[];
  renderCount?: { current: number };
}): JSX.Element;

export const ExpensiveList: React.MemoExoticComponent<
  (props: { query: string; items: string[]; renderCount?: { current: number } }) => JSX.Element
>;
```

- `FilterList` renders an input labelled `Filter` and, below it,
  `<ExpensiveList>`.
- The input is **fully controlled and urgent**: typing updates it immediately.
- `ExpensiveList` receives a **deferred** copy of the query, not the live one.
- While the live and deferred values disagree, the list's wrapping `<div>` has
  `aria-busy="true"` and `data-stale="true"`; when they agree, both are
  `"false"`.
- `ExpensiveList` renders one `<li>` per item whose lowercase form contains the
  lowercase query, and increments `renderCount.current` once per render — the
  gate uses it to prove the list is not re-rendering on every keystroke at high
  priority.
- `ExpensiveList` must be wrapped in `React.memo`, or deferring buys nothing:
  the parent re-renders on every keystroke and would re-render the child anyway.

The gate types six characters, asserts the input's value tracked every
keystroke exactly, and asserts the stale flag went true and then false.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb03_suspense_streaming ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two values and it matters which one goes where. The **live** value
belongs to the input — that is what makes typing feel instant. The **deferred**
value belongs to the expensive subtree. Deferring the input's own `value` is
the classic mistake and produces exactly the laggy typing you were trying to
avoid.

```tsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);
```

## Hint 2

`query !== deferredQuery` is the staleness signal, and it is genuinely useful:
it is true exactly while the screen is showing results for an older query. Dim
the region, set `aria-busy`, and the user reads "this is updating" rather than
"this is wrong".

## Hint 3

`React.memo` on the child is load-bearing, not decoration. Without it, the
parent re-renders on every keystroke (because `query` changed), and re-rendering
a parent re-renders its children regardless of whether their props changed —
so the expensive list runs at urgent priority anyway and the deferral achieves
nothing. `memo` makes the child skip when `deferredQuery` has not moved.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what `useDeferredValue` actually does, because the mental model
"it's a debounce" leads to wrong decisions. On the render triggered by the new
value, it returns the *old* one, then immediately schedules a second, low
priority render with the new one. On a fast machine both happen within one
frame and there is no visible delay at all. A debounce would have waited 300ms
regardless. On a slow machine, the low-priority render is interruptible, so the
next keystroke abandons it — a debounce cannot abandon work it already started.

## Hint 2

The corollary is when a debounce is still right: when the goal is fewer
*network requests*. Deferring does not reduce work, it reschedules it, so a
deferred value that triggers a fetch triggers just as many fetches. Deferring is
for expensive *rendering*; debouncing is for expensive *asking*. Real search
boxes often use both — debounce the request, defer the render.

## Hint 3

Watch for the trap where deferring makes things worse. If the expensive child
is expensive because it rebuilds thousands of objects that did not change, the
low-priority render can be started and abandoned several times, doing that work
repeatedly. Deferring is the last optimisation after memoisation and stable
props, not a substitute for them. If a profile shows a transition making things
slower, this is nearly always why.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the spinner that refuses to flash Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export a hook and a component. ```tsx export function useDelayedFlag( active: boolean, options?: { delayMs?: number; minVisibleMs?: number; now?: () => number }, ): boolean; export function SaveIndicator({ saving }: { saving: boolean }): JSX.Element | null; ``` `useDelayedFlag` returns `false` until `active` has been true continuously for `delayMs` (default `200`). Once it returns `true`, it keeps returning `true` for at least `minVisibleMs` (default `400`) even after `active` goes false. The four cases the gate walks, with fake timers: | `active` true for | flag ever true? | for how long | | --- | --- | --- | | 80ms | no | — | | 210ms | yes | 400ms from when it appeared | | 600ms | yes | 600ms | | 3000ms | yes | 3000ms | `SaveIndicator` renders `

Saving

` when the flag is true and `null` otherwise. Both timers must be cleaned up: the gate asserts no pending timers after unmount, and that unmounting during the delay never sets state. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rb03_suspense_streaming ex6 ```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The numbers have a source and knowing it makes them defensible. Robert Miller
(1968) and Jakob Nielsen (1993): 0.1s is the threshold at which a system feels
instantaneous, 1s is the limit for uninterrupted flow of thought, 10s is the
limit of attention. Below 100ms, showing an indicator is *worse* than showing
nothing, because the appearance and removal of an element is itself a change
the eye has to process. The 200ms delay sits just above that threshold with
margin for scheduling.

## Hint 2

There is a third state most implementations forget: `active` goes false *during
the delay*. Nothing was ever shown, so nothing needs a floor, and the correct
behaviour is simply to cancel the timer and show nothing at all. If your code
routes that case through the floor logic you will get a spinner appearing after
the work has finished, which is the most confusing possible outcome.

## Hint 3

Consider the composition with `isPending` from ex4, because that is how this is
actually used. A transition keeps the old content on screen with no progress
indication, which is right for a second and wrong for five. Feeding `isPending`
into this hook with a delay around 500ms gives you: instant swaps show nothing,
slow ones eventually admit that something is happening. That combination is
what a polished app does and it is two lines.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1 The mechanism you need is already in the semantics of a boundary: everything inside a boundary is hidden while anything inside it suspends. So if panel two is *inside* panel one's boundary, panel two cannot possibly appear before panel one does. Ordering is nesting. ## Hint 2 `reduceRight` builds the nest from the inside out: ```tsx panels.reduceRight( (rest, panel) => ( Loading {panel.id}

}> {rest} ), null, ); ``` Reading it outside-in: the first boundary contains panel one *and* the second boundary, which contains panel two and the third, and so on. ## Hint 3 Two details the gate will catch. The fallback of the outer boundary is the only thing visible at the start, so if you want all three "Loading" lines shown up front you have to put them there deliberately — nesting means the inner fallbacks are not rendered at all until the outer boundary reveals. And keys still matter on the boundaries, because you are producing them from a map.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Know why `SuspenseList` is not in React 19, because it explains the shape of
this workaround. It lived in experimental builds for years with a `revealOrder`
prop and was never stabilised — coordinating reveal across independently
scheduled boundaries turned out to interact badly with concurrent features and
with streaming, where the server has already committed to an order. Nesting
gives you `revealOrder="forwards"` and nothing else, which is the case that
actually comes up.

## Hint 2

Be precise about the cost, because it is the reason not to do this by default.
With three siblings settling at 100ms, 500ms and 200ms, unordered reveals
progressively and everything is visible at 500ms. Nested reveals in order and
everything is visible at 500ms too — but nothing at all is visible until the
*first* one settles, and if the first is the slow one, the fast ones wait for it
with nothing on screen. You have traded early partial content for a stable
reading order.

## Hint 3

There is a third option worth knowing that this exercise does not build:
reveal unordered but reserve the space, so nothing reflows even though things
appear out of order. Geometry-matched skeletons at every position achieve the
main benefit of ordering — no jumping — without any of the latency cost. Order
matters for meaning (a narrative, numbered steps); geometry matters for
stability. Do not use the expensive fix for the cheap problem.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — skeletons that reserve the space

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export shared geometry and two components.

```tsx
export const ROW_HEIGHT = 44;
export const HEADER_HEIGHT = 56;

export function OrderTable({ rows }: { rows: { id: string; total: string }[] }): JSX.Element;

export function OrderTableSkeleton({ rowCount }: { rowCount: number }): JSX.Element;
```

- Both render an outer `<div data-testid="orders">` whose inline
  `style.height` is `HEADER_HEIGHT + rowCount * ROW_HEIGHT` pixels, where
  `rowCount` is `rows.length` for the real table.
- The real table renders a header row of height `HEADER_HEIGHT` and one row per
  order of height `ROW_HEIGHT`, each row showing `id` and `total`.
- The skeleton renders the same header height and `rowCount` placeholder rows of
  the same height, each with `aria-hidden="true"`, and the container carries
  `role="status"` and `aria-label="Loading orders"`.
- **Neither** may hard-code a pixel number: both must read the exported
  constants, so the two cannot drift.

The gate renders the skeleton with `rowCount={8}`, records the container's
`style.height`, renders the real table with 8 rows, and asserts the heights are
**identical strings**. It then asserts the skeleton exposes exactly one
accessible name and that its placeholder rows are hidden from the accessibility
tree — a screen reader should hear "Loading orders", not eight empty rows.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb03_suspense_streaming ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A skeleton's job is to reserve space, not to entertain. If it is 120px tall and
the content is 180px, the reveal shifts everything below it by 60px — a layout
shift the user experiences as the page moving under their cursor mid-click, and
one that shows up directly in Cumulative Layout Shift.

## Hint 2

Sharing the constants is the mechanism that keeps them equal. The moment one
component says `height: 44` and the other says `height: "2.75rem"`, they will
drift the first time somebody adjusts padding. Export the numbers, compute both
heights from the same expression, and the drift becomes impossible rather than
unlikely.

## Hint 3

`aria-hidden="true"` on the placeholder rows is not cosmetic. Without it, a
screen reader announces eight empty rows, which is noise that actively
obstructs. With `role="status"` on the container and a label, the user hears
one useful sentence. The general rule for loading UI: one announcement, no
decoration in the accessibility tree.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about which loading placeholder is right for which situation, because
skeletons are not always the answer. A skeleton is right when the shape of the
content is known and stable — a table, a card grid, a profile header. A spinner
is right when the shape is unknown or the region is small. And *nothing* is
right when the wait is under ~100ms, which is why this composes with the
delayed-flag hook: reserve the geometry always, show the shimmer only after the
delay.

## Hint 2

There is a subtle failure worth avoiding: a skeleton whose row count differs
from the real row count. Eight placeholder rows followed by three real ones
shrinks the container on reveal, which is the same layout shift in the other
direction. When the count is unknown, prefer a fixed container height with a
scroll region, or a count that matches the page size you are about to request —
you usually know it, because you asked for it.

## Hint 3

Test layout stability the way the gate does: render both, compare the computed
geometry, and fail on a mismatch. That check is cheap to add to a real codebase
and catches the whole class of bug, which is otherwise only visible as a
gradually worsening CLS number that nobody can attribute to a particular
change.
