exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — normalise without moving the caret

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Export two components.

```tsx
export function NaiveCode({ onChange }: { onChange?: (v: string) => void }): JSX.Element;
export function SteadyCode({ onChange }: { onChange?: (v: string) => void }): JSX.Element;
```

Both render an input labelled `Code` whose value is always uppercase and
contains only `A-Z` and `0-9` — anything else the user types is dropped.

- `NaiveCode` transforms in `onChange` and does nothing about the caret. This is
  the version you are diagnosing.
- `SteadyCode` keeps the caret where the user left it.

The gate types `abc`, then places the caret between `A` and `B`, types `x`, and
asserts:

- `NaiveCode` ends with value `AXBC` and `selectionStart === 4` — the caret
  jumped to the end;
- `SteadyCode` ends with value `AXBC` and `selectionStart === 2` — immediately
  after the inserted character.

It also types a character that gets **dropped** (a `-`) in the middle and
asserts `SteadyCode`'s caret does not advance past it, because nothing was
inserted.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb05_form_state_location ex1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a much simpler answer available and knowing when to prefer it is part
of the exercise: **normalise on blur**. The caret is leaving the field anyway,
so nothing can jump, and the user sees exactly what they typed while they are
typing it. Most design systems format phone numbers, card numbers and postcodes
this way for precisely this reason. Live transformation is for cases where the
transformed form must be visible during typing.

## Hint 2

Notice how you would discover this bug in a real codebase, because it is
instructive. It never appears in development, because a developer testing their
own field types the whole value from the start, always at the end. It appears
when a user corrects a typo in the middle. Any field with a live transform
needs a test that types into the middle, and almost none have one.

## Hint 3

Watch out for a subtle failure mode of the layout-effect approach: it runs on
*every* commit, including ones not caused by typing. Guarding on the ref being
non-null and clearing it after use — as the hint above does — is what keeps a
parent re-render from yanking the caret to a stale position while the user is
elsewhere in the field.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new FormData(formElement)` walks the form's *named* controls and reads the
DOM. It does not know or care whether a field is controlled. Any field without
a `name` is invisible to it, which is the number one cause of "my form data is
missing a field" — and a good reason to be suspicious of component libraries
that do not forward `name`.

## Hint 2

The two traps, spelled out:

```tsx
const newsletter = data.has("newsletter");              // absent when unchecked
const interests = data.getAll("interests").map(String); // get() returns only the first
```

`data.get("newsletter")` returns `"on"` when checked and `null` when not, so
`Boolean(...)` happens to work — but `has` says what you mean and survives a
checkbox with an explicit `value=""`.

## Hint 3

`FormDataEntryValue` is `string | File`, so coerce deliberately rather than
casting. And for `referrer`, the empty-string-to-null conversion belongs in the
reader, not in the form: the reader is the boundary where DOM strings become
your domain types, and putting the conversion there means every caller gets it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what you did not have to write: no `useState`, no `onChange` per field,
no assembling an object at submit, no risk of the state and the DOM disagreeing.
For a form where nothing needs the values during typing — which is most forms —
that is the whole implementation, and it is faster, shorter and less likely to
be wrong than the mirrored version.

## Hint 2

This is also what makes progressive enhancement possible. A form built this way
works before React has hydrated and works with JavaScript disabled if the action
points at a server endpoint. React 19's `<form action={fn}>` is built directly
on it. A mirrored form cannot do either, because its values only exist once the
JavaScript is running.

## Hint 3

The cost you accept is that everything arrives as a string or a `File`. Numbers,
booleans, dates and enums all need parsing, and the parsing has to live
somewhere — which is the reader. Putting it there rather than scattering
`Number(...)` calls through the submit handler gives you one place to validate,
one place to change, and one function that is trivial to unit-test without
rendering anything.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the warning nobody reads

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export three things.

```tsx
export type ProfileRecord = { name?: string; bio?: string | null; age?: number };

export function BrokenProfile({ record }: { record: ProfileRecord }): JSX.Element;

export function toFormValues(record: ProfileRecord): { name: string; bio: string; age: string };

export function Profile({ record }: { record: ProfileRecord }): JSX.Element;
```

- `BrokenProfile` puts `record.name`, `record.bio` and `record.age` straight
  into `value` props. Given `{}` it produces uncontrolled inputs; when the gate
  re-renders it with `{ name: "Ada" }`, React logs *A component is changing an
  uncontrolled input to be controlled*. The gate asserts that warning appears —
  you are reproducing it deliberately.
- `toFormValues` normalises **once, at the boundary**: `undefined` and `null`
  become `""`, and a number becomes its string form. `age: 0` must become
  `"0"`, not `""`.
- `Profile` seeds its state from `toFormValues(record)` and renders three
  controlled inputs labelled `Name`, `Bio` and `Age`. The gate asserts **no**
  React warnings for the same sequence of props.

Do not use `value={x ?? ""}` inline in `Profile`. The point is to fix the data
at the edge rather than patch every consumer — the gate greps for `??` inside a
`value` prop and fails if it finds one.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb05_form_state_location ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the warning literally. React decides whether an input is controlled by
whether `value` is `undefined` on that render. `{}` gives `undefined` — React
steps back and lets the DOM own the field. A later render supplies `"Ada"` —
React steps in and takes over. The transition is the thing it is warning about,
because the field's behaviour changes underneath the user.

## Hint 2

`null` and `undefined` behave differently and both are wrong in different ways.
`value={undefined}` is uncontrolled. `value={null}` is *also* treated as
uncontrolled by React, and additionally warns about `null` specifically. Your
normaliser has to handle both, which `?? ""` does — the question is *where* it
runs.

## Hint 3

Watch the `age: 0` case, which is the trap in `toFormValues`. `record.age ?? ""`
is correct (`??` only falls through for `null`/`undefined`), but
`record.age || ""` is not — `0` is falsy and becomes an empty field, so a user
whose age is zero cannot see it. This is the same falsy-versus-nullish
distinction as the stray `0` in conditional rendering, in a different costume.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason to fix this at the boundary rather than at every `value` is that
`?? ""` at the input hides the actual bug. If `record.nmae` is a typo, `?? ""`
turns it into a silently empty field that saves an empty string over real data.
A normaliser with an explicit shape — three named fields, each converted — fails
loudly at the type level when the source shape changes.

## Hint 2

Think about what the boundary is in a real application: it is where the server's
JSON becomes your form's initial values. Servers omit fields, send `null` for
"not set", and send numbers for numeric columns. All three arrive as something
an input cannot render as a value. One conversion function per form, applied
once, is the cheapest place to absorb that.

## Hint 3

The reverse conversion matters just as much and this exercise only does half of
it. On submit you have three strings and the server wants `age` as a number and
`bio` as `null` when empty. That is `fromFormValues`, and forms that skip it end
up sending `age: "31"` and discovering the type error in production. Whenever
you write a `toFormValues`, write its inverse in the same file.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The cost model in one sentence: a `setState` re-renders the component that owns
the state and everything below it. So the question "where does the note's state
live?" is exactly the question "what re-renders when the user types?". Put it in
`OrderForm` and the answer is the whole form; put it inside `NoteField` and the
answer is one input.

## Hint 2

`useImperativeHandle` is how a parent reads a child's private state without
subscribing to it:

```tsx
const NoteField = forwardRef<NoteHandle, Props>(function NoteField({ label, defaultValue = "" }, ref) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(defaultValue);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ getValue: () => value }), [value]);
  // ...
});
```

The dependency array matters: without `[value]` the handle closes over the
first render's value forever.

## Hint 3

`React.memo` on `ExpensiveField` is necessary but not sufficient — memo compares
props, so a prop that is a new object or arrow function every render defeats it.
`renderCount` is a stable ref object, and `label` is a string, so this one is
fine. In a real form, watch for `onChange={() => ...}` inline handlers, which
are the usual reason memo appears to do nothing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the entire architecture of React Hook Form, compressed into one
exercise. Fields own their own values (or are uncontrolled), the form
subscribes to nothing by default, and reading happens at submit. That is why
typing in field 12 of a 30-field RHF form re-renders one component, while the
same form built on a single `formState` object re-renders thirty.

## Hint 2

Know the cost of the imperative escape hatch, because it is real. A value the
parent can only read imperatively is a value the parent cannot *react* to: no
live validation across fields, no dependent field, no summary that updates as
you type. If you need any of those, the field must be controlled from higher up,
and the right optimisation is memo plus a stable handler rather than isolation.

## Hint 3

`useImperativeHandle`'s dependency array is where this exercise is usually got
wrong, and the failure is silent: with `[]`, `getValue()` returns the initial
value forever, the gate's submit assertion fails, and nothing warns you. The
alternative that avoids the trap entirely is to keep the value in a ref and read
`inputRef.current.value` — genuinely uncontrolled — which is what you would do
if the field needed no local reaction at all.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — reset with a key, not an effect Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Export three components. ```tsx type Record = { id: string; title: string; notes: string }; export function EffectSyncedForm({ record }: { record: Record }): JSX.Element; export function EditForm({ record }: { record: Record }): JSX.Element; export function EditPanel({ record }: { record: Record }): JSX.Element; ``` - `EditForm` renders inputs labelled `Title` and `Notes`, seeded from `record` with `useState`, plus a `

` showing an internal `expanded` boolean that starts `false` and toggles with a `Toggle details` button. It does **not** watch `record` at all. - `EditPanel` renders ``. - `EffectSyncedForm` is the version you are diagnosing: same fields, but with `useEffect(() => { setTitle(record.title); setNotes(record.notes); }, [record])` and no key. The gate, for each: edits the title, toggles `expanded` to `true`, then re-renders with a **different record**, and asserts: - `EditPanel` shows the new record's title and notes, and `expanded` is back to `false` — a `key` resets *all* state, including state the author of the reset never thought about; - `EffectSyncedForm` shows the new title but `expanded` is **still true**, and there is a render in between where the *new* record is present but the *old* title is still displayed. The gate captures that intermediate render with a spy on the title input's value. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rb05_form_state_location ex5 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

State in React belongs to a *position in the tree*, identified by component
type and key. Two renders that put the same component at the same position
share state. `key` is how you say "this is a different thing now" — and React
then discards the old instance entirely, without you having to enumerate what
its state was.

## Hint 2

The enumeration problem is the whole argument. The effect resets `title` and
`notes` because those are the fields its author knew about. `expanded` was
added later by somebody else, and nothing connected the two. Every piece of
state added after the effect is written is a piece of state the effect forgets
to reset, and nothing warns you.

## Hint 3

The intermediate render is the second argument and it is subtler. An effect runs
*after* the commit, so there is a painted frame in which React has rendered
with the new `record` prop and the old state. On a fast machine that is one
frame; in a user's hands, clicking quickly through a list, it is a screenshot in
a bug report titled "sometimes it shows the wrong data".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Know the counter-argument, because `key` is not free. Remounting throws away
DOM state as well as React state: focus, selection, scroll position of anything
inside, and the identity of any element an animation was running on. If the
user is mid-edit when the key changes, their cursor is gone. That is a good
trade when the record genuinely changed, and a bad one if you key on something
that changes for unrelated reasons.

## Hint 2

There is a middle option worth knowing for when you want to reset *some* state
without a remount: adjust state during render.

```tsx
const [seenId, setSeenId] = useState(record.id);
if (seenId !== record.id) {
  setSeenId(record.id);
  setTitle(record.title);
}
```

React re-runs the component immediately, before touching the DOM, so there is
no intermediate paint and no remount. It is React's own documented answer, and
it costs an extra render pass rather than a commit.

## Hint 3

Ask *what identity means* for your data, because that determines the key. Keying
on `record.id` resets when you switch records — right. Keying on the whole
record object resets on every fetch that returns a new object with identical
contents — wrong, and a common accident when the record comes from a query that
does not do structural sharing. The key should be the thing whose change means
"this is a different subject".

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The failure of a stored flag is precise: type `a`, `setDirty(true)`; press
backspace, and nothing sets it back, because no handler knows that the field
just returned to its original value. The form is byte-identical to how it
started and the button says there are unsaved changes. Deriving cannot get this
wrong, because there is nothing to get out of sync.

## Hint 2

Two pieces of state, one derived value:

```tsx
const [baseline, setBaseline] = useState(initial);
const [values, setValues] = useState(initial);

const dirtyFields = (Object.keys(baseline) as (keyof T)[]).filter(
  (k) => values[k] !== baseline[k],
);
const isDirty = dirtyFields.length > 0;
```

`Object.keys(baseline)` rather than `Object.keys(values)` keeps the order
stable and stops an extra key in `values` from appearing as dirty.

## Hint 3

"After a save the new values become the baseline" is what `setBaseline(values)`
is for, and it is why the baseline is state rather than a prop or a ref. Doing
it this way means the form goes clean without a remount, so focus and the
user's scroll position survive — a `key`-based reset would have discarded both
after a successful save, which is a bad experience for a settings page.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Generalise the rule: anything that is a pure function of state you already have
should be computed, not stored. `isDirty`, `canSubmit`, `errors`, `isComplete`,
the filtered list, the total — all of them. Storing a derived value creates a
second source of truth and a synchronisation obligation, and the bug always
takes the same form: an edge case where somebody forgot to update the copy.

## Hint 2

Notice the cost you are accepting, and know its limits. Deriving means
recomputing on every render. Comparing ten string fields is free. Deep-comparing
a thousand-row array on every keystroke is not, and that is when `useMemo` — or
a smarter representation, like tracking which fields have been touched — becomes
appropriate. The order is: derive first, measure, memoise if measurement says
so.

## Hint 3

There is a design question hiding in `dirtyFields` order. Deriving it from
`Object.keys(baseline)` gives you the declaration order, which is stable and
matches the form's visual order if the object was written to match. Deriving it
from the order fields were *touched* would give a different, also-defensible
answer. Whichever you choose, make it deterministic — a `Set` iterated in
insertion order will surprise somebody eventually.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The rule: **never `Number(e.target.value)` in the handler.** Trace what happens
to each intermediate string a user passes through while typing `-1.5`:
`"-"` → `NaN`, `"-1"` → `-1`, `"-1."` → `-1` (the dot is deleted from under the
caret), `"-1.5"` → `-1.5`. Storing the number and rendering it back means two of
those four keystrokes fight the user.

## Hint 2

`problem` is a classification of the *string*, and separating "incomplete" from
"invalid" is what makes the UI civil. A user halfway through typing `1.5` has a
string that is not a number *yet*; telling them so is noise. A user who typed
`abc` has a string that will never be a number; telling them so is help. Only
the second gets a message.

## Hint 3

Normalising on `commit` (blur) rather than on change is the same decision as
ex1's caret problem, arrived at from the other direction. On blur the caret is
leaving, so rewriting `007` to `7` disturbs nothing. Do it on change and the
user typing `0`, `0`, `7` sees their first two keystrokes deleted as they make
them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider `<input type="number">` itself, because it has a reputation and the
reputation is earned. Its `value` is `""` for anything the browser considers
invalid — so a user who types `1e` sees the field's value read as empty, and
you cannot recover what they typed. Its spinner buttons change values on scroll
in some browsers. And localisation is inconsistent: a comma decimal separator
works in some locales and not others. `type="text"` with `inputMode="decimal"`
gives you the numeric keyboard on mobile and full control of the string, which
is why most design systems ship exactly that.

## Hint 2

Think about where the parsed value is actually needed and you will find it is
almost never during typing. It is needed at submit, in a total displayed
elsewhere, or in a validation that runs on blur. All three are boundaries. The
general shape — raw string in state, parsed value derived, normalisation at a
boundary — applies identically to dates, durations, currencies and any field
where the display form and the domain form differ.

## Hint 3

Be careful with `Number("")`, which is `0`, and `Number(" ")`, which is also
`0`. A naive `Number(raw)` treats an empty field as a zero, which silently
writes `0` into a nullable column. Check for emptiness before parsing, and
prefer an explicit regex test over trusting `Number` to reject what you think
it rejects — `Number("0x10")` is 16 and `Number("1e3")` is 1000, both of which
may or may not be what your field means.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start with the one that bites hardest: a checkbox's `value` property is the
string `"on"` unless you set `value` explicitly, and it stays `"on"` whether the
box is checked or not. `e.target.value` on a checkbox therefore gives you the
same answer forever, which is why "my checkbox does not update" is the single
most common form bug in React codebases.

## Hint 2

Narrow with `instanceof` rather than by reading `type` off a union, so
TypeScript follows you:

```tsx
if (el instanceof HTMLSelectElement) {
  return el.multiple ? Array.from(el.selectedOptions, (o) => o.value) : el.value;
}
if (el instanceof HTMLInputElement) {
  if (el.type === "checkbox") return el.checked;
  // ...
}
return el.value;
```

`el.selectedOptions` is an `HTMLCollection`, so `Array.from` — spread works too
but `Array.from` with a mapper is one pass.

## Hint 3

The radio rule exists because of how radio groups fire events. Changing the
selection fires `change` on the newly checked input only, so you receive one
event with `checked: true`. But a handler attached generically may also see
events from inputs that are *not* checked (a programmatic click, a form reset),
and returning `null` there would wipe the group. Guarding in `register` — ignore
a `null` from a radio — is the cheapest correct answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice the shape of the abstraction you are building. `register(name)` returning
props to spread is exactly React Hook Form's API, and the reason for that shape
is that it puts the control's own behaviour — its `name`, its handler, its ref —
in one place that the field can spread without knowing anything. A form library
is largely this function plus a subscription model.

## Hint 2

File inputs deserve a specific warning: they are the one control that **cannot**
be controlled. Setting `value` on a file input is a security restriction — a
page must not be able to make you upload a file you did not choose — so React
gives you a warning and the DOM ignores you. File inputs are always
uncontrolled, always read through `ref.current.files` or `FormData`, and always
reset by resetting the form.

## Hint 3

Think about the ordering hazard in a radio group specifically. If you store
`values["choice"]` and each radio's handler writes to it, then a group where two
inputs share a name works — but only because the browser guarantees one is
checked at a time. If two groups accidentally share a name, or a name is
misspelled on one member, the group silently splits and neither behaves. Reading
`name` from the control rather than from the closure is a small habit that makes
that class of bug visible.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Sort the six fields into the three categories from the briefing before writing
anything. Nothing needs `recipient` or `notes` during typing → uncontrolled.
`region` needs `country` during typing → `country` controlled. `weightKg` needs
a live warning → controlled, as a string. `express` is a checkbox that nothing
watches → could be either, and uncontrolled is simpler. That sorting *is* the
design.

## Hint 2

Requirement 5 is the `key` trick applied to a whole form:

```tsx
const [generation, setGeneration] = useState(0);
return <ShipmentFields key={generation} ... />;
```

with `Reset` doing `setGeneration(g => g + 1)`. That discards the controlled
state *and* remounts the uncontrolled inputs, which restores their
`defaultValue`s — the one mechanism that resets both kinds at once.

## Hint 3

Requirement 2's reset has an ordering subtlety. Setting `country` and `region`
in two separate `setState` calls is fine (React batches), but computing the new
region requires calling `regionsFor(nextCountry)` in the handler rather than
reading a memoised list from the previous render. Write it as one handler that
computes both values from the new country and sets both.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Requirement 6 is a small lesson in itself. You cannot disable a submit button
based on an uncontrolled field's value without either reading the DOM on every
keystroke (defeating the point) or making it controlled (also defeating the
point). So the honest design is: let them submit, validate at submit, report the
problem clearly. That is also better for accessibility — a disabled button gives
a screen reader user no explanation of *why* they cannot proceed.

## Hint 2

Watch the interaction between `key`-based reset and focus. Remounting moves
focus to `<body>`, which for a keyboard user means their position is gone. A
polished version moves focus to the first field after a reset, deliberately.
That is one `useEffect` with a ref, and noticing that it is needed is the mark
of somebody who has actually used a keyboard to fill in a form.

## Hint 3

The `initial` prop being `Partial` is deliberate and it is where the ex3 lesson
returns. Every access to it must have a defined fallback, and the place to do
that is once, at the top, producing a fully-populated defaults object that the
rest of the component uses. Sprinkling `?? ""` at each `defaultValue` works and
scatters the knowledge of what the defaults are across six places.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — a wizard whose steps do not lose their answers `review1/solution.tsx`. State location, from the direction of a multi-step form. ```tsx export type WizardData = Record; export function Wizard({ steps, onFinish, }: { steps: { id: string; title: string; fields: string[] }[]; onFinish: (data: WizardData) => void; }): JSX.Element; ``` - One step visible at a time. `

` with the step title, then one text input per field, labelled with the field name. - `Back` and `Next` buttons; `Next` becomes `Finish` on the last step and calls `onFinish` with **every** field from **every** step. - The fields are **uncontrolled** within a step — no `useState` per field — and read with `FormData` when the user leaves the step in either direction. - Going back must show exactly what the user typed. Going forward again must also show it. The accumulated answers live **above** the step component. - Each step is rendered with `key={step.id}` so that moving between steps remounts the fields and their `defaultValue`s apply. - `

Step {n} of {total}

`. - The first field of the newly shown step receives focus, so a keyboard user is not dropped at the top of the document after every transition. The gate fills step one, goes next, fills step two, goes back, asserts step one's values are intact, goes forward, asserts step two's are too, and finishes, asserting the merged object. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rb05_form_state_location review1 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The architecture in one sentence: **answers live above, fields live below, and
the transition is where they meet.** Every navigation — forward or back — is
"read the current step's DOM into the accumulator, then change the step". Both
directions do the same read, which is why `Back` losing data is such a common
bug: the author only wired the read into `Next`.

## Hint 2

`key={step.id}` is doing the same job as in ex5, and here it is essential
rather than tidy. Without it, moving from step one to step two reuses the same
input DOM nodes at the same positions; their `defaultValue`s were read at mount
and will not reapply, so step two's fields show step one's text.

## Hint 3

Focus management after the remount:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  formRef.current?.querySelector("input")?.focus();
}, [stepIndex]);
```

Without it, focus falls to `<body>` on every transition, and a keyboard user
has to tab from the top of the document to reach the first field of every step.
This is the single most common accessibility failure in multi-step forms.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice the division of responsibility, because it generalises. The step
component knows how to render fields and nothing about navigation. The wizard
knows about navigation and nothing about fields. The `FormData` read at the
boundary is the only place they touch. That is why adding a step is a data
change rather than a code change, and it is the shape you want any
data-driven form to have.

## Hint 2

Ask what would break if the fields were controlled and hoisted into the
wizard's state instead. It would work, and it would re-render every step's
worth of structure on every keystroke, and it would need an explicit reset when
steps change, and the `key` trick would no longer help because the values would
be props. The uncontrolled version is not merely faster; it is *smaller*,
because the browser is doing the remembering.

## Hint 3

There is a real limitation to name: with uncontrolled fields you cannot validate
live or enable `Next` conditionally without reading the DOM on every keystroke.
For a wizard that usually does not matter — validate at the transition, block it
if invalid, and report — but if a step genuinely needs live cross-field
validation, that step's fields should be controlled while the others stay as
they are. Mixed is normal; uniform is a preference, not a requirement.

lessons.title: V3·RB6 — Validation and accessible error reporting
lessons.summary: Most validation code is correct and unusable: it fires on the first keystroke, announces a red message no screen reader ever reads, and leaves focus at the bottom of a form the user cannot submit for reasons they cannot find. This sector separates the two halves — deciding what is wrong, and telling somebody — and gets the second one right, which is the half that is nearly always wrong.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RB6 — Validation and accessible error reporting

The previous sector was about where a form's values live. This one is about
what happens when they are wrong, and it is a bigger topic than it looks
because it is really two topics that get conflated.

**Deciding what is wrong** is a pure function: values in, errors out. It is
easy to test, easy to share with a server, and easy to get right. Almost nobody
gets it wrong.

**Telling somebody** is an interaction design problem with an accessibility
specification attached, and almost everybody gets it wrong. The failures are so
consistent that you can list them from memory: validation that fires on the
first keystroke, so the field is red before the user has finished typing their
own name; a message rendered in red text with no programmatic relationship to
the input, so a screen reader announces the field as if nothing were wrong; a
submit button that does nothing, with the reason four hundred pixels below the
fold; and focus left exactly where it was, so a keyboard user has no idea
anything happened at all.

## When to validate

The rule that has survived contact with real users is **validate late,
revalidate early**.

Do not validate a field the user has not finished with. "Finished" means
blurred, or the form was submitted. A required-field error on an empty box the
user has not yet reached is not information, it is an accusation.

Once a field *has* an error, switch to validating on every change. The user is
now actively fixing something, and waiting for another blur to tell them they
have fixed it is a needlessly long feedback loop. The error should disappear
the moment it stops being true.

That asymmetry is the whole rule and it maps to one piece of state per field:
`touched`. Untouched fields are silent. Touched fields validate live.

There is one common exception worth knowing: a field with an unambiguous format
where early feedback is genuinely helpful — a password strength meter, a
username availability check. Those are *hints*, not errors, and they should be
`aria-live="polite"` status text rather than `role="alert"`.

## How to tell somebody

There are exactly four things to wire up, and doing three of them is the same
as doing none.

**`aria-invalid`** on the control. This is what makes a screen reader say
"invalid entry" when the user focuses the field. Without it, the field sounds
completely normal no matter how red it is.

**`aria-describedby`** pointing at the error element's `id`. This is what makes
the *message* readable. `aria-describedby` is announced after the label and the
value, so the user hears "Email, edit text, not a valid address, invalid
entry". Note that `aria-describedby` accepts a space-separated list, so a field
with both a hint and an error references both.

**A stable `id`** on the error element. `useId` exists for this; hand-rolled
ids collide the moment a form is rendered twice on one page.

**Focus management on submit.** If a submit fails, focus must move — to the
error summary, or to the first invalid field. Otherwise a keyboard or screen
reader user presses the button, nothing appears to happen, and they have no way
to discover why.

## The error summary

For anything longer than three fields, the pattern that works — and the one the
UK Government Digital Service, the US Web Design System and the WCAG techniques
all converge on — is an error summary at the top of the form: a heading, a list
of every error, each item a link to the field it describes. On a failed submit,
focus moves to the summary. The user hears "There is a problem: 3 errors" and
can jump straight to any of them.

It costs about thirty lines and it is the single highest-value accessibility
improvement available to a form.

## Native validation, and why you will still write your own

The browser has a validation engine: `required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`,
`min`, `max`, `minlength`, and the `ValidityState` object describing exactly
which constraint failed. It is well-tested, localised, and free.

It is also unusable on its own for most applications, for three specific
reasons. The bubble UI cannot be styled, positioned or made to persist. The
messages cannot be customised without `setCustomValidity`, which then blocks
submission until you clear it. And `:invalid` matches from page load, so an
empty required field is styled as an error before the user has touched it —
which is why `:user-invalid` was added, and why you still need a fallback.

The productive position is to use the platform's *engine* — read `validity` to
find out what is wrong — and supply your own *messages and presentation*. That
is what exercise 4 builds.

## What you will build

Touched-based timing; the four attributes wired correctly; an error summary
with focus management; native `ValidityState` with custom messages; async
availability checking that is debounced, abortable and non-blocking;
cross-field rules and where their errors belong; a schema-shaped validator with
DOM-ordered results; and server errors mapped back onto fields. The challenge
is a complete accessible signup form built on `useActionState`; the review is
an audit — a form with six specific accessibility defects, to be found and
fixed.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3rb06_validation_a11y

## Notes

**Validation is a pure function; reporting is an interaction.** Keep them in
separate code. A `validate(values): Errors` function with no React in it can be
unit-tested exhaustively, shared with the server, and reasoned about. Mixing it
into components is what produces validation logic that only runs in one place
and disagrees with the server.

**`touched` is the timing mechanism.** One boolean per field, set on blur, and
set for all fields on submit. Errors are computed always and *displayed* only
for touched fields. That single indirection implements "validate late,
revalidate early" completely.

**`aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` are not optional decoration.** Colour is
not information: a red border conveys nothing to a screen reader, nothing to a
user with a colour vision deficiency, and nothing when the page is printed.
`aria-invalid="true"` is what makes assistive technology announce the state, and
`aria-describedby` is what makes the message reachable.

**`role="alert"` is an assertive live region.** It interrupts whatever the
screen reader is saying. That is right for a submit failure and wrong for a
per-keystroke message — an alert that fires on every character is unusable. Use
`role="alert"` for the summary and for errors that appear on submit; for
messages that update as the user types, use `aria-live="polite"` or nothing at
all, relying on `aria-describedby` to make the text available on focus.

**A live region must exist before its content.** Screen readers watch a live
region for mutations. If the region itself is inserted already containing text,
some readers do not announce it. Render the container unconditionally and put
only the text inside conditionally.

**Focus on failure, and put it somewhere useful.** Moving focus to the summary
container — which needs `tabIndex={-1}` to be focusable — is the standard,
because the user then hears the count and can navigate the list. Moving focus to
the first invalid field is also acceptable and loses the overview.

**Disabled submit buttons are an accessibility trap.** They cannot be focused,
so a keyboard user tabbing through the form never encounters them and gets no
explanation. Keep the button enabled, let the submit fail, and report.

## ex1 — touched

Tests timing. The classic mistake is validating in `onChange` from the first
keystroke, which paints an error on a field the user is halfway through filling
in. The model answer computes errors always and gates *display* on `touched`,
which also makes the revalidate-early half fall out for free.

## ex2 — the four attributes

Tests the wiring. The classic mistake is a red `<span>` with no relationship to
the input, which is invisible to assistive technology. The model answer uses
`useId` for the message id, `aria-describedby` to link it, `aria-invalid` to
announce the state, and joins multiple ids when a hint is present too.

## ex3 — the summary

Tests focus management. The classic mistake is rendering a summary and never
moving focus to it, so the user who most needs it never learns it exists. The
model answer focuses a `tabIndex={-1}` container on each failed submit — keyed
on a submit counter, so a second identical failure still moves focus.

## ex4 — native validity, custom messages

Tests the platform. The classic mistake is either ignoring `ValidityState`
entirely or calling `setCustomValidity` and forgetting to clear it, which blocks
submission forever. The model answer reads the validity flags to *choose* a
message and keeps presentation entirely in React, with `noValidate` on the form
so the browser's bubbles never appear.

## ex5 — async availability

Tests non-blocking validation. The classic mistake is awaiting the check inside
submit, which makes the user wait for a request whose answer they mostly know.
The model answer debounces, aborts superseded checks, exposes the result as a
status rather than an error, and does not gate submission on it — the server is
the authority.

## ex6 — cross-field rules

Tests error placement. The classic mistake is attaching a "passwords do not
match" error to both fields, so the user hears it twice and fixing one does not
clear the other. The model answer attaches it to the second field — the one the
user can act on — and clears it when either changes.

## ex7 — a schema, in DOM order

Tests ordering. The classic mistake is returning errors in object-key order,
so the summary lists them in an order unrelated to the form, and "go to the
first error" jumps to the middle. The model answer orders results by the field
order the schema declares, which is the form's order.

## ex8 — server errors

Tests the round trip. The classic mistake is showing the server's error as a
single string at the top, discarding the per-field information a 422 carries.
The model answer maps the response's field errors onto the fields, keeps
unmapped ones as a form-level error, and moves focus to the first affected
field.

## Further reading

- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: form instructions](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/)
- [WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html)
- [MDN: `ValidityState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ValidityState)
- [MDN: `aria-describedby`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby)
- [MDN: `:user-invalid`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:user-invalid)
- [GOV.UK Design System: error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
