exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do not store errors in state. Compute them on every render from the current
values, and keep a separate piece of state for *whether to show* each one:

```tsx
const errors = validate(values);
const [touched, setTouched] = useState<Partial<Record<keyof Values, boolean>>>({});
const show = (field: keyof Values) => Boolean(touched[field] && errors[field]);
```

Stored errors can disagree with the values they describe; derived ones cannot.

## Hint 2

That one indirection gives you both halves of the rule and it is worth checking
why. An untouched field: `touched.email` is false, so nothing shows — validate
late. A touched field: `errors` is recomputed on every keystroke and `show`
reads it fresh, so the message disappears the moment the value becomes
valid — revalidate early. No extra code for the second half at all.

## Hint 3

Submit is "touch everything":

```tsx
setTouched({ email: true, password: true });
if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) return;
onSubmit(values);
```

Note the guard reads `errors`, which was computed during this render from the
current values — not from a stale copy, and not from something the submit
handler has to recompute.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what an early error actually communicates. The user has typed `a`
of `ada@example.com`, and the form says "Enter a valid email address". That is
not feedback, it is a system telling somebody they are wrong while they are
mid-sentence. Every user learns to ignore it, which means when a *real* error
appears they ignore that too.

## Hint 2

There is one legitimate exception and it is worth being able to name: live
*hints* rather than live *errors*. A password strength meter, a character
counter, a username availability indicator — these update as you type and are
genuinely useful because they are not accusations. They should be
`aria-live="polite"` status text, not `role="alert"`, and they should not gate
submission.

## Hint 3

Note what the "never disabled" requirement buys. A disabled submit button is
removed from the tab order entirely, so a keyboard user never reaches it and
never learns it exists; and there is no standard way to explain *why* it is
disabled. Letting the submit fail and reporting the reason is strictly more
informative. The general principle: prefer explaining a failure over preventing
an attempt.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Think about what a screen reader announces when a user tabs into the field, in
order: the accessible name from the label, the role, the value, the
*description* from `aria-describedby`, and the *state* from `aria-invalid`. Each
attribute supplies exactly one of those, and a missing one means that part is
simply not spoken. A red border supplies none of them.

## Hint 2

The describedby list is the fiddly part:

```tsx
const describedBy = [hint ? hintId : null, error ? errorId : null]
  .filter(Boolean)
  .join(" ") || undefined;
```

`|| undefined` matters: `aria-describedby=""` is an empty reference that some
implementations treat as an error, so the attribute should be absent rather
than empty.

## Hint 3

`useId` returns one opaque string per component instance; derive the rest from
it (`${id}-error`, `${id}-hint`). Do not call `useId` three times — it works,
but the ids are then unrelated and harder to debug in the accessibility
inspector. And never build ids from the label text: two fields labelled
`Amount` in different sections would collide silently.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Test the claim rather than trusting it. Open any form you have written, focus a
field with a visible error, and read the accessibility tree in devtools. If the
"description" row is empty, the error message you can see is invisible to
assistive technology — and that is the default outcome, because nothing in JSX
connects a `<span>` to an `<input>` automatically.

## Hint 2

`aria-invalid` has values beyond `"true"` and `"false"` — `"grammar"` and
`"spelling"` — which exist for editors and are worth knowing about mostly so
you recognise them. The reason to omit the attribute rather than set `"false"`
is that absence and `"false"` are computed identically, and a DOM full of
`aria-invalid="false"` is noise that makes the real ones harder to spot when
auditing.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens when the error appears while focus is *already* inside
the field. `aria-describedby` is read when the field receives focus, so a
description that appears afterwards is not announced — the user is sitting in a
field that has silently become invalid. That is the case a polite live region
around the error text solves, and it is why some design systems wrap the error
element in `aria-live="polite"` as well as referencing it. Know the gap; do not
paper over it with `role="alert"`.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The requirement "including two identical failures in a row" is what forces the
design. An effect keyed on `errors` or on a `hasErrors` boolean does not re-run
when the second submit produces the same errors — nothing changed. Key it on a
counter that increments on every submit attempt, and the effect fires every
time.

```tsx
const [attempt, setAttempt] = useState(0);
useEffect(() => {
  if (attempt > 0 && errorList.length > 0) summaryRef.current?.focus();
}, [attempt]);
```

## Hint 2

`tabIndex={-1}` makes a `<div>` programmatically focusable without adding it to
the tab order — exactly what you want for a container the user should land on
after an action but should not tab into during normal navigation. Without it,
`.focus()` on a `<div>` silently does nothing.

## Hint 3

DOM order is the requirement people skip. `Object.entries(errors)` gives you
insertion order, which is whatever order the validator happened to assign in —
often unrelated to the form. Iterate `fields` and pick out the ones that have
errors, and the list matches the form by construction:

```tsx
const errorList = fields
  .filter((f) => errors[f.name])
  .map((f) => ({ ...f, message: errors[f.name] }));
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand the interaction you are fixing, because it is the most common
accessibility failure in web forms. A screen-reader user fills in a long form,
presses Submit, and... nothing. No announcement, no movement, no change they can
perceive. The errors are inline, four hundred pixels away, in a part of the
document their virtual cursor is not near. From their point of view the button
is broken.

## Hint 2

The summary pattern was arrived at independently by the UK Government Digital
Service, the US Web Design System and the W3C's form tutorials — all after
usability testing with disabled users. The specific findings it encodes: a
count up front ("There is a problem: 3 errors") orients the user; links let
them jump rather than traverse; focusing the container guarantees the
announcement rather than depending on live-region quirks; and DOM order means
"the first error" means the same thing to everyone.

## Hint 3

Note that `role="alert"` on the summary is doing a *second*, redundant job here
and that redundancy is deliberate. Moving focus announces the container's
contents in most screen readers; the alert role covers the ones where it does
not, and the case where the summary changes while focus is already inside it.
Belt and braces is acceptable for a region that appears at most once per submit;
it would not be acceptable on something that updates as the user types.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`noValidate` is the key that unlocks this. It turns off two things — the
browser's bubble UI and its blocking of submission — while leaving `validity`
fully populated on every element. So you keep the engine (eight named booleans,
localised, well-tested) and take over the presentation entirely.

## Hint 2

Order the checks from most specific to least, because more than one flag can be
true at once. An empty `required` `type="email"` field has `valueMissing` true;
whether `typeMismatch` is also true varies. Checking `valueMissing` first means
"you left it blank" wins over "that is not an email address", which is the more
useful message.

## Hint 3

Walking the form's controls:

```tsx
const controls = Array.from(form.elements).filter(
  (el): el is HTMLInputElement => el instanceof HTMLInputElement,
);
```

`form.elements` is an `HTMLFormControlsCollection` and includes buttons, so the
`instanceof` narrow does double duty — it filters and it gives TypeScript the
`validity` property.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Know why `setCustomValidity` is forbidden here, because it is the obvious API
and it is a trap. Calling it makes the control permanently invalid — `customError`
stays true — until you call it again with `""`. Every code path that changes the
value must remember to clear it, and forgetting one produces a form that can
never be submitted, whose symptom is a button that silently does nothing. Half
the "my form won't submit" questions online are this.

## Hint 2

Consider the CSS side, which this exercise does not build but which every real
form needs. `input:invalid` matches from page load, so an empty `required`
field is styled as an error before the user has seen it — the CSS equivalent of
validating on the first keystroke. `:user-invalid` fixes it by matching only
after interaction, and it is the CSS spelling of the same `touched` concept from
ex1. Support is good in current browsers, which is why most design systems
still drive styling from their own state attribute.

## Hint 3

The fallback to `el.validationMessage` is worth defending in an interview. It
gives you the browser's own message — correctly localised into the user's
language, which your hard-coded English strings are not — for any constraint you
have not written a message for. That means a new constraint added to the markup
degrades to something sensible rather than to `null`. Graceful degradation, at
the cost of one line.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three separate mechanisms, all from earlier sectors, in one effect: a debounce
timer whose cleanup cancels it, an `AbortController` whose cleanup aborts it,
and a guard on the answer. Because both cleanups belong to the same effect run,
one `return` handles both:

```tsx
return () => { clearTimeout(timer); controller.abort(); };
```

## Hint 2

The politeness level is the accessibility content of this exercise. A status
that changes as the user types must be `aria-live="polite"` — it waits for a
pause. `role="alert"` is assertive and interrupts, so with an alert the screen
reader would talk over the user on every keystroke, and they would be unable to
hear what they are typing.

## Hint 3

"The region still renders" when empty is not a detail. Screen readers watch a
live region for *mutations*, so a region inserted already containing text may
not be announced at all — from the reader's point of view a new node appeared
rather than an existing region changing. Render the container unconditionally
and put only the text inside it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be clear about what this check is *for*. It is not validation; it is a
courtesy that saves the user a round trip. Treating it as validation leads
directly to the two failures: blocking submission on it (so a network hiccup
locks somebody out of signing up) and rendering it as an error (so a perfectly
reasonable username is announced as a problem before the user has finished
typing it).

## Hint 2

Note the race that a naive version has even with a debounce. Debouncing reduces
requests but does not order the answers: if the user pauses, types more, and
pauses again, two requests exist and the first can answer last. That is sector
one's race in a new costume, and the abort is what actually fixes it — the
debounce only makes it rarer, which is worse than not fixing it because the bug
becomes intermittent.

## Hint 3

Think about the `unknown` state and why it deserves a name. Collapsing a failed
check into `idle` loses the distinction between "we have not asked" and "we
asked and could not find out", and a UI that wants to say "we could not check
this right now" needs the second. Naming states you might not render yet is
cheap; discovering you cannot express one after the fact is not.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — rules that span two fields

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Export a validator and a form.

```tsx
export type TripValues = {
  password: string;
  confirm: string;
  start: string;   // yyyy-mm-dd
  end: string;
};

export function validateTrip(values: TripValues): Partial<Record<keyof TripValues, string>>;

export function TripForm({ onSubmit }: { onSubmit: (v: TripValues) => void }): JSX.Element;
```

Single-field rules:

- `password` shorter than 12 → `Use at least 12 characters`;
- `start` empty → `Enter a start date`; `end` empty → `Enter an end date`.

Cross-field rules, and **where they go** is the exercise:

- `confirm !== password` → the error goes on **`confirm` only**, reading
  `Passwords do not match`. Never on `password`.
- `end` earlier than `start` → the error goes on **`end` only**, reading
  `End date must be after the start date`.
- A cross-field error is **suppressed** while the field it depends on has its
  own error: if `password` is too short, `confirm` shows nothing, because
  telling somebody their confirmation does not match a password that is itself
  invalid is noise.

`TripForm` uses the ex1 timing rule (touched + submit) and the ex2 wiring, and
additionally: **a cross-field error clears when either of its two fields
changes**, not only the one it is attached to. The gate fixes the mismatch by
editing `password` and asserts the error on `confirm` disappears.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb06_validation_a11y ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The placement rule in one sentence: **attach the error to the input the user
will change to fix it.** For a confirmation field that is the confirmation, not
the original. For a date range it is the end date. Attaching it to both means
the user hears it twice and fixing one leaves the other stale.

## Hint 2

The suppression rule falls out of ordering the checks in the validator:

```tsx
if (values.password.length < 12) errors.password = "Use at least 12 characters";
else if (values.confirm !== values.password) errors.confirm = "Passwords do not match";
```

The `else` is doing real work — while the password itself is invalid, "does not
match" is noise about a value that is about to change anyway.

## Hint 3

"Clears when either field changes" is free if you derive errors rather than
storing them, which is the whole point of ex1's design: `validateTrip` runs on
every render with the current values, so editing `password` recomputes
`confirm`'s error immediately. If you had stored errors per field and cleared
them in each field's own handler, you would need explicit cross-clearing — and
that is exactly the bug the derived approach prevents.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about the *touched* interaction with cross-field errors, which is subtler
than it looks. If the user fills `password`, then `confirm`, and they do not
match, the error should appear when they blur `confirm` — which works. But if
they then go back and edit `password`, `confirm` is still touched, so the error
updates live. That is the behaviour you want, and it happens automatically with
derived errors. With stored errors you would have to notice and implement it.

## Hint 2

Date comparison as strings is safe here specifically because the format is
`yyyy-mm-dd`, which sorts lexicographically in the same order as
chronologically. That is a genuine property of ISO 8601 and a good reason to
prefer that format for stored dates. The moment the format changes, string
comparison silently becomes wrong — so it deserves a comment saying why it
works.

## Hint 3

Consider the wider family of cross-field rules and how they generalise:
"either email or phone is required" (the error belongs on... both? a fieldset?),
"total must not exceed budget" (on the field being edited), "at least one option
selected" (on the group). The ones with no single obvious owner belong on a
`<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` and an error inside it, which is the accessible
way to attach a message to a group rather than to a control.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reason the schema is an array rather than an object is the whole point of
the exercise. An object's key order is insertion order, which is whatever the
author happened to type, and it drifts as fields are added. An array is
explicitly ordered, and that order is the form's — which is what the summary
needs and what "jump to the first error" depends on.

## Hint 2

First failure wins, per field:

```tsx
for (const { field, label, rules } of schema) {
  const value = values[field] ?? "";
  const failed = rules.find((rule) => !safeTest(rule, value, values));
  if (!failed) continue;
  byField[field] = failed.message;
  issues.push({ field, label, message: failed.message });
}
```

Because you iterate `schema`, `issues` is in schema order by construction — no
sorting step, nothing to get wrong later.

## Hint 3

Rule order within a field matters as much as field order. `[required(...),
minLength(8)]` on an empty field says "required"; the reverse says "use at
least 8 characters", which is technically true and unhelpful. Cheap rules and
fundamental ones go first, expensive and specific ones after.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that this is a small validation library and that the design decisions in
it are the same ones Zod, Yup and Valibot make. Rules as composable predicates
with messages; a schema as an ordered description; a result that carries both a
lookup and a list. The reason to build one is that once you have, the libraries
stop looking like magic and start looking like decisions you can evaluate.

## Hint 2

The "first failure wins" choice deserves defending because some libraries
collect all failures. Both are defensible; per-field-single-message is better
for a form UI because it fits in the space beside the field, is one thing to
fix, and is what an error summary can list one line per field. Collecting all
of them is better for an API response, where the caller is a program that can
handle a list.

## Hint 3

The try/catch around a rule's `test` is not paranoia. A rule that reads
`all.otherField.trim()` throws when the other field is absent, and without the
guard one missing key in a partially-filled form takes down the entire
validation — meaning the form cannot be submitted and cannot say why. Failing
the rule instead degrades to a message that is at worst slightly wrong.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The unknown-field bucket is the requirement people skip and it matters. A
server that validates a field your form does not render — because the form is
older than the API, or because the field is derived — must not produce an error
that goes nowhere. Silently dropping it means the user sees a form that failed
to save with no explanation at all.

## Hint 2

Focus in `fields` order, not in the server's order:

```tsx
const first = fields.find((f) => byField[f.name]);
if (first) document.getElementById(idFor(first.name))?.focus();
```

The server's object-key order is an implementation detail of its serialiser.
"First error" must mean first *on screen*, or the focus lands somewhere the user
does not expect.

## Hint 3

Clearing on change is the same "revalidate early" instinct from ex1, applied to
errors that came from elsewhere. The server said the email was already
registered; the user is now typing a different one; keeping the message is
actively wrong. Clear the server error for that field in its `onChange` and let
the next submit produce a fresh answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be clear on why the client validates at all if the server is the authority.
Client validation is a *user experience* feature: it catches the easy problems
in 0ms instead of 300ms and without a network round trip. It is never a
security boundary — the server must check everything regardless — and it should
never be *stricter* than the server, because then it rejects things the system
would have accepted.

## Hint 2

The ideal is one schema executed in both places, and it is genuinely achievable
in a TypeScript monorepo with a shared validation library. The payoff is that
the rules cannot drift and the messages are identical, so a user never sees the
client say one thing and the server another. Where it is not achievable, the
minimum contract worth insisting on is that the server's errors are **per
field**: a 422 that says "invalid" and nothing else forces the client to guess.

## Hint 3

Watch a subtle ordering problem in the focus move. If you call `.focus()` in
the same tick as `setState`, the error elements may not be in the DOM yet and
the field's `aria-describedby` will point at nothing at the moment focus lands —
so the screen reader announces the field without its error. Moving focus in an
effect that runs after the state has committed avoids it, which is the same
reason ex3's summary focus lives in an effect.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Let the action be the single decision point. It receives `FormData`, so it can
read every field without any per-field state; it runs the schema; it either
returns errors or calls the API and returns the result of that. Everything the
component renders comes out of the returned state. That is the discipline that
keeps error and success from disagreeing.

## Hint 2

Requirement 5's "every failed attempt" needs the counter, and here it lives in
the returned state rather than in a separate `useState` — which is neater,
because the action is the only thing that knows an attempt happened:

```tsx
return { byField, formError, attempt: previous.attempt + 1, values };
```

Then `useEffect(..., [state.attempt])` focuses the summary.

## Hint 3

Requirement 6 is why `values` is in the state at all. React resets an
uncontrolled form after an action returns, so without carrying the submitted
values back and feeding them to `defaultValue`, a failed submit would clear
everything the user typed — the single most infuriating form bug there is.
Build `values` from the same `FormData` the validation read.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in layers and check each one with a screen reader or the accessibility
inspector before adding the next: labels and ids first, then `aria-invalid` and
`aria-describedby`, then the summary, then focus, then the live region. Each
layer is independently verifiable, and stacking them without checking is how
you end up with a form that has every attribute and still announces nothing —
usually because one id is wrong.

## Hint 2

Watch the interaction between the summary's `role="alert"` and the live region
in requirement 8. Two assertive regions competing on the same submit is a
genuine problem: the screen reader announces one and may drop the other. The
resolution is that the summary is assertive (it appears only on failure and the
user must act) and the outcome region is polite (it reports a completed
action). Do not make both assertive because it seems safer.

## Hint 3

Requirement 7's "never disabled" combines with `isPending` in a way worth
thinking about: the button stays enabled while the request is in flight, so a
user can click twice. `useActionState` queues submissions rather than racing
them, so the second one runs after the first — which is usually fine and
occasionally creates two accounts. If double submission is genuinely dangerous,
the answer is an idempotency key from the optimistic-updates sector, not a
disabled button.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — the audit

`review1/solution.tsx`. A working form with six specific accessibility
defects. It looks correct, it validates correctly, and it is unusable with a
screen reader or a keyboard.

```tsx
export function DonationForm({ onSubmit }: { onSubmit: (v: Values) => void }): JSX.Element;
```

The stub contains all six. Find and fix each one:

1. **No label association.** The field text sits in a `<span>` beside the
   input. Give each input a real `<label htmlFor>` with an `id` from `useId`.
2. **A radio group with no grouping.** Three "Amount" radios with individual
   labels and nothing tying them together. Wrap them in a `<fieldset>` with a
   `<legend>` reading `Amount`, which is how a group gets an accessible name.
3. **Colour as the only signal.** Errors are a red `<span>` with no `id`, no
   `aria-invalid`, no `aria-describedby`. Wire all three.
4. **An error message announced on every keystroke.** The inline error is
   inside `role="alert"`. Change it: the error text is linked with
   `aria-describedby` and is **not** a live region; only the submit-time
   summary is `role="alert"`.
5. **`required` used as the only signal.** The mandatory fields are marked with
   a red asterisk in a `<span>`. Add `required` to the input **and** put the
   word `(required)` inside the `<label>` text, so it is announced.
6. **A disabled submit button.** It is `disabled` until the form is valid.
   Enable it always, validate on submit, and move focus to the first invalid
   field.

The gate asserts each fix specifically: accessible names for every control, the
group's accessible name, `aria-invalid`/`aria-describedby` on an invalid field,
that no `role="alert"` exists on an inline error, that the label text contains
`required`, and that the submit button is focusable.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb06_validation_a11y review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Work with the accessibility tree open rather than by reading code. For each
control ask: does it have a name? a description? a state? For the group ask:
does it have a name? Every one of the six defects shows up as a missing row in
that inspector, which is much faster than reasoning about attributes.

## Hint 2

Defect 2 is the one people have not met. A radio group's accessible name comes
from the `<fieldset>`'s `<legend>` — there is no other mechanism. Without it, a
screen reader announces "Amount 25, radio button, 1 of 3" with no indication of
what the group is *for*; the user hears three unrelated radios. `role="radiogroup"`
with `aria-labelledby` is the ARIA equivalent, but the native elements are
better supported and need no JavaScript.

## Hint 3

Defect 5 has a subtlety. `required` on the input makes assistive technology
announce "required", which handles most cases — but the visible asterisk is
still meaningless to a sighted user who does not know the convention, and some
older combinations do not announce the attribute. Putting the word in the label
is belt and braces, is visible to everyone, and costs nothing. The general
rule: never encode meaning in a symbol or a colour alone.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that all six defects come from the same underlying assumption: that
appearance is communication. A red border, a red asterisk, a red message, a
greyed-out button — each of them conveys the intended meaning to a sighted user
with good colour vision and nothing at all to anybody else. The fix in every
case is to say the thing programmatically as well as visually.

## Hint 2

Defect 4 is the interesting one because it is an *over*-correction. Somebody
knew about live regions and applied one to the wrong thing. An assertive region
on a message that updates per keystroke means the reader interrupts itself
constantly and the user cannot hear what they are typing. The rule that keeps it
straight: **announce state changes that happen to the user; describe state the
user can query.** A submit failure happened to them; a field's current error is
something they can ask about by focusing it.

## Hint 3

Defect 6 is worth having an argument about, because designers request disabled
buttons constantly. The counter-argument, in order: it leaves the tab order, so
a keyboard user never finds it; there is no standard way to explain why it is
disabled; and the resulting experience — a complete-looking form with an inert
button — reads as a broken site rather than as user error. Enabling it and
explaining the failure is strictly more informative and no harder to build.

lessons.title: V3·RB7 — Large lists: pagination, infinite scroll, virtualization
lessons.summary: A list stops being a list somewhere around a thousand rows: the DOM gets heavy, the scrollbar starts lying, and every naive fix introduces a new bug — duplicate rows from a shifting cursor, a sentinel that fires twice, a focused row that unmounts under the user. This sector builds all three strategies and is honest about what each one costs.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RB7 — Large lists: pagination, infinite scroll, virtualization

There are three strategies for a list that is too big, they solve different
problems, and choosing the wrong one is a common and expensive mistake.

**Pagination** limits what you fetch and what you render. It is the only one of
the three that is simple, and it has a property the others lack: every position
in the data is addressable. Page 4 of the results is a URL you can share, come
back to, and open in a new tab. It is also the only strategy where "how many
are there?" has an answer on screen.

**Infinite scroll** limits what you fetch but not what you render. After twenty
"load more"s you have four hundred rows in the DOM, and the page is slower than
when you started. It solves a network problem and creates a rendering one. It
also breaks the footer, breaks the back button unless you work at it, and
cannot address a position.

**Virtualization** limits what you render but not what you fetch. It is the
only one that makes a 50,000-row list feel like a 20-row one — because as far
as the DOM is concerned it *is* a 20-row list. It costs you find-in-page,
native scroll anchoring, and a great deal of care about measurement.

Real applications combine them. A feed is infinite scroll plus virtualization.
A data table is pagination plus virtualization within the page. A search result
is pagination, because the user needs to be able to say "the third page".

## What actually goes wrong

**The shifting cursor.** Offset pagination — `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40` — is
computed against the data as it is right now. If a row is inserted before your
offset between page two and page three, one row shifts from page three into
page two's territory: the user sees it twice. If a row is deleted, one is
skipped entirely. On a busy dataset this happens constantly and is nearly
impossible to reproduce. Cursor pagination — "give me twenty after this
record" — is stable under insertion, and is why every serious API has moved to
it.

**The sentinel that fires twice.** An `IntersectionObserver` on a div at the
bottom of the list fires when it becomes visible. It also fires when the list
grows and the sentinel is *still* visible, which happens whenever the new page
does not fill the viewport. Without a guard you send the next request
immediately, and the one after that, until you run out of data — the whole
dataset loaded in one burst, which is the opposite of what infinite scroll is
for.

**The unmounted focus.** In a virtualized list, the row the user is on can
scroll out of the rendered window and be removed from the DOM. Focus falls to
`<body>`, keyboard navigation dies, and the screen reader loses its place. This
is the single hardest problem in virtualization and the reason most virtualized
tables are inaccessible.

**The measurement lie.** Fixed-height windowing is arithmetic and it works.
Variable-height windowing needs to know each row's height *before* it renders,
which it cannot, so it guesses, renders, measures, and corrects — and every
correction changes the scroll offset of everything below, which can move the
content under the user's cursor mid-read.

## The scroll anchoring problem

Prepending items to a list — new messages arriving above, a "load older" at the
top — moves everything down, so the browser's scroll position now points at
different content. The user is reading paragraph five and suddenly they are
looking at paragraph two.

Browsers implement CSS scroll anchoring to fix this automatically, and it works
well enough that most people never learn it exists — until they turn it off, or
until they virtualize (which defeats it, because the anchor element gets
unmounted). The manual fix is to record `scrollHeight` before the insertion and
add the difference to `scrollTop` after, in a layout effect so it happens before
paint.

## Accessibility, which is where infinite scroll usually fails

Three specific failures, all avoidable. A scroll-triggered load with no button
cannot be triggered by a keyboard user at all — they tab to the last row and
there is nothing after it. A list that grows silently gives a screen reader user
no indication that anything happened. And a `role="feed"` — the ARIA pattern
designed for exactly this — is almost never used, so assistive technology has no
way to know the list is incrementally loaded.

The fixes are: always ship a real `Load more` button (the observer is an
enhancement, not the mechanism), announce the new count politely, and set
`aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset` so the user knows where they are in a list whose
DOM does not contain all of it.

## What you will build

Offset pagination with a page window; cursor pagination with deduplication; an
`IntersectionObserver` sentinel with a correct lifecycle; the accessible
version of infinite scroll; fixed-height windowing from scratch; variable-height
windowing with a measurement cache; scroll restoration and prepend anchoring;
and keyboard navigation over a windowed list. The challenge combines
virtualization with infinite loading and sticky headers; the review is a
performance bug hunt on a list that stutters.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3rb07_large_lists

## Notes

**Offset pagination is unstable; cursor pagination is not.** `OFFSET 40` means
"skip the first forty rows *of the current ordering, right now*". Insert a row
above and everything shifts. A cursor — "after id X, ordered by (created_at,
id)" — describes a position in the data rather than a count, so insertions
elsewhere do not move it. The tie-breaker in the sort key matters: a cursor on a
non-unique column can skip or repeat rows with equal values.

**Deduplicate anyway.** Even with cursors, a row can appear twice if it is
updated in a way that changes its sort position. A `Set` of seen ids on append
costs almost nothing and turns a visible bug into a non-event.

**`IntersectionObserver` needs three things done right.** Observe the sentinel
node, not a ref that may be null on first render; re-observe when the node
changes; and disconnect in cleanup. The callback fires on *changes* in
intersection, including the initial observation — so it fires once immediately
for an already-visible sentinel, which is usually what you want and always
surprises people.

**The guard is not the same as the disabled attribute.** A `Load more` that is
disabled while loading still gets called by the observer, because the observer
does not consult the DOM. Guard inside the handler.

**Windowing is four numbers.** `scrollTop`, row height, viewport height,
overscan. From those: `start = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - overscan`,
`end = start + ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight) + 2 * overscan`. The container
gets `height: total * rowHeight` so the scrollbar is honest, and the rendered
rows get `transform: translateY(start * rowHeight)` — `transform` rather than
`top`, because it does not trigger layout.

**Overscan is not an optimisation, it is a correctness measure for
scrolling.** Without it, fast scrolling shows blank space where rows have not
been rendered yet. Two to five rows is usually enough.

**Variable heights need estimate, measure, correct.** Keep a cache of measured
heights and a prefix-sum of offsets. Render with estimates for unmeasured rows,
measure with a `ResizeObserver`, and rebuild the offsets when a measurement
differs from the estimate. Rebuilding shifts everything below, which is why
measurement should happen as early as possible and why the estimate should be
close.

**Virtualization breaks find-in-page.** Ctrl+F searches the DOM, and the DOM
does not contain the rows that are not rendered. There is no workaround; it is a
cost you accept. Mention it before a designer discovers it.

## ex1 — offset pagination

Tests the arithmetic and the edges. The classic mistake is a page control that
lets the user reach page 0 or page `total + 1`, and a page count computed with
`total / size` rather than `ceil`. The model answer derives everything from
`total` and `size`, clamps, and renders a windowed range of page numbers rather
than 400 buttons.

## ex2 — cursors and duplicates

Tests append correctness. The classic mistake is a blind `[...prev, ...page]`,
which duplicates a row whenever the underlying data shifts. The model answer
filters against a `Set` built from the current list inside the updater, so it
compares against the present rather than against a captured past.

## ex3 — the sentinel

Tests observer lifecycle. The classic mistake is a `useEffect` with `[]` deps
that observes `ref.current` before it exists, so nothing ever fires. The model
answer uses a callback ref so the observer attaches when the node arrives, and
guards against re-entry when the sentinel stays visible after a load.

## ex4 — accessible infinite scroll

Tests whether the feature works without a mouse. The classic mistake is a
scroll-only trigger, which a keyboard user cannot reach. The model answer has a
real button as the mechanism and the observer as an enhancement, announces the
count politely, and sets `aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset`.

## ex5 — fixed-height windowing

Tests the arithmetic. The classic mistake is rendering the visible slice
without a spacer, so the scrollbar reflects twenty rows instead of fifty
thousand. The model answer sizes an inner element to the full height and
translates the window into place.

## ex6 — variable heights

Tests measurement. The classic mistake is measuring in `useEffect` after paint,
which produces a visible jump on every scroll. The model answer measures with a
`ResizeObserver`, keeps a prefix-sum for offsets, and only rebuilds from the
first changed index.

## ex7 — anchoring and restoration

Tests scroll position. The classic mistake is restoring scroll in an effect
after the rows render, which paints at the top first. The model answer adjusts
`scrollTop` in a layout effect using the `scrollHeight` delta, so nothing moves
visibly.

## ex8 — keyboard over a window

Tests the hardest part. The classic mistake is `tabIndex={0}` on every row,
which makes a 50,000-row list require 50,000 tabs. The model answer uses roving
tabindex with one focusable row, moves focus with arrow keys, scrolls the target
into the window *before* focusing it, and handles the case where the focused row
has been unmounted.

## Further reading

- [MDN: `IntersectionObserver`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API)
- [MDN: `ResizeObserver`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ResizeObserver)
- [MDN: CSS scroll anchoring](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/overflow-anchor)
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: feed pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/feed/)
- [`content-visibility`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/content-visibility)

# V3·RB7 — Large lists: pagination, infinite scroll, virtualization The archive version: the three strategies, the arithmetic, the traps, the interview answer and a question bank. ## 1. Choosing a strategy | | fetch | render | addressable | total known | a11y | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | pagination | bounded | bounded | yes | yes | easy | | infinite scroll | bounded | **unbounded** | no | no | hard | | virtualization | **unbounded** | bounded | yes | yes | hard | Read the two bold cells as the costs. Infinite scroll leaves the DOM growing; virtualization leaves the fetch unsolved. Combining them solves both and inherits both accessibility problems. The decision heuristic that holds up: if the user might want to *return to a position*, paginate. If the content is a stream they consume forwards, infinite scroll. If the list is long enough that the DOM is the bottleneck, virtualize — in addition to, not instead of, one of the other two. ## 2. Offset versus cursor ```sql -- Offset: unstable under concurrent writes. SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40; -- Cursor: stable, and uses the index. SELECT * FROM posts WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20; ``` The offset version has two problems. Correctness: a row inserted above the offset shifts everything, so page three repeats a row from page two. And performance: the database must produce and discard 40 rows — at `OFFSET 100000` it discards a hundred thousand, on every request. The cursor version needs a **unique** sort key. `ORDER BY created_at` alone cannot distinguish rows with identical timestamps, so the cursor can skip or repeat them; appending `id` makes the ordering total. Client-side, cursors mean you cannot jump to page 7, cannot show "page 3 of 40", and cannot go backwards without a separate reverse cursor. That is the trade. ## 3. Deduplicating on append ```tsx setItems((prev) => { const seen = new Set(prev.map((item) => item.id)); return [...prev, ...page.filter((item) => !seen.has(item.id))]; }); ``` Inside the updater, so the comparison is against the *current* list rather than the one captured when the request went out. Two duplicate React keys is a console warning and a rendering bug; this is three lines of insurance. ## 4. The sentinel ```tsx const [sentinel, setSentinel] = useState(null); useEffect(() => { if (!sentinel || !hasMore) return; const observer = new IntersectionObserver( ([entry]) => { if (entry.isIntersecting) onReachEnd(); }, { rootMargin: "200px" }, ); observer.observe(sentinel); return () => observer.disconnect(); }, [sentinel, hasMore, onReachEnd]); // ...
``` Four decisions in there: - **A callback ref in state**, not `useRef`. `ref.current` is `null` during the effect of the first render if the node is conditionally rendered; a state setter as the ref re-runs the effect when the node actually arrives. - **`rootMargin`** starts the load before the sentinel is visible, so the content is there by the time the user gets to it. - **`hasMore` in the deps** means the observer is torn down when there is nothing left, rather than firing into a no-op forever. - **`disconnect` in cleanup**, or you accumulate observers. And the re-entry guard, which belongs in the handler rather than in the JSX: ```tsx const onReachEnd = useCallback(() => { if (loadingRef.current || !hasMoreRef.current) return; loadingRef.current = true; void loadNextPage().finally(() => { loadingRef.current = false; }); }, []); ``` A `disabled` attribute does not help: the observer does not consult the DOM. ## 5. Fixed-height windowing ```tsx const ROW = 40; const OVERSCAN = 3; const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW) - OVERSCAN); const visible = Math.ceil(height / ROW) + OVERSCAN * 2; const end = Math.min(items.length, start + visible);
setScrollTop(e.currentTarget.scrollTop)} style={{ height, overflowY: "auto" }}>
{items.slice(start, end).map((item) => (
{item.label}
))}
``` Three details that are load-bearing. The **spacer** (`items.length * ROW`) is what makes the scrollbar honest — without it the browser thinks there are twenty rows. **`transform`** rather than `top`, because transforms are composited and do not trigger layout. And **overscan** prevents blank space during fast scrolling, which is a correctness issue rather than a nicety. Browsers have a maximum element height (around 33 million pixels in Chrome, lower in Firefox). At 40px per row that is roughly 800,000 rows before the spacer approach breaks and you need a scaled-offset scheme. ## 6. Variable heights ```tsx const measured = useRef(new Map()); const offsets = useMemo(() => { const out = [0]; for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) out.push(out[i] + (measured.current.get(i) ?? estimate)); return out; }, [count, version, estimate]); const start = binarySearch(offsets, scrollTop); ``` Estimate, render, measure, correct. The measurement happens in a `ResizeObserver` on each rendered row; when a measured height differs from what the prefix-sum assumed, bump `version` and the offsets rebuild. The unavoidable artefact: correcting a row's height changes the offsets of everything below it, so the scrollbar's meaning shifts slightly as the user scrolls into unmeasured territory. Good estimates minimise it; nothing eliminates it. ## 7. Anchoring and restoration Prepending content moves everything down. The manual fix: ```tsx useLayoutEffect(() => { const el = viewport.current; if (!el || prependedCount === 0) return; const delta = el.scrollHeight - previousHeight.current; el.scrollTop += delta; }, [prependedCount]); ``` `useLayoutEffect`, so the correction happens before paint and the user sees nothing move. Browsers do this automatically via CSS scroll anchoring (`overflow-anchor`), which virtualization defeats because the anchor element gets unmounted. Restoration on back-navigation is the same idea with the number stored somewhere that survives the unmount — `sessionStorage`, a router's state, or a module-level `Map` keyed by list id. ## 8. Keyboard navigation ```tsx // Roving tabindex: exactly one row is tabbable.
{visible.map((item, i) => (
{item.label}
))}
``` The hard part is that the target of an arrow key may not be rendered. The sequence has to be: update the index, scroll it into the window, wait for the render, *then* focus. A layout effect keyed on the index does the last two. `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` are how a screen reader knows "item 400 of 50,000" when the DOM contains twenty items. ## Common mistakes, ranked 1. Offset pagination on a dataset with concurrent inserts. 2. A sentinel with no re-entry guard, loading everything at once. 3. `useRef` for the sentinel node, so the observer never attaches. 4. No spacer, so the scrollbar reflects the window rather than the data. 5. `top` instead of `transform` for the window offset. 6. No overscan, so fast scrolling shows blank rows. 7. `tabIndex={0}` on every row in a 50,000-row list. 8. Restoring scroll in `useEffect` rather than `useLayoutEffect`. 9. No dedupe on append. 10. Infinite scroll with no `Load more` button — unusable by keyboard. ## The interview answer *"How would you render a list of 50,000 rows?"* First ask which problem is actually being solved, because there are two. If fetching 50,000 rows is the problem, that is pagination or cursor-based infinite loading, and I would use cursors rather than offsets because offset pagination duplicates and skips rows whenever anything is inserted concurrently, and because the database discards every skipped row on every request. If *rendering* is the problem, that is virtualization: keep a scroll container whose inner spacer is the full height so the scrollbar is honest, compute the visible index range from `scrollTop` and the row height, render that slice plus a few rows of overscan, and translate it into place with a transform. For variable heights you need a measurement cache and a prefix-sum of offsets, with a `ResizeObserver` correcting the estimates. Then name what it costs: find-in-page stops working, native scroll anchoring stops working, and keyboard focus can land on a row that then unmounts — which is why roving tabindex plus `aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset` is not optional. In practice a feed is infinite loading plus virtualization, and a table is pagination plus virtualization within the page. ## Check yourself 1. Give the exact sequence in which offset pagination shows a row twice. 2. Why does a cursor need a unique sort key? 3. What does `OFFSET 100000` cost the database? 4. Why does an `IntersectionObserver` sentinel fire repeatedly, and what stops it? 5. Why a callback ref rather than `useRef` for the sentinel? 6. What is the spacer element for? 7. Why `transform` rather than `top`? 8. What does overscan prevent, and how much is enough? 9. What is the browser's maximum element height, roughly, and when does it matter? 10. Describe estimate-measure-correct for variable heights, and its artefact. 11. Why `useLayoutEffect` for scroll restoration? 12. Name three things virtualization breaks. 13. What do `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` communicate? 14. Why is a `Load more` button required even when the observer works?

# Long reading — the list that does not fit

## The DOM is the bottleneck, and why

A DOM node is not free. Each element carries a layout box, computed styles,
event-listener bookkeeping, and a slot in the accessibility tree. Rendering
10,000 rows of five elements each means 50,000 nodes, and the cost shows up in
four separate places: the initial parse and construction; every subsequent
layout pass, which must walk the tree; every style recalculation, which must
match selectors against every node; and memory, which on a low-end mobile
device is the constraint that actually bites.

The number where this starts to matter is lower than people expect. A few
thousand simple rows is usually fine on a desktop. The same list on a
mid-range Android phone from three years ago will take several hundred
milliseconds to lay out and will jank on every scroll. And "simple" is doing a
lot of work in that sentence — a row with a flexbox layout, an avatar, a
tooltip wrapper and a menu button is fifteen nodes, not five.

React's own overhead compounds it: 10,000 rows is 10,000 fibers to
reconcile on every update, even when nothing changed, unless the rows are
memoised and their props are referentially stable — which is the connection back
to the structural-sharing sector.

## Why offset pagination is still everywhere

Cursor pagination is better and offset pagination is what most applications
ship, for reasons worth understanding rather than dismissing.

Offset is trivially implementable on any data source. It gives you a total count
and therefore a page count, which the design almost always asks for. It lets a
user jump to page 40. And its instability only manifests on datasets with
concurrent writes at a rate that matters — a settings list of 200 items will
never exhibit the bug.

Cursor pagination gives up random access. You cannot show "page 3 of 40", you
cannot let the user jump, and going backwards requires a second cursor in the
other direction. GraphQL's Relay connection specification, which is the most
widely-copied cursor design, addresses this with `first`/`after` and
`last`/`before` plus a `pageInfo` object, and it is notably more complicated
than `?page=3`.

The pragmatic position: use offsets for small, mostly-static datasets where the
UI needs page numbers, and cursors for feeds, activity streams, logs, and
anything where new rows arrive at the top. If you must have both, cursor for
the "next page" flow and a separate count query for the display.

## Infinite scroll, and the case against it

Infinite scroll is the default for feeds and it has a well-documented set of
harms that are worth being able to argue about, because you will be asked to
implement it and sometimes the right answer is not to.

It destroys the footer. Anything below the list — contact details, legal links,
site navigation — becomes unreachable, because the list grows faster than the
user scrolls. Sites that need a footer end up putting it in a sidebar, which is
a design compromise forced by an implementation choice.

It breaks position memory. The user scrolls for two minutes, clicks a result,
presses back, and lands at the top of an empty list. Fixing this properly means
persisting both the loaded pages and the scroll offset, and restoring both
before paint — which is the exercise in this sector — and most implementations
do not.

It removes the sense of progress. A paginated list tells the user there are
four pages; an infinite list tells them nothing, which is comfortable for
consumption and hostile for search. Users looking *for* something rather than
browsing consistently prefer pagination in usability studies.

And it is the accessibility failure case: without a real button the feature does
not exist for keyboard users, and without announcements a screen reader user
has no way to know that content appeared.

The hybrid that avoids most of this is "load more" — a button, clicked
explicitly, with the observer as an optional enhancement for a few automatic
loads before it stops. That is what this sector's exercise builds.

## Virtualization, honestly

The technique is straightforward: render a window, size a spacer so the
scrollbar tells the truth, and translate the window as the user scrolls. What
is not straightforward is everything it breaks.

**Find-in-page.** Ctrl+F searches the DOM. Rows that are not rendered are not
findable. There is no workaround short of implementing your own search UI,
which most virtualized tables do — and which is a worse experience than the
browser's.

**Native scroll anchoring.** Browsers keep the visible content stable when
things change above it by anchoring to a visible element. Virtualization
unmounts that element continuously, so the feature stops working and you
implement it by hand.

**Printing and "save as PDF".** The page prints the window.

**Ctrl+A / select-all and copy.** The user copies twenty rows out of fifty
thousand and does not necessarily notice.

**SEO and no-JS.** The content is not in the initial HTML.

**Accessibility**, which is the deepest one. A `role="listbox"` whose DOM
contains 20 of 50,000 options is lying unless every option carries
`aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset`. Focus can land on a row that then unmounts.
Screen reader virtual cursors, which navigate the DOM independently of focus,
cannot reach unrendered content at all — so a screen reader user cannot browse
the list the way they browse any other list, and there is no complete fix.

None of this means do not virtualize. It means virtualize when the list is
genuinely large, not because it seems more advanced, and know what you are
signing up for.

There is also a much cheaper option that people forget. CSS
`content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size` tells the browser to
skip rendering work for off-screen elements while keeping them in the DOM. It
is one CSS declaration, it preserves find-in-page and accessibility, and it
gets a large fraction of the benefit for lists in the low thousands. It does
not scale to 50,000 rows, because the nodes still exist — but for the very
common case of "a few thousand rows and it feels sluggish", it should be the
first thing you try.

## The measurement problem, in depth

Fixed-height virtualization is arithmetic and is always correct. Variable-height
virtualization is a feedback loop and is always approximately correct.

The loop: to know which rows are visible you need the offsets; to know the
offsets you need the heights; to know the heights you must render the rows. So
you estimate, render, measure, and correct — and the correction changes the
offsets, which changes which rows are visible.

The artefacts this produces are real and users notice them. The scrollbar thumb
changes size as you scroll into unmeasured territory, because the estimated
total height is being revised. Scrolling to a position and back does not
necessarily return you to the same place, because the offsets changed in
between. And a fast scroll into unmeasured territory can overshoot and
correct visibly.

Mitigations, in order of effectiveness: make the estimate good (measure a
sample and use the median, or have the server tell you); cache measurements
across sessions when the content is stable; and measure eagerly during scroll
rather than after, using a `ResizeObserver` rather than a post-paint effect.

The reason libraries exist for this — TanStack Virtual, react-virtuoso —is that
the correction logic has a long tail of edge cases: dynamic content that
changes height after measurement, images that load and reflow, rows removed
from the middle, and browsers that report subpixel heights inconsistently.
Writing it once teaches you what the library is doing; shipping your own is a
decision that should be deliberate.

## When to do none of this

The best fix for a list that is too long is often not to have a list that is
too long. Search and filtering reduce 50,000 rows to 12. Grouping with
collapsed sections reduces the rendered count without hiding anything.
Aggregation answers the question the list was being scrolled to answer.

A useful diagnostic question: *why is the user scrolling?* If they are looking
for something, give them search. If they are scanning for anomalies, give them
sorting and highlighting. If they are genuinely consuming everything in order —
a feed, a log, a chat history — then the list is the right shape and this
sector's techniques apply. In a surprising number of cases the answer is the
first two, and the virtualization work never needed to happen.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The sliding-window rule is what separates this from a three-line
implementation. Compute an ideal start of `current - span`, then push it back
inside the bounds *without changing the length*:

```tsx
const size = Math.min(span * 2 + 1, totalPages);
let start = Math.min(Math.max(1, current - span), totalPages - size + 1);
```

The second clamp is the one people miss — it is what makes the window slide at
the right-hand edge rather than run off the end.

## Hint 2

`Math.ceil(total / pageSize)` is the page count, and `total === 0` is the case
that breaks the naive version: `Math.ceil(0 / 10)` is `0`, which is correct, but
every downstream calculation then has to cope with zero pages. Handle the empty
case first and return early.

## Hint 3

The range display has two off-by-ones waiting. `from` is `(page - 1) * pageSize
+ 1`, which is one-based. `to` is `Math.min(page * pageSize, total)`, and the
`min` is what stops the last page claiming more items than exist. Both are
worth writing as named constants rather than inline, because they will be read
by somebody checking a bug report against them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice why offset pagination is worth building despite being the inferior
strategy. It gives you a total, a page count, and random access — three things
cursors cannot provide — and its weakness only appears on data with concurrent
writes. For a settings list of 200 rows it is exactly right, and reaching for
cursors there is complexity with no payoff.

## Hint 2

`aria-current="page"` is doing real work and is not decoration. Without it, a
screen reader user tabbing through ten identical-sounding buttons has no way to
know which page they are on — the visual highlight conveys nothing. It is one
attribute and it is the difference between a usable and an unusable pager.

## Hint 3

Think about what a disabled `Previous` button costs, given the previous
sector's argument against disabled controls. Here it is defensible, and it is
worth knowing why: the reason for disablement is obvious from context (you are
on page one), it needs no explanation, and the alternative — a button that does
nothing — is worse. The rule is about buttons whose disablement encodes a
*hidden* condition, not about the ends of a range.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The duplicate is not a bug in your code — it is a property of paginating live
data. A cursor says "give me twenty after this position"; if a row is updated
in a way that moves it, or inserted at that boundary, it can legitimately
appear in two consecutive pages. Dedupe is insurance you always want, not a
workaround for a specific server bug.

## Hint 2

Comparing against the current list means doing it inside the updater:

```tsx
setRows((prev) => {
  const seen = new Set(prev.map((row) => row.id));
  const fresh = page.rows.filter((row) => !seen.has(row.id));
  dropped.current += page.rows.length - fresh.length;
  return [...prev, ...fresh];
});
```

A `Set` built outside the updater captures the list as it was when the request
went out, which is exactly the stale comparison the gate's out-of-order test
catches.

## Hint 3

`duplicatesDropped` is counted in a ref but must be *rendered*, which is a
conflict. Two honest resolutions: keep the count in state and set it alongside
the rows, or keep both rows and count in one state object. The second is
tidier and avoids two updates describing one event — the same reasoning as the
base-plus-layer state in the optimistic-updates sector.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Know why the cursor needs a unique sort key, because it is the same class of
bug one level down. `ORDER BY created_at` cannot distinguish two rows with
identical timestamps, so "everything after this timestamp" either skips the
other rows sharing it or repeats them. `ORDER BY created_at, id` makes the
ordering total and the cursor unambiguous. Any API that hands you an opaque
cursor is encoding exactly that tuple.

## Hint 2

Compare the failure modes of the two pagination styles when the data changes
underneath you. Offset: a row inserted above shifts everything, so a later page
repeats a row and a deletion skips one — and you cannot detect either from the
client. Cursor: the boundary is stable, so only a row that *moves across the
cursor* can duplicate — rarer, and the dedupe catches it. Neither is
duplicate-free; one is much closer.

## Hint 3

Watch the interaction between `reset` and an in-flight request. If `reset`
clears the list but does not abort, the outstanding page appends onto the
freshly-emptied list and the user sees page three of the old query as the first
page of the new one. Abort *and* bump a generation counter — the abort stops the
work, the generation stops any answer that slips through.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a sentinel with a correct lifecycle

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Export a hook.

```tsx
export function useReachEnd({
  onReachEnd,
  enabled,
  rootMargin,
}: {
  onReachEnd: () => void;
  enabled: boolean;
  rootMargin?: string;
}): (node: HTMLElement | null) => void;
```

It returns a **callback ref** to attach to a sentinel element.

- When the sentinel intersects the viewport and `enabled` is true, call
  `onReachEnd` once.
- The observer must be created with `rootMargin` (default `"200px"`) so the
  load starts before the sentinel is on screen.
- When `enabled` is false — no more pages, or a request in flight — the observer
  must be **disconnected**, not merely ignored.
- Attaching to a new node re-observes it; attaching `null` disconnects.
- The observer is disconnected on unmount.
- **Re-entry**: if the sentinel is still intersecting after `enabled` flips back
  to true, it may fire again — that is correct, and the caller's guard handles
  it. But a single continuous intersection must not produce two calls.

The gate uses a fake `IntersectionObserver` it controls. It asserts: no
observer while the ref is null; exactly one call per intersection transition;
disconnection when `enabled` goes false; a fresh observation when the node
changes identity; and no observers left after unmount.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb07_large_lists ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`IntersectionObserver` fires once immediately when it starts observing, with the
element's current state. That surprises people and it is usually what you want:
if the sentinel is already visible — because the first page did not fill the
viewport — you *should* load the next one. The bug is not the initial fire; it
is the absence of a guard, which turns "load the next page" into "load every
page as fast as the network allows".

## Hint 2

`rootMargin` is the single highest-value tuning knob here and it is worth
understanding as a design decision rather than a number. `"200px"` means "start
loading when the sentinel is 200 pixels below the fold", which buys you roughly
one scroll-flick of latency. Too small and the user hits a spinner every time;
too large and you fetch pages nobody looks at. Scale it with the row height and
the typical scroll speed, not with taste.

## Hint 3

Consider what a `threshold` option would add and why it is usually unnecessary
here. `threshold` controls what fraction of the element must be visible to
count as intersecting; for a zero-height sentinel it is meaningless. If your
sentinel is a real row rather than an empty div, a threshold of `0.5` gives you
"half of the last row is visible", which is a more natural trigger — and a good
reason to make the sentinel the last item rather than an empty div after it.

## Exercise 4 — infinite scroll that works without a mouse

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. Export one component.

```tsx
export function Feed({
  rows,
  hasMore,
  isLoading,
  onLoadMore,
}: {
  rows: { id: string; label: string }[];
  hasMore: boolean;
  isLoading: boolean;
  onLoadMore: () => void;
}): JSX.Element;
```

Required:

- `<ul>` of `<li>`s, each carrying `aria-posinset={index + 1}` and
  `aria-setsize={-1}` — the list's true size is unknown, and `-1` is the
  standard way to say so.
- A **real `Load more` button** after the list whenever `hasMore` is true. It
  is the mechanism; the observer is an enhancement. The gate removes
  `IntersectionObserver` from the environment entirely and asserts the button
  still loads.
- The button carries the sentinel ref from `../ex3/solution`, so it doubles as
  the trigger element — one node, one purpose, nothing invisible.
- **Automatic loading stops after three consecutive automatic loads.** After
  that the user must click. The gate scrolls repeatedly and asserts exactly
  three automatic loads before it goes manual. A click resets the counter.
- `<div aria-live="polite">` rendered unconditionally, whose text becomes
  `Showing {n} items` after each load and is empty before the first.
- While `isLoading`, the button reads `Loading` and is **not** disabled — see
  the previous sector.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb07_large_lists ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Putting the sentinel ref on the button itself is the design decision that makes
this accessible. There is no invisible trigger div, so there is nothing that
exists for the mouse and not for the keyboard: the same element is what the
observer watches and what a keyboard user activates. The observer becomes a
convenience layered on a working control.

## Hint 2

The three-load limit is a real pattern, not an exercise contrivance. It bounds
the DOM growth, it preserves the footer's reachability, and it gives the user a
moment to decide whether they want more. Track it with a counter that
increments on automatic loads and resets on a click:

```tsx
const autoLoads = useRef(0);
const canAuto = hasMore && !isLoading && autoLoads.current < 3;
```

`canAuto` becomes the `enabled` flag for the sentinel hook.

## Hint 3

`aria-setsize={-1}` is the specified way to say "the total is unknown", and it
matters here because it is *true*: with cursor pagination you genuinely do not
know how many rows exist. Passing a wrong number is worse than passing `-1`,
because a screen reader will announce "3 of 20" for a list that turns out to
have two thousand.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take the accessibility argument seriously rather than as a checkbox. An infinite
list with a scroll-only trigger does not exist for a keyboard user: they tab to
the last row and there is nothing after it, no matter how far the page could
have scrolled. That is not a degraded experience, it is a missing feature, and
it is the single most common way this pattern ships broken.

## Hint 2

The live region has a specific job that is easy to get wrong. Announcing every
row that arrives would be unusable. Announcing the *count* after each load —
"Showing 60 items" — tells the user something happened and how much, in one
short utterance, at the moment they can act on it. Polite, so it waits for a
pause; unconditionally rendered, so the region exists before its content
changes.

## Hint 3

Be able to argue about infinite scroll itself. It removes the footer, breaks
position memory on back-navigation, and takes away any sense of progress —
which is comfortable for browsing and hostile for searching. Usability research
is consistent that users looking *for* something prefer pagination. "Load more"
with a bounded number of automatic loads, which is what this exercise builds, is
the compromise that keeps most of the convenience without the harms.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three elements, three jobs, and mixing them up is the usual failure. The
**viewport** is the scroll container and has the fixed height. The **spacer**
has the full content height and exists purely so the browser's scrollbar
reflects the data rather than the window. The **translated wrapper** holds the
rendered rows and is moved into position. Remove the spacer and the scrollbar
thinks there are seventeen rows.

## Hint 2

`transform: translateY(...)` rather than `top` is a performance decision with a
concrete mechanism: `top` triggers layout, which walks the tree; `transform` is
handled by the compositor and skips layout and paint entirely. On a list that
updates on every scroll event, that is the difference between smooth and janky.

## Hint 3

The bottom edge is where off-by-ones live. `end` must clamp to `count`, or
`items.slice(start, end)` silently returns fewer rows and the last screen shows
blank space below the final row. Test it by scrolling to `spacerHeight -
viewportHeight` exactly, which is the maximum `scrollTop` the browser will
report.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Overscan is a correctness measure, not an optimisation, and understanding why
tells you how to size it. Scroll events are dispatched *after* the browser has
already scrolled and painted — so between the paint and your re-render, the user
is looking at rows you have not rendered. Overscan means those rows already
exist. Two to five is usually enough; on a fast-flicking mobile list, more.

## Hint 2

Know the ceiling. Browsers cap element height — around 33.5 million pixels in
Chrome, and lower in Firefox. At 40px per row that is roughly 800,000 rows
before the spacer stops growing and the scrollbar starts lying again. Beyond
that you need a scaled scheme where the spacer represents the content at a
compressed ratio and you translate scroll positions between the two spaces.
Knowing the limit exists is more important than implementing it.

## Hint 3

Say what this costs before somebody discovers it. Ctrl+F finds nothing outside
the window. Select-all copies seventeen rows. Print produces one screen. Native
scroll anchoring stops working, because the anchor element keeps unmounting. And
a screen reader's virtual cursor — which walks the DOM independently of focus —
cannot reach unrendered rows at all. These are not bugs to fix; they are the
price, and the decision to pay it should be deliberate.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The loop you are implementing is estimate → render → measure → correct, and it
is genuinely circular: to know which rows are visible you need the offsets, to
know the offsets you need the heights, to know the heights you must render the
rows. Accepting that it converges rather than being immediately correct is the
conceptual step.

## Hint 2

The prefix sum makes both lookups cheap:

```tsx
// offsets[i] is the top of row i; offsets[count] is the total height.
private offsets: number[];

offsetOf(i) { return this.offsets[i]; }
totalHeight() { return this.offsets[this.offsets.length - 1]; }
```

`measure` recomputes only from the changed index forward — everything above it
is unaffected, which is what keeps the correction O(n - i) rather than O(n) from
zero.

## Hint 3

The no-loop rule is what `measure` returning a boolean is for. `ResizeObserver`
fires on every layout of the observed element, including ones your own
correction caused. If `measure` returns `false` for an unchanged height and the
component only re-renders when it returns `true`, the loop terminates. Without
that check you get an infinite render cycle that is very hard to diagnose.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be honest about the artefacts, because users notice them and you will be asked.
The scrollbar thumb changes size as you scroll into unmeasured territory,
because the estimated total is being revised. Scrolling somewhere and back does
not necessarily land in the same place, because the offsets changed underneath.
And a fast scroll into unmeasured rows can overshoot and visibly correct. Good
estimates minimise all three; nothing eliminates them.

## Hint 2

`ResizeObserver` rather than a post-paint `useEffect` measurement is a real
difference. An effect measures after the browser has painted, so the wrong
height is visible for a frame and every scroll produces a small jump. A
`ResizeObserver` callback runs in the same frame, before paint in modern
browsers, so the correction is invisible. It also catches heights that change
*after* mount — an image loading, a font swapping — which an effect on mount
never sees.

## Hint 3

This is where the argument for a library is strongest, and it is worth being
able to make it. The long tail here includes: content that changes height after
measurement, images that load and reflow, rows removed from the middle
invalidating cached indices, subpixel height reporting that differs between
browsers, and the interaction with sticky headers. TanStack Virtual and
react-virtuoso have absorbed years of those. Write it once to understand it;
ship your own only when you have a reason.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The mechanism is arithmetic on one number. Prepending content increases
`scrollHeight` by exactly the height of what was added; adding that same
difference to `scrollTop` leaves the visible content where it was. You need the
"before" value, which means recording it during render or in a ref that the
layout effect can compare against.

## Hint 2

`useLayoutEffect` is the whole difference between the two failure modes:

| hook | what the user sees |
| --- | --- |
| `useEffect` | the browser paints the new scroll position, then you correct it — a visible jump |
| `useLayoutEffect` | you correct before paint — nothing moves |

The rule generalises: any DOM measurement or correction whose result must not
be visible mid-flight belongs in `useLayoutEffect`.

## Hint 3

Browsers do this automatically via CSS scroll anchoring
(`overflow-anchor: auto`, the default), which is why most people never learn
the technique. It stops working the moment you virtualize, because the anchor
element is unmounted as it leaves the window. Knowing that the browser feature
exists — and exactly why virtualization defeats it — is the interesting half of
this exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider what "restore the scroll position" actually requires, because it is
more than a number. The rows have to exist before the position is meaningful:
setting `scrollTop = 4000` on a container that currently holds ten rows clamps
to its maximum and silently loses the position. So restoration is really two
things — restore the *data* (which pages were loaded) and then the offset — and
implementations that only do the second work in development and fail with a
real fetch.

## Hint 2

The module-level `Map` in this exercise is deliberately crude and worth
critiquing. It never evicts, so a long session accumulates an entry per list
ever visited; it does not survive a page reload; and it is keyed by a string
the caller supplies, which two components could collide on. `sessionStorage`
survives reloads, a router's location state survives navigation properly, and
either needs a cleanup story. The crude version is fine for a demo and should
be labelled as such.

## Hint 3

Think about where the "before" measurement comes from, since there is no
`useBeforeLayoutEffect`. Two respectable answers: read `scrollHeight` during
render into a ref (a read, not a write, so it does not violate purity in
practice though it does read the DOM during render), or record it in the
handler that triggers the prepend, which is where you know it is about to
happen. The second is cleaner and only works when there is a single trigger.
