## Exercise 8 — the keyboard, over a window

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Export one component.

```tsx
export function VirtualListbox({
  items,
  rowHeight,
  height,
  onActivate,
}: {
  items: { id: string; label: string }[];
  rowHeight: number;
  height: number;
  onActivate: (id: string) => void;
}): JSX.Element;
```

Windowing as in ex5, plus a working keyboard:

- The container is `role="listbox"`; rendered rows are `role="option"` with
  `aria-selected`, `aria-posinset={index + 1}` and
  `aria-setsize={items.length}` — a screen reader must be able to say
  "item 4,200 of 50,000" from a DOM containing seventeen.
- **Roving tabindex**: exactly one row has `tabIndex={0}` — the active one — and
  every other has `-1`. The gate asserts the container has exactly one tabbable
  descendant with 50,000 items.
- `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp` move the active index by one, `Home`/`End` to the ends,
  `PageDown`/`PageUp` by a viewport's worth. All clamp.
- **When the active index moves outside the rendered window, the list must
  scroll it into view *before* focusing it.** The gate presses `End` from index
  0 and asserts the last row is focused, not that focus was lost to `<body>`.
- `Enter` and `Space` call `onActivate` with the active id and prevent the
  default scroll.
- If the active row is unmounted by scrolling, focus must return to it when it
  comes back — the gate scrolls away with the mouse, then presses `ArrowDown`,
  and asserts focus lands on the correct row.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb07_large_lists ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The ordering is the exercise and it must be: update the index → set
`scrollTop` so the row is inside the window → let React render → focus. Try to
focus first and the element does not exist. Three of those four steps happen
synchronously; the fourth needs a layout effect keyed on the active index.

## Hint 2

Scrolling the index into view is arithmetic, not `scrollIntoView`:

```tsx
const top = index * rowHeight;
const bottom = top + rowHeight;
if (top < scrollTop) next = top;
else if (bottom > scrollTop + height) next = bottom - height;
```

`scrollIntoView` needs the element, which is the thing you do not have yet.

## Hint 3

Roving tabindex is the standard answer to "a composite widget with many
children". One element in the tab order, arrow keys to move within, so a user
tabs *past* the whole listbox in one keystroke rather than through 50,000 rows.
Every APG composite pattern — listbox, grid, toolbar, tree — uses it, and
`tabIndex={0}` on every row is the mistake it exists to prevent.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the hardest problem in virtualization and it is worth understanding why
it has no complete solution. Focus lives on a DOM node. Virtualization removes
DOM nodes. So focus can be destroyed by a scroll the user initiated with the
mouse or the scrollbar, entirely outside your keyboard handler. You can restore
it when the row returns, which is what this exercise does — but between the
unmount and the return, focus is on `<body>` and there is nothing to be done
about it.

## Hint 2

`aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` are the mechanism that makes a windowed list
truthful. Without them a screen reader inspects the DOM, finds seventeen
options, and announces "item 3 of 17" for row 4,200 of 50,000. With them the
announcement is correct. They are two attributes and they are the difference
between a lie and the truth.

## Hint 3

There remains a failure this cannot fix, and being able to name it is the
honest end of the argument. A screen reader's *virtual cursor* navigates the
DOM independently of focus — it is how a user reads a page without tabbing — and
it cannot reach rows that are not rendered. So a screen-reader user cannot
browse a virtualized list the way they browse any other list, no matter how
correct your ARIA is. For genuinely large lists the accessible answer is often
search and filtering rather than virtualization.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a virtualized infinite list with sticky headers

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. Combine the sector.

```tsx
export type Section = { id: string; title: string; rows: { id: string; label: string }[] };

export function SectionedFeed({
  sections,
  hasMore,
  isLoading,
  onLoadMore,
  rowHeight,
  headerHeight,
  height,
}: {
  sections: Section[];
  hasMore: boolean;
  isLoading: boolean;
  onLoadMore: () => void;
  rowHeight: number;
  headerHeight: number;
  height: number;
}): JSX.Element;
```

All of this at once:

1. **Flatten** the sections into a single indexed list of items, each either a
   header (height `headerHeight`) or a row (height `rowHeight`). Offsets are a
   prefix sum, so a mixed list of 100,000 entries is still O(log n) to look up.
2. **Window** it: spacer sized to the total, a translated wrapper, overscan of
   3.
3. **Sticky header**: the header of the section containing the top of the
   viewport is rendered *additionally*, pinned at the top with
   `position: "sticky"` semantics — the gate reads
   `<div data-testid="sticky">` and asserts it holds the correct title as it
   scrolls through sections.
4. **Infinite loading**: when the window's `end` is within 10 items of the
   flattened length and `hasMore` and not `isLoading`, call `onLoadMore` — at
   most once per window position. A `Load more` button is rendered after the
   list as the keyboard-accessible mechanism.
5. **Jump to index**: an exported ref handle
   `{ scrollToIndex(index: number): void }` via `useImperativeHandle`, setting
   `scrollTop` to the item's offset.
6. **Anchoring**: appending sections must not move the visible content.
7. `aria-setsize={-1}` on rows while `hasMore`, and the real total when not.

The gate scrolls through 2,000 rows in 40 sections, checks the sticky title at
five positions, asserts the load trigger fired the right number of times, and
uses `scrollToIndex` to jump to item 1,500.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb07_large_lists challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Flattening first makes everything else ordinary. Build one array of
`{ kind: "header" | "row", sectionIndex, item }` with a parallel prefix-sum of
offsets, and the windowing code from ex5 works unchanged — it does not care
that the heights differ, only that `offsetOf` and `indexAt` exist. Do that
before anything else and the sticky header becomes a lookup rather than a
special case.

## Hint 2

The sticky header is `indexAt(scrollTop)` followed by "walk back to the nearest
header":

```tsx
const topIndex = indexAt(scrollTop);
const section = flat[topIndex].sectionIndex;
const title = sections[section].title;
```

Which is O(1) if each flattened entry carries its section index — which is why
the flattening step should store it rather than recomputing it.

## Hint 3

Requirement 4's "at most once per window position" is the re-entry guard again,
in a new costume. The window's `end` changes on every scroll event, so a naive
check fires continuously while the user sits near the bottom. Guard on
`isLoading` *and* remember the length at which you last triggered:

```tsx
if (lastTriggeredLength.current === flat.length) return;
lastTriggeredLength.current = flat.length;
onLoadMore();
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice the order the requirements should be built in, because two of them
constrain everything else. Flattening (1) and windowing (2) are the
foundation — get those right and requirements 3, 4, 5 and 7 are each about ten
lines on top. Requirement 6 is the one that touches the others, because
anchoring interacts with the scroll position that windowing reads. Build it
last and test it separately.

## Hint 2

Real sticky headers via CSS `position: sticky` do not work inside a virtualized
list, and understanding why is the point of doing it manually. `sticky` pins an
element within its scrolling ancestor as long as the element is in the DOM —
and virtualization removes the header the moment it scrolls out of the window,
so it un-sticks. Rendering the current section's header *separately*, outside
the translated wrapper, is the standard workaround.

## Hint 3

Requirement 5's imperative handle is worth thinking about as an API decision.
`scrollToIndex` is imperative because scrolling is an *action*, not a state:
"the list is scrolled to item 1500" is not a thing the parent should own,
because the user can scroll away from it immediately. Modelling it as a prop
would create exactly the controlled-input problem from the forms sector — React
would keep re-asserting a position the user is fighting.

exercises.prompt:
## Review — the list that stutters

`review1/solution.tsx`. A 3,000-row list that renders correctly and scrolls
badly. Four distinct causes, all visible in a render count.

```tsx
export function OrdersTable({
  orders,
  onSelect,
  renderCounts,
}: {
  orders: Order[];
  onSelect: (id: string) => void;
  renderCounts: { table: { current: number }; row: { current: number } };
}): JSX.Element;
```

The stub has all four defects. Fix each:

1. **Rows are not memoised.** Every parent render re-renders 3,000 rows. Wrap
   the row in `React.memo`.
2. **An inline arrow prop defeats the memo.** `onClick={() => onSelect(o.id)}`
   is a new function every render, so `memo` never skips. Pass the stable
   `onSelect` and the `id`, and let the row build its own handler — or use
   event delegation on the container.
3. **A new object prop per render.** `style={{ padding: 8 }}` is a fresh object
   every time. Hoist it to a module constant.
4. **Derived data recomputed and re-identified.** The stub sorts inside the
   render body, producing a new array every render even when `orders` has not
   changed, which re-renders every row via the array identity. Memoise it —
   and copy before sorting, because `sort` mutates.

The gate renders, asserts a baseline row-render count, then triggers **ten
unrelated parent re-renders** (a state change that does not touch `orders`)
and asserts:

- `renderCounts.table.current` increased by 10 — the parent must still render;
- `renderCounts.row.current` increased by **0** — no row re-rendered.

It then changes one order's status and asserts exactly **one** row re-rendered.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rb07_large_lists review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Fix them in order and re-run after each, because they mask one another.
`React.memo` alone changes nothing while the inline arrow is there — memo
compares props, and a new function fails the comparison every time. That is why
"I added memo and it did not help" is such a common report: the memo was
working, the props were lying.

## Hint 2

Event delegation is the alternative to a stable per-row handler and it scales
better:

```tsx
<tbody onClick={(e) => {
  const id = (e.target as HTMLElement).closest("[data-id]")?.getAttribute("data-id");
  if (id) onSelect(id);
}}>
```

One listener for 3,000 rows, no per-row function identity at all. React already
delegates internally, so the win here is prop stability rather than listener
count.

## Hint 3

Defect 4 has two halves and both matter. `useMemo` stops the recomputation, and
copying with `[...orders]` before sorting stops `sort` mutating the caller's
array — which in a parent that memoised on `orders` would mean the parent never
re-renders even though its data changed. A mutation bug hiding inside a
performance fix.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Measure before you fix, always, and this exercise's `renderCounts` is the
cheapest possible instrument. A counter incremented in the component body tells
you exactly how many times something rendered, needs no tooling, and works in
tests. The React DevTools profiler gives you the same information with timings
and a flame graph; both are better than reasoning about what *should* re-render.

## Hint 2

Know when memoisation is the wrong fix, because reaching for it reflexively has
a cost. `memo` is not free — it stores the previous props and compares them on
every render — and on a component that almost always receives new props it is
pure overhead. It pays off exactly where this exercise puts it: many instances,
props that usually do not change, a parent that re-renders often. React
Compiler, where it is available, does this automatically and makes most manual
memoisation unnecessary.

## Hint 3

Consider the fix this exercise does not make: virtualization. 3,000 rows is in
the band where memoisation plus stable props is usually enough, and where CSS
`content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size` would help further for
one declaration while keeping find-in-page and accessibility intact.
Virtualization is the answer at 50,000, not at 3,000 — reaching for it first is
how a list ends up inaccessible for a problem that a `memo` would have solved.
